EFFECTS OF FALSE HAIR. —At Dieppe, in France, the following notice has been issued by the police: "The bathing police are requested., when a lady is in danger of drowning, to seize her by the dress, and not by the hair, which oftens times remains in their grasp. Newfoundland clogi will govern themselves accordingly." EVIDENCE OF BELIEF.—A correspondent of a Scotch contemporary, in referring to Lord Camp- bell's assertion that in Scotland a man can scarcely ; tell whether he is married or not, states: "'think Lon.' Campbell labours under a mistake. You will believe that I am really married ; I keep my mother in-law and her three maiden davgisters in the house." "WHEN you were last here," said the Magistrate to the prisoner, "you promised me, if I released you, you would go to work. Why haven't you kept your word ?" "Judge," returned the victim meekly, "I didn't want to insult honest working people by joining their ranks. lam such a vaga- bond, you know, that I should disgrace any calling I took up."

Lord Tennyson, whilst making a flying visit to town, lunched with Mr. Henry Irving at the Garrick Club. It is not improbable that., when Mr. Irving produces Lord Tennyson's " Becket," at the Lyceum, the title may be changed to the more . romantic title " Fair Rosamond,' by which it was originally called. It may be noted that the play was read in manuscript by Mr. Irving more than ten years ago, and was then accepted by him for representation at the Lyceum. -- 1 Garotters are having a successful winter season in Melbourne. They secured a sum of £175 by one performance on a dark night in Fitzroy-gardens. No arrest was ro2de in this or other cases of violent assault, the victims being left helpless and uncon- scious. The Melbourne Press is strongl advocat- ing the lash as punishment for such offences, but clearly arrest and conviction are the first processes to be secured. The unfrequented parts of the city are quite dangerous after nightfall, and are dreaded by all peaceful citizens.

CHARLFS, EARL STANHOPE, a very worthy man and a good chemist, concerned himself usually so little with public life, that, on his going down on one occasion in his workaday clothes to the House • of Lords, the doorkeeper refused him admission: "Honest man, you have no business here." "I am sorry," replied the gentle Earl, "that honest men have no business here." "How I pity the poor such a night as this," said Blande, as he sat in his comfortable apartment. "Then why," asked Biuff, "Don't you put on your coat and go out and see if you cannot render assistance to some of them?" "Ali," replied Blande, "then I should not be so comfortable as I am now," "and I might forgft the poor and begin to pity myself. That would be selfish you know." "WELL, pop," said Jimmy Tuff boy, "he a goin' ter the circus in the afternoon or evening?' "James," said his mother, “.1 hardly think your father intends to take you at all." "Not take me! Then the circus might as well not show." "You can go this evening my son," interjected his father. " Evening ! I was in hopes you'd take me this afternoon, 'cos Uncle Ben's promised to take me in the evening." THE funny man who seeks in the mother-in-law of English society a target for his wit would find his occupation gone in Persia. There the bride's mother takes charge of the household for a year, and instructs the young wife in the mysteries of baking asad brewing, while the son-in-law makes her his counsellor and guide. Civilisation has not introduced clubs and latch-keys into Persia, and, strange to say, the barbarians are happy without them. "You see," said a seedy-looking, broken-down gentleman, there is a point at whieh our trust in our fellow-men gives way. I reached that point last night, when, wishing to leave my hotel with- out disturbing the repose of its inmates, I quietly lowered my valise from my bedroom window, and suddenly heard the dissonant voice of the landlord crying out, All right, I've got the valise! Let go the rope " THE following conversation occurred between • two elegantly-dressed young ladies on one of the most fashionable streets of Chicago. " Were you in the Court-room when the guilty wife gave her testimoney in that divorce suit ?" "Yes, and I was so shocked, so completely prostrated by the dis- gusting revelations that I couldn't get up and leave the Court-room. I had to wait until the Court adjourned. I'm going again to-morrow." THE MILLER AND THE FOOL.—A miller, who attempted to be witty at the expense of a youth • of weak intellect, accosted him with : "John, people say you are a fool." On this John replied: " I.don't know that I am, sir. I know some things, sir, and some things I don't know, sir." "Well, John, what do you know ?" "I know that millers always have fat hogs, sir." "And what don't you know ?" "I don't know whose corn they eat, sir." A MAN going into a railroad car at Louisville, and finding all the seats occupied, exclaimed in a loud voice, "This car isn't going !" During the stampede which followed, the practical joker got a comfortable seat, and the train soon made off. In the midst of the indignation telt at him, an angry passenger came up and said, " Didn't you say this car wasn't going ?" " Yes," was the quiet answer, "and it wasn't going then, was it 2" A TEACHER having told the class in literature to write a abort essay on the idea involved in the line The pen is mightier than the sword," a boy produced the foll Owing : A goat browsing on a green sward approached a pig-pen and said to its intelligent occupant, "Why do you stay in that ungenteel place when there is such a lovely spot as this so handy? " " Because the pen is mightier than the sward," grunted the pig in reply to yie intrusive goat. "S' " exclaimed the sick woman, at last, to her son-in,a "you might at least have the decency to let" me die Ili-154466. You know very well that I auly have another month to live." " Oh," replied the unforgiving visitor "only another month you say, eh? Well, judging by what that meant when you used to come to stop with us for one, I shall find you still alive when I come back to England next Christmas !" Snz "As a crank on the subject of music. In the Munich Criminal Courtitwo scholars of the Gymnasium there Lave just been tried for placing an explosive substance in the stcve of a class-room. It appeared that at about nine o'clock in the even- ing one of them went to the stove and fired the imaterial. Much damage was done. The two boys were under the impression that the effect of the explosion would only be to bring down the soot, and that the smoke would so disfigure the objects , in the class-room that reboot work would be Impos- sible for some time. The two boxepl sentenced to a year's imprisonment each.

During Sir George Dibb's visit to this country be met the Prince of Wales several times. His Royal Highness was interested in Australia, and naturally found Sir George Dibbs able to gratify his interest. When the Duke of York went round the. world as a midshipman in the Bacchante,Sir George Dibbs was among those who welcomed him and the late Duke of Clarence at Sydney. Here Sir George had again the opportunity of meeting the Duke of York. No doubt when begets to New York at the end of this week, the American interviewers will be anxious to "pump" Sir George on his hobnobbing with the royalties.

Lord Bathurst, who aied. on Bank Holiday at his Gloucestershire seat, Cirencester House, and one of whose last wishes was that a tete to be held, in his beautiful grounds on that day should not, in the event of his death, he interfered . withrwas only in his sixtieth year. For more than twenty years the late Earl was member for Cirencester, before he succeeded his uncle in the title in 1878, and he was extremely popular in Gloucestershire. Cirencester House is a rather gloomy • looking building of the seventeenth or early eighteenth century, but. the grounds are extensive and very beautiful, well wooded, and full of quaint.nnd pipturesquesnpoks and corners. .:-w

The sixty-second meeting of the British Associa- ' tion is, according to all accounts, to be as great' a success as its predecessors have been. This will make the fourth time the.association has met in the, Scotch capital, the last three by a curious Coimiid- ence having been separated by intervals of twenty- one years. This time geologists will be in good force in anticipation of Sir Archibald Geikie's presi- nential address. Many more eminent foreign scientists are expected to attend than on former occasions, and papers have been promised by them on structural geology and petrology. Section F discussion on the subject of old ageArsions will also be specially interesting.

Sir Archibald Geikie, who must not be confounded with his brother, Professor James Geiltie, president of the Geographical Section, is too well known in geological circles to need any introduction or recom- mendation. He is, and has been for some time a member of the Geological Society and director of the Museum of Practical Geology. His associations with Sir Roderick Murchison in the working out of the true structure of the Highlands, and with the geological survey of which he was eleven years ago Director-General, have placed him in the front rank of famous scientists. He is as eloquent in his des- criptions as he is clear in his arguments. His me- moirs and works make a valuable addition to the literature of the country. - -

- - The Oxford honor lists, of which the last, that of Classical Greats, appeared on Tuesday, have not contained cuch well-known names as was the case last year. It may, however, be remarked that Vis- count St. Cyres, the grandson of the late Earl of Iddesleigh 'better known as Sir Stafford Northcote) obtained a first class in history. " Stuffy " in his day took two first and had many marks. This young viscount is a cultured and studious person- age, whose historical studies have led him to the Church of Rome. Ile spent one of his vacations at Lampeter, in Cardiganshire, and wrote an interest- ing letter on his sojourn in that Welsh district, which appeared in some of the Welsh periodicals.

"F. J. Cestr."—that is the Right Rev. Francis John Jayne, D.D., late of fieble College, Oxford, and now Bishop of Chester—who writes a long letter to the "Times," advocating a reconstruction of the "public- house system "on lines that shall "invest" tempe- rance drinks "with prestige" at the same time that alcoholic beverages are "frankly recognised," is remembered as the divine who some time ago stated before a large audience that his great ambition in life was to properly conduct a public-house. Fail- ing the example of a bishop turned licensed victual- ler, we are given, at any rate, some excellent pre- cepts of a kind that is characteristic of Bishop Jayne's well-known desire for rather heterodox ori- ginality.

Four hours a day is the average of time devoted by Miss Ellen Terry to correspondence, and she has confided to Mrs. George Augustus Sala that the numerous letters she receives include perpetual applications from would-be actresses for help and advice. Miss Terry's advice always is " Don't." "Madness." she says, "lies that way. The" market" is overcrowded ; but still they come. Why is it? Simply because it is such a delightful life ; such an attractive life. I remember," the famous actress continued, "telling one lady that it was no use to make the attempt unless she were possessed of extreme beauty (I was thinking of Mrs. Langtry) or genius. She replied that my advice only made her the more resolved, because she had both."

The Marquis of Ormonde, vice-commodore of the Royal Yacht Squadron, and virtual dictator of the club, came on to Cowes on Saturday, and was busy on Monday. Lord Ormonde is a very fine spepmen of a yachtsman, for he stands over six feet in his stockings. Be is no fair weather sailor, for besides the mimic performances in the Solent he has taken his fine yacht, the Mirage, up into the Arctic seas, along the dangerous coast of Spitzbergen. As one of the leading nobles of Ireland, he is invested with the mediteval office of Chief Butler. He is married to a daughter of the Duke of Westminster, who in good looks and sweetness of disposition strongly resembles her mother. By this marriage be is connected with the powerful families of the Dukes of Devonshire, Nortliumberland,Argyll, and Suther- land.

Richard Daft is not only a famous cricketer but a good story-teller.. Here is one of his yarns about umpires :—" This. umpire stuttered very much. Tarrant was bowling, and cried How's that?' for leg before wicket. The umpire being appealed to so sharply could not for some time speak a word, al- though it was plain to be seen he was endeavouring to give his decision; but Tarrant, who was very impatient, took up the ball, saying, 'Oh, I can't wait any longer bowled another ball which knock-

ed the batsman's middle stump down just as the umpire called out, • N-n-not out 1" Not out ?' said Tarrant, why, look at his middle stump !' It was a long time before the poor umpire was able to make Tarrant understand that the decision ref erred to his appeal for the leg-before of the previous ball." Good cricket requires smartness all round.

40 - KICKED TO D EATII. TRAGIC OCCURREI,CE A L WINWICK. An accident of a startling and tragic character, and by which a Warrington cabman lost his life, took place at Winwick early on Saturday morning. About a quarter to eleven on Friday night Mr. Thomas Dowell, who is a telegraphist living at Nantwich and employed by the London and North- Western Railway Company, arrived at Bank Quay station, Warrington. His intention was to get to the signal box at Winwick junction to take charge of the telegraphing arrangements during the pres- sure of traffic in connection with bank holiday. About twelve o'clock he engaged Patrick Flannery, a cab driver employed at the Patten Arms hotel, to take him to near Wargrave. When they had reached Winwick, on the way thither, Dowell I notice i that Flannery was taking the wrong turn and he shouted this out to him. Almost immedi- ately the cab collided with something or other, and was violently overturned. Dowell,although severely shaken, scrambled out of the window. It was now about two o'clock and very dark, but he noticed the ' horse was still on its feet but kicking violently. He cut the traces to release it. Ile did not see the driver at the time, but he was afterwards found under the cab, dead, having, evidently, been killed by tt e kicking of the horse. An inquest was held at Winwick as to the occurrence by Mr. Brighouse, coroner, on Tuesday afternoon. The first witness called was Edward O'Toole, of 2, Stoney- yard, off Bank-st., Warrington. Ile said he was a driver at the Patten Arms establishment. Patrick Flannery, the deceased, had also been a driver there, and had lodged at 38, Scotland-road. He knew Flan- nery's age in this way. On Friday morning Flannery joking about getting grey. " Why," witness said, "lam as old as you." Flannery thereupon asked him what age he was, and lie said he was 32. " Then lam older than you " Flannery answered, " for I am 38." Flannery had to his (witness's) knowledge been a driver in Warrington for three and a half years. He under- , stood horses very well and was a careful driver. They , were both at the station all day on Friday, and it was About half-past eleven when they put their horses away. He parted with Flannery about a quarter to twelve, and the latter was then sober. The cab that he afterwards was taking to Winwick Junction was a full lock cab, but the horse he took was very light of mouth, and turned sharply on the lightest touch, but the deceased knew of this characteristic of the animal. Thom ai Dowell said that he found on arriving at Bank Quay Station that ne had missed the St. Helens train. He waited about a while in the hope that he might get a lift on a bank engine. About 12 o'clock, however, he left the station,and he met Flannery before he had got to the end of Sankey-st. He asked Flannery the way through the town towards Winwick, and in fact, asked him to show him through. It was then that deceased sug- gested that a cab might be taken, and to this suggestion witness agreed. They drove on satisfactorily till Win- wick was reached, but there he noticedthat Flannery was taking the road to the right instead of to the left. 'He shouted out to him to keep to the left, and almost 'directly the cab went over. Witness scarcely re- membered how he got out, but he thought he must have scrambled through the window. He saw the horse was standing and kicking, and, failing to unbuckle the traces, he out them. Be called for the driver but I there was no answer, and afterwards he detected what looked like the shadow of a body under the cab. He , went to a cottage near at hand in which there was a tight, and knocked, but the people inside advised him to go to the public-house. He knocked at the public-houses but they said they could not assist because there were only woman in the house. Whilst lie was knocking he saw the lights of the mail cart, and he went back to the' scene of the accident. He then found that the mail driver had caught the horse. With the aid of the lamas they found Flannery's body, and the mail driver said he ' was dead, as his chest had been kicked in. Wittess then got on to the mail cart and drove to Newton for Dr. Watkins, who came back with him. The doctor said the man must have been killed at once. The doctorossisted by his driver, witness, and a young man, he believed, from the public house, released the body.—The Coroner I thought they said there were no men there.—Witness It appears there were. Witness added that he knocked at a third house below, but they declined to give any assistance, and gave no reason for it.—A juryman said that in one case the man in the house is an invalid.— The Coroner remarked that there was a landlord at that public-house. Ile added that in the present case nobody could have done anything for the deceased. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned, the verdict stating that deceased had been kicked to death by a horse.
THE NEW ST. HELENS AND LIVERPOOL
RAILWAY.

The directors' report of this railway for the half- year ended June 30, states that the whole of the works on the portion under construction have been satisfactorily proceeded with. Several bridges have been built, others are well in hand, and the works in connection with the bridges and viaducts in St.flelens will be commenced at an early day. The Go[borne em- bankment is now completed up to Wigan-lane, and a considerable length of permanent way laid down. A satisfactory settlement has been arrived at for the ac- quisition of the land in St. Helens belonging to the United Alkali Company, and the directors hope to ob- tain early possession of the remaining land required. The statement of accounts shows that the company have been authorised to raise capital on stocks and shares £550,000, and on loins £183,000 ; total £733,000. The capital created or sanctioned amounted in stock or shares to £280,000. The amount received was £130,148; calls in arrear £1,038, amount uncalled £19,256, and amount unissued £129,560. No capital has been raised by loans or debenture stock. The amount expended on lines in course of construction to 31st December, 1891, was £81,228 135. 3d., and the amount expended in the six months ending 30th June 1892, was £49,559, making a total expenditure of £130,788 3s. 10d. The details of the £49,559 expended are given :—Land purchase and compensation, £9,224 13s. 5d.; construction of way and stations, £31,317 15s. 2d. ; law and Parliamentary charges, £225 13s. sd. ; engineering expenses, £8,250 ; and general expenses, £541 Bs. 7d. The estimated fur- ther expenditure is as follows :—During the half-year to 31st December, 1892, £75,000 ; in subsequent half-years, £3,522,000 ; total £BOO,OOO. The company has capital powers and other assets available to meet further expen- diture of £602,211 16s. 21. The mileage statement shows , that nineteen miles are being or to be constructed be- tween Lowton and Liverpool.

SHOPEREAKING AT WIDNES. On Monday at the Liverpool Assizes before Mr. Justice Denman, William Barker (19), labourer, Thomas Collins (17), labourer, and Charles Parr (19), labourer' were indicted for having, at Widnes on or about the 25th of June, broken into the shop of Horatio Syred, and stolen a gold watch, two sil- ver watches, one gold chain, two ladies' silver chains, seven gold wedding rings, Pine gold keeper rings, seven gold dress rings, four diamond studs, and a quantity of wearing apparel. Barker and Collins pleaded guilty, and Parr not guilty. It appeared from the evidence that the shop of the prosecutor was locked up in safety on Saturday night, the 25th of June. On Monday morning it was found to have been broken into, an entrance having been obtained through the skylight. The articles in question were found to have been stolen, and some of the articles were traced to the prisoners. The jury found Parr guilty—His Lordship, in address- ing Barker,said he had been twice convicted before 1890. On the 7th of October, 1890, he was committed at the City Sessions for one month for shopbreaking. On the 2nd of June, 1891, he was committed for six weeks with hard labour. On the 24th of August, at the same City Sessions he was sentenced to one calendar month with hard labour. Then on the 18th of January, 1892—his fourth offence for shopbreakiug—he received the re- markable sentence of one day's imprisonment. (Laughter) He (the learned judge) did not, therefore, wonder to see him there again. But there were other surkmary convictions against the prisoner. This kind of thing would not do. The prisoner was old enough to know better, and something must be done by way of setting an example to young scoundrels like the prisoner. The sentence of the court was that the prisoner must be kept in penal servitude for three years. Addressing Collins, his lordship said the prisoner han been convicted on the 16th April, 1889. for warehouse breaking, and got one month. On the 17th March, 1890, for burglary, he got four months. At the City Sessions on the 27th October, for shopbreaking, he was sentenced to fourteen days. On the 24th August, 1891, for shopbreaking, he got twenty-one days. At the Petty Sessions, on the 26th September, for a small offence, he got three months. At the City Sessions again, in January, 1892, for shopbreaking, he got one day— (laughter)—in company, apparently, with the other man who got one day for shopbreaking. The sentence of the court now was that he be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for fifteen months. He sent the prisoner to gaol for this period because he was the younger of the two. Parr was as old as Barkert hut there was no such record of previous convictions against him. There was a conviction against him at the Manchester Petty Sessions. Parr must go to gaol for eight months with hard labour.

A. THRILLING LOVE STOBY. BY LAURA JEAN LIBDEY. .•• • CHAPTER I. "THE YOUNG MAN RAISED HIS HAT AND TURNED AWAY, LEAVING THE MEMORY OF HIS HANDSOME FACE AND DARK EYES BE- HIND HIM." To love him and be beloved Is the one grand dream of a maiden's life. F. N. CROUCH. It was on the tenth of January, and intensely cold in New York city. I am particular as to the date, for it marked the bitterest tragedy that ever ' darkened a beautiful young girl's Ill.:. All the night before a thick, steady storm of snowflakes had been coming down, until it seemed on this fatally event( I day that the world lay lost under a shroud of whiteness, and it was snowing ' still. Great icicles hung from the bare branches of the trees and from the eaves of the houses. A cold north wind was blowing—a wind that chilled every- thing it touched. One this bitter cold morning, hurrying along with the crowd that surged up Broadway, was a young girl, who, despite her shabby attire, was rarely beautiful. She was not more than seventeen, this fair maiden who was destined to meet so strange—aye, so wonderful—a fate, with a face dark and piquant, framed in a wealth of nut-brown curls; dimpled cheeks, which the cutting wind had kissed into twin roses; lips like the heart of a crimson blossom ; and these eyes, dark as stars, looking out from the rose-leaf face, would have startled any one with their vivid loveliness. She had the grace of a daint3 young princess, though lonic Lawrence was but a working- girl—the daughter of a Knight of Labour. lonic had been the pride and darling of her father's heart. Six months before our story opens he had passed away, joining the wife of his youth, who had been dead several years, leaving two daughters be- hind him. On his death-bed he had called Barbara, his eldest daughter, to his bedside, and drawing her face down to his own cold, clammy one, he whispered, solemnly: "You are three-and-twenty, Barbara, and lonie is but seventeen. I leave her to your care. You must be both mother and sister to her, Barbara, she is so young. She is gay, impetuous, and wilful, but you must be patient with her. She will be more beauti- ful than it seldoms falls to the lot of women to be, Barbara, and a great beauty in a young and unpro- tected girl brings with it either a blessing or a curse. Oh, my dear, I have such strange fears for lonie's future, I cannot tell why. I trust to Heaven this premonition of coming evil is but a sick man's morbid fancy. I could not rest in my grave if harm befell her. Guard our treasure well, Barbara." " I will, father," said the weeping girL "Yon may safely leave lonie to me." Barbara had kept her promise well. She guaided her treasure too well, perhaps; and that was how she came to lose it. Barbara Lawrence had taken up the thread of life when her father had laid it down, and sought work in an adjacent mill; but lonie was kept' at school. Then a sudden change came. Barbara was stricken ill. LThe doctor who was summoned saw at once hat he dared not tell lonie—that the end was hear; she would soon be alone in this pitiless "Oh, my darling " Barbara had moaned, rwhat shall we do now? I—l dare not look the future in the face. The money we have laid by will soon be run through with." I "Do not fear, dear,' cried beautiful, brave lonie. ." We shall not starve. I can take your place in the mill." , At first Barbara demurred; but there was no help Ifor it. lonic must be bread-winner now by force of necessity; but, ah, how Barbara dreaded it. Her darling knew so little of the great hard world of men and women! How would it end? . On this eventful morning that our story opens, 1 Barbara kissed her darling good-bye with a wistful I sigh, asking, anxiously: " Are you sure you can find the way to the mill, darling " • lonic threw back the brown head running over with curls, and looked at her, a gay rollicking laugh that sounded like the chiming of silver bells rippling over the cherry-red lips "Don't be a goose, Barbara," she cried. "Why shouldn't I find my way? One would think, to hear , you talk, that I was a child of seven, instead of a young lady of seventeen." With a hearty kiss and a bear-like hug, lonic darted away before her sister had time to reply; and Barbara remembered afterward she had watched the girl out of sight. More than one pair of eyes turned to gaze admir- ingly after the slim, girlish figure, but lonic Law- rence paid no heed. Turning hurriedly off Broadway, and crossing Canal-street, she paused at length before a large brick structure which bore aboye the broad entrance door the sign: ROCHESTER AND LELAND. NOTTINGHAM LACE MILLS.

" This is the place," murmured lonie, her heart In a flutter as she ascended the steps, nervously, that led to the office. "Oh, they will, they must take me in Barbara's place, when I tell them she has fallen ill, and that I—" The sentence never was finished. All in an instant Joule was conscious of a swift, dizzy sen- sation; the earth and sky seemed to meet, and then— "I hope you are not hurt," said a deep musical voice. "Those ice-covered steps are treacherous. I am so fortunate as to have saved you from an ugly fall." lonic struggled out of a pair of masculine arms, and, raising her bewildered eyes, saw a tall, fair- haired gentleman standing before her. He and a gentleman friend had but a moment since alighted from a sleigh that had dashed up to the pavement. "I sincerely trust you are not hurt," he repeated, looking earnestly at the lovely young face flushing and paling in evident embarrassment, as she mur- mured she was "not hurt, only stunned." "You can go into the office through the private door, if you like. These steps are such a sheet of ice, they are actually dangerous." He could not account for the impulse that led him to add: "Allow me to introduce myself, and to apologise for the condition of them."' He drew a card from his card case, and handing it to her, lonie read the name—" ARTHUR Ro- CHESTER." "Are you, sir, one of the owners of the mill ?"' asked lonie, with timid eagerness. "The son of the senior member of the firm," he replied. Then her eyes involuntarily travelled toward his companion; and she saw a face that left its memory on her heart while her life lasted—a dark, handsome face that usually won women's hearts at the first glance, a pair of dark, laughing, eyes that met her Owe, and seemed to hold hbfespell-bound by their magic power. • Poor, beautiful lonic! She might have led a happy enough life if her path had not been crossed by this handsome young man. • Although Arthur Rochester had made himself known to her, he did not offer to introduce his companion, lonie noticed. On the contrary, he seemed annoyed when he glanced suddenly around and saw that his friend was regarding the girl with apparent admiration. A frown came over Arthur Rochester's fine face; and, raising his hat, he hurried his companion quickly away. But not before the darkly splendid eyes had flashed another glance full of unbounded admira- tion into the lovely, girlish face; for Frank Lyons had promised himself that he should see this petty young girl again, at whatevet cost. He permitted himself to be hurried away; but a strange smile crept up to the lips the dark, curling moustache shaded. He had left the memory of his handsome face and dark eyes behind him,. as he knew he should. As the gentlemen turned away, lonie hurried on to the office. Upon making known her errand, she was sent to the foreman, Who had charge of those affairs. A few minutes later, pale as death, she emerged upon the street. She would have sobbed aloud but that so many were passing. "Father," she cried below her breath, raising her eyes to the storm-swept sky," can you understand your poor lonie's terrible woe? "Ah me! ah me I how can I return to Barbara, lyidg sick unto death this bitter cold winter day, and tell her they refused to take me in her place. "Can I tell her howl pleaded with them, telling them I must find employment or we would starve? I am too proud to apply to the labour league for aid, while I have health and strength; they expended so

• much for poor papa daring hie- long illness: Oh, what shall I do? Oft, Heaven-help me! What shall Ido Where shall I turn? I shall not go back to Barbara until I have found some place." , It eo happened that for some little time after Arthatltochester had entered the mill in company with his friend, it did not occur to him as to the loVely young girl's object in coming there on that bitter cold morning. t' It must be she is in search a work,", he argued with himself,. gazing thoughtfrilly ~into the - fire. "Traverse, the foreman, will 'be sure to And her away," he mused.-" for he was speaking only yester ; d 4 of the advisability of discharging some of the hapds, for work is slack now; but that isn't to be thbught of as long as have a voice in the matter," 1211uminated, with a determined shake of the 'head. "We must manage to Apd something for them to do for this is a bitterly hard wieterrfOr the poor. I Must intercede in this young girl's behllf." It was for his kindly consideration of their inter- ests that the employees loved him, end sabre than one recipient, of his bounty had cried out from an over-wrought heart: God bless Mr. Arthur He's a noble, trim friend to the poor!" *rid in proportion as young Arthur Rochester -was revered and loved by those about him, his father, the proud old-raillionaire owner of the mill, was hated. ...Hurrying to the office, Arthur Rochestei called foX the foreman, and found his surmise had been quite correct; the girl had come in. search of work, and he found, to his dismay, that she had been already sent away. A strange regret that he could scarcely have defined thrilled in the young man's heart. The result was, however, an office boy was hurriedly:: dispatched to overtake the slim figure hurrying down the street almost lost to sight by the blind- ing storm, and lonie was recalled and given her Sister's place in the mill. All that day thoughts of pretty lonie filled twe different masculine hearts. Arther Rochester, who had been hastily summoned from the city by a telegram, thought of lonic as the train whirled him on his journey. His friend, Frank Lyons, had thought of nothing else. • "Confound it I " he _muttered, teaching for his sealskin overcoat, and throwing it on somewhat hastily, "what is coming over me, I wonder. I have seen a pretty, girlish face, and I cannot forget it.' There's but one ,:say to cure myself of this mad TancY, and that is to 'see the same ,faceagqin " ;aud 'he laughed a little, hard, cynical latigh.ll' I oughiF lint to give one thought to the •pretty little gipsy ; the fates have forbidden A, that's certain." - 'All day long the stormhad raged on, gicl nitht, dark as Hades, had set in early. ' • At length six ,o'clock- sounded shrilly from the clocks and adjoining belfries,' and a few 'Moments later throngs of nimble4ooted lasses -emerged from the broad entrance door of the Nottingham Mills to battle with the , storm and the darkness,, as they, made their way to the elevated roads and street cars, anxious to get to their homes. lonie could not afford the expensive luxury-Pt riding, so she made her, way alone,en foot. The night was growing colder and colder"; the very breath seemed to freeze on poor' Tonie'elips, and the snow had drifted to such great depths, and beneath tlie street was covered with a glaze of ice, that making one's way was almost impossible. Suddenly she heard the sound of sleigh bells, and a few moments later a sleigh dashed up the street: and when it was abreast. lonie, to her surprise it stopped short. Hoy was she to know that its 'oCcupant had•purpoiely followed her from the mill? Glancing up, she saw by the yellow gleam of the street lamp the dark, handsome face of the 'stranger whom she had Met that morning with Mr. liochestar. "If you are going my way," he called out, plea- santly, as he raised his hat to her, "won't you let me persuade you to ride? Walking is &meg the, impossibilities. I hope you recognise me; I am your employer's friend." Me hu sprung from the t sleigh, and was stand.' ing, hat in hand, before her knee deep in the drift- ing snow. " I almost envied my friend being of assistance to you this morning," he went on, laughingly. "Fate' Is kind in placing me in that position now. He did not introduce me to you; he best knows why. . Let'- me introduce myself; lam rank Lyons, his college chum, from Philadelphia " ; adding: "And. you ale ?" " Tonle' Lawrence," the girl answered, timidly, a 1 vely flash covering her shy sweet face. • • "Do allow me to insist upon taking you home, Miss Lawrence," he pleaded. "You can see for yourself you will never be able to make your way 'there on foot; you would meet the fate of poor I Gretchen; you would be found frozen stiff and cold:1 in death in the snow-drifts to-morrow mornine'

was a Mile delighted—a little bewildered and just a little frightened. If she could have foreseen the future she would have turned from him and fled ere the first steps that were to end in so bitter a tragedy were taken. With girlish, .bashful hesitancy, elle allowed her- self to be persuaded afid Placed,in the sleigh. He took up thereins,, and the mettlesome horse fairly flew over the frozen Emow.drifts.

' THE FIRST .13E0RM • SOX HAS • EYER'. KEPT LIES LIKE A DEAD WEIgHT, IN lONIICS HEART. " Ah, what a fatal web we weave, :When first we practice to, deceive." lonie•Lawrence never forgot that sleigh-ride; It was destined to live in her mereory for many a long year afterward. Frank Lyons was a clever man, quick of compre-, hension,; he had the great gift of understanding character, and of adapting himself to the people into whose company he was thrown. He misused the gift terribly, even fatally; but he had it, and Used ft like a-chi:rm. ' Although he haetexchanged but a few indifferent words with Joule, he understood her perfectly. • He talked with her of the books she had read, as the gleigh dashed on over the frozen drifts; he quoted sweet, 'passionate wordiefrom the, pets; he cited the beautiful love story of Romeo and Juliet as the sweetest he had ever heard, and ' complimented her by. remarking, she was strangely like the picture of sweet Juliet which hung In the Art Academy, adding that he intended to purchase the pieture, that the face be admired so sincerely might be ever before him. It was pleasant to sit there and hear such kind words; it was pleasant to read the admiration so clearly revealed in those dark eyes. It was very romantic,.too,, to think that he thought her so like Juliet. Although he did not say it in words—he was too clever for that—he made lonie understand that the brightness of life had just begun for him that morn- ing; for, like Romeo, he had seen for the first time a fair face wlaich he should never forget. Listening to him, lonie believed him to be the brightest, kindliest, truest man upoit earth. ' She was very young and inexperienced, or a pair of dark eyes, a dark, curling moustache, and a musical voice, could not have charmed her so. The drive home had been of scarcely twenty minutes' duration, but it seemed to lonie she had lived long ages during that time in another world.. " Ali L here LQ the number," he said at length, stopping short before her bumble home. He was satisfied with the impression he had made when be saw her start back and exclaim, in

_ wonder: "Have we reached my home so soon 7" He helped her to alight with as much courtly grace as though she had been a princess instead of a poor little working girl, and expressed the hope, very earnestly, that he might see her again some time. The next instant the slim little figure was lost to sight in the darkness. "You are late, my darling," said Barbara, as the door opened and lonian sprang into the room, and up to the couch on which the sufferer lay. Aa she took her darling in her arma she inquired ?Thal. llati hushed her fair young face with such a new and tender beauty. "Has it been a hard day, dear 1" she asked, as ;he white arms twined about her, and the dark, nurly head nestled down on the pillow beside her men. "It must have been," she, added, "for it was tour first " day as a brea-Livinner, facing the cold, hard world of men and women," "It was the happiest day of my life, Barbara," she answered. "Every one was so good to me." Then she, told her how near the foreman had come to not taking her into the mill, but bad changed his mind; and of the accident at the slippery steps which would have happened if young lir. Rochester 11;ici not been ahr at hand. ' "God blessaMr. Arthur !" returned Barbara, "He is as noble as he is good—a king among men,' "PM you ever 9ce his friend, Mr.—Mr. Lyons?' stammered lonic, co.,fusedly. And if Barbara had bat glanced at the girl's blushing face, she would have seen a look on it that would have alarmed her at once.. " Yes," answered Barbara hoarsely, her face darkening strangely. "1 have seen him. Why 7" " YOU like him 2" faltered joule, in a low voice.

-" NO, edfiarbara, siowly. A.lcatitY "Why-1"- persisted Joule, the colour fading front her pretty, dimpled cheeks. "I cannot tell you all, ply reasons, but I will say he has a false face. There is cunning in the sharp era qnd cruelty on the thin lips," " You are prejudiced," said Joule, drawing been Coldly. "I have never heard of any sensible per- son disliking a man for the colour of hi s eyes or the shape of his lips." "Nature never makes a mistake in her handwrit- ing," returned Barbara Lawrence, gravely, "and she has Written 'Beware' on every lineament of his face." A gleam of defiance flashed into the dark eyes, and lonie turned abruptly away, with the words she was about to utter unsaid. How could she tell Barbara—after that—that he had ridden home with him from the mill, and all he had said to her? "A. false, face," . /mile repeated indignantly to herself, as she turned away. • Barbara certainly was prejudiced against him. It was the handsomest face, She had ever seen, and the remembrance of that .one glance froth those dark eyes, as they had parted, made her heart beat. It was a break in the monotony of her life—it was something agreeable to think of--the first dawning of that sun that was to shine sO.briglitlrfor a time—then destroy her. The first secret lonia had ever kept was then and there buried down' deep in her heart from Barbara's wat4hful eyes. If; lonie had not tamed silently away, this story would never have been written. ' Leng and earnestly Barbara thought over that conVersation, during the still solemn hours of the night, as she tossed restlessly cm her pillow. "Shall I tell her the reason I have for hating— yes, Vtatipg Frank 'Lyons ?" she asked herself, with a bitter sobbing Aigh. "Oh, Heaven! heir can I ? and yet she should be told the whole truth, no matter how great the shock may be." "To-morrow I will tell her," murmured Barbara, huskily, "when she returns at night from the mill." lonie met the invalid with a strangely flushed face the next morning. The first secret she had ever kept from Barbara lay like a heavy weight in her teart, "*ill tell her that / know him, when I come home to-night," she thought, tenderly kissing the pallld face as she bade her good-bye. It was long after dark when lone returned home that evening. 'A -sadden chill seemed to oppress her, as she opened-MCI-dor: -The fire in the-grate-was out-4.-the lamp she had left on the small stand, beside the sufferer's couch, was not lighted—the room was in total darkness, save for a little strip of moon- light that drifted in. Nb welcome voice greeted her. Was Barbara asleep.? Nbiselessly she stole up to the couch and knelt dowea beside it. . ~. "Harhara," she said, softly, "I have sting to tell you, dear. It has been weighing on raYthind all day long. You won't scold me for not telling youllast night, will you. Barbara 1 Promise me in advence." The thin, patient face did not-. " toward lin her! ,The lips that .were wont'„ '„).breathe wo aof consolation were strangely silent 11'. No gentle hand was laid caressingly on the curly head; no tender voice answered that faltering appeal. Heaven help her I Barbara Lawrence's voice would ansWer her never again. "Do you hear me, Barbara?" she cried, laying her face down beside the one turned from her on the rallevi,.. What was there i'n that icy touch that sent such a thrill of horror through the girl's heart?' lirith.sa low!, startled cry, joule gazed down into the rigid face lying po Ftill and whiteatritlifiethe little strip of white mooldight. The half-dieri'eazitd-eyes flashel! no look of recognition up,into her own. Then a piercing shriek rang 'through the lonely room ; aaelat) 'l Oh, God! Barbara is diced I' ~ • Yes, she waa dead, leaving lonic, hiA/idearlitig, her Idol, 'friendless 'and alone, to the ' its of the bitter world. ~ lonie's wild cries brought in a kind.hearted neighbourotho found her in a deep swoon on the floor. It was quite a week after Barbara was laid to rest, that•lome opened her eyes to consciousness, and realised with a bitter moan what had happened. "You nearly went off in brain fever, too, my dear," said Mrs., Gregory,, the; kind neighbourt, to whose house she had been removed. a. "I. wish I had," sobbed lonie. "I have nothing to live for now I" "It's wicked in the sight of God to think that, let alone saying it," declared Mrs. Gregory. "You have youth and strength, and, no doubt, a long life before you. You are to make the best of it. You mist not worry. You ean stay here with me until you are able to go back to the mill again." It was several„weekii before lonia was able to take up the thread of life again; and in the face of another 'terrible.. snew-atorm she set out,, heavy- hearted, for the mill once more. As she was about to pass through the weaving- room, where a', score or more of pretty girls were bending over their looms,' toward the cloak-room to 'divest herself of her wraps, she was confronted by the foreman, who tapped, her insolently on the shoulder. .. "Never mind hanging up your wraps, Miss—

Mika Lawrence." he said sharply, " step up to the deSk with me, and we will settle your account. We do not keep 'young ladies here who gay, out from worm when it suits their fancy, You, are dis- charged." " Oh, sir 1" she began. "Ii—"• "No excuses, please,' returned the foreman. "/ decline to discuss the matter—to listen to another word. You are discharged, I say." Fairly dazed with pain, lonic staggered from the weaving-room, with the miserable pittance that had been handed to her, out into the street and the ter- rible snow-storm. . "What shall I do ?" she groaned, pressing her hands to her throbbing temples as she raised her eyes te the stormy sky. "Not a dollar left—no borne—no money to pay for a day's board. Oh,. God og the orphans and the friendless, show me which way to trim," she moaned, blinding tears falling down her cheeks.

Only those who know what ftll horror 'is ' compassed in the awful word "discharged," and in the dead of winter, oan. pity poor lonia. Only those who have had a. page of just such a experience in their own past lives, can understand what this beautiful, hapless working-girl suffered, and an answering chord, will; thrill in their hearts for her. ; All day long lonie wandered through the stormy streets, heedless of hunger and; cold. .At length dusk set in, soon giving place to the darkness of night. lonie ;dreaded returning to. liTrs. Gregory, and telling hen she was out of worte-;, for; that lady had impressivelY hinted she would bepleased to receive as much as she eoald spare each week, in addition to her board bill, to pay up for tb e time already spent beneath her roof during her illness. "AM how 'can return there?" moaned lonia, threading her way with the bus. 7 thong that surged • up Broadway. She found herself at last upon Lexington Avenue; and just as she made that iliscovery, a gentleman passed her, directly beneath the glaring light of the gas-lamp. Although be did not glance in her direction, and hi., seal overcoat CVP9 fs,tened close up about the chin, she recognised him at nice as young Mr. itochester, the mill owner's son. And she remem- bered now that he was. called "the friend of the poor." If she could but plead with him to take her back, telling him why she remained away frem the mill that ten days, perhaps he wcuald grant her request. Acting upon the impulse, lonie sprang forward; hut she was not quiek enough. At that moment Arthur Rochester had run lightly up the broad marble steps of an adjacent mansion, and had ad- mitted himself with his pass-key. lonie atood silent and motionless before the house, her hands clasped in despair, her lovely eyes drowned in tears. There seemed to be something going on inside,. for the house was lighted from "garret to base— ment ;" and while she stood there, coaches corer menced to arrive and deposit their fair burdens at the canopy-covered door. "‘Oh, if I could only see him for but one little moment I" thought lonie, catching her breath uith a bitter sob. "In cases like this, even the aaost timid aro driven by necessity to desperate mea- uares."

She hurriedly ascended the steps and toucled the bell. The liveried footman gazed in Indisguised amaze- ment at the shivering, ili-clad, slim figure standing before him, "What are you doing here? What do you want T Why didn't you go below to the gervaLts' hail 7" ho asked, all in a breath. "I wanted to see Mr. Arthur Dichester for but a few minutes," pleaded lone, earnestly. " I saw him enter just now. I must see An insolent laugh answered her : , "Must l" he repeated, sneeringly. "That's pretty good u ca move on my You n't see him, Come, pretty,"

div.p: " Who is it Wants to see Arthur, Peters 7" asked a cnrious voice from within.
Peters, the footman, drew back with a low, ob-

sequious bow. "Only a working girl from the mill, I should Imagine. Miss Elaine—a mere nobody. l've told her it is simply !impossible; she couldn't see Mr. Rochester." - - - "A would see me, if he only knew my errand,' soblie lonic: . f m The young girl who Retire had called Elaine I came swiftly forward, and then lonie saw the most ! magnificent being she had ever be- held. A slim, petite young - girl, with dark eyes b.nd hair, robed • in a •fleecy • white ball dress. Diamonds encircled her, white throat, 4 flashed from her arms and small white hands, swung from the tiny shell-like ears, and caught back the meshes of her jetty coil. "Why do you wish to see Mr. Rochester so par- ticularly 2" she asked, peering eagerly down into the white upturned face which she saw at a glance was as beautiful as a poet's dream. " I—l could hardly tell you," murmured lonie, choking back a sob. The heart of the little heiress, who loved Arthur • Rochester with a mad, passionate love, was fired with bitter jealousy at once, and she made up her mind that this lovely working-girl should never Bee him, if she could prevent it. r WARRINGTON TOWN - • COUNCIL. .1 The monthly meting of this Council was held dn 'uesday evening, in the Town Rail. The Mayor (Alderman E. Geeenall) presided, and there were 51s present Aldermen Sutton, Harrison, Burgess, ttolmes, Chandley, Platt, Franconab ; Councillors Illackhurst, It. T. Fairclough, J. Shaw-Oreen. Cannel], Hill, Smethurst, Muir, Olonks, Plumptoro Garner, H. Roberts, Heaton, Bolton, Dixon' Ashton, Hepherd, Hutchinson, Browne; Messrs. J. Loion Whittle (Town 'Clerk), and T. Longdiu .(Borough %tory eyor) THE DEATH OF LORD RHNMARLEIGH. The Mayor said :—Before proceeding with the ordin- ary business of the Council it is my duty, as Mayor of the borough, officially to announce to the Council the death of that illustrious and venerable nobleman' Lord Winmarleigh. We are assembled in the hal! which was for many years of his valuable life his private residence; and the walls of the very chamber in which we sit mist have witnessed man- scenes of his private life. You know his many virtues, his high moral standard, his blameless and highly honoured and useful life, His name will be ever remembered with those of the noblest and best of his time. He was fevered and loved by all men, and England mourns his, loss. Warrington has been foremost in her expression of sorrow.and it remairis for us only to place upon the record of this borough the Written testimony of our sincere grief and our unbounded admiration of thanoblenesa of character of the great man We have lost. 1 therefore beg to propose that this Council desires to record its deep sorrow on the occasion of the death of Lord Winmarleigh, who for many years el his beneficial life resided among us, and whose asso- ciation bestowed distinction on the town. We desire also to express our warm admiration of his noble and , Illustrious life spent in the service of his country, of his moral ani distinguished public career, and his high domestic virtues. We further desire to express to he daughters of the late Lord Winmarleigh, the Hon. Misses Wilson Patten, the sincere and heartfelt sympathy. net sOnlY of the Council but of the town at large with them In their sad hezeavernent. Alderman HARRISON seconded the proposal, and in the course of his remarks, he pointed out that Lord Win- Marleigh had been a trusted minister of State, and had served his sovereign and his country faithfully, and well both at home and abroad, and In positions civil as well as military. So far as,Warrington was concerned, Lord Winmarleigh had been identified with the growth and Progress of the valuable institutions which had been established from time to time. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Bootees said he entirely united with the rxPreesions made use of, and joined - most heartily and sineerely in all that had been said in favour of such a Man as Lord Wintnarleigh. Lord Winmarleigh Was known to him, as to all the rest of the Council, and they had had very good opportenities of judging his Work in every department. He (Alderman Holmes) had been one of the three gentlemen who waited upon Lord Winmarleigh with regard to the purchase ot that Hall and Park for the town; and he should never forget tie, aind reception' they had met with and the desire that was shown that the Council should acquire the property' for the benefit of the town. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Reetoess said he had harra good deal of ex- , Perience of Lord Winmarleigh, and he had said many times, and he repeated it again, that his idea of a true .English gentleman was embodied In Lord Winmarleigh In every sense of the word—his 'conduct, his career, his charities, and his utmost desire to be of the greatest Possible service to his common humanity during the pro. areas df his passing through this life, and he felt per- suaded that no gentleman ever achieved a higher distinc- • tion in that department than did Lord Winmarleigh. He had left behind him a lasting remembrance amongst all those whose good fortune it had been to oeme in con- . tact with him, and they did not expect, and they hardly had any right to expect, to see his like again. Warring- ton owed a great deal to Lord Winmarleigh, and he kat persuaded that the time would not soon COMP, if it ever did come, when the benefits that he conferred I'„.Port the town would be lost to the memory of its inha- ottants. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CHANDLET said there was one gratifying cir- cumstance, and that was that whatever praise might he !add in favour qf Lord Winmarleigh they all of thean felt 'lt was a tribute of true feeling. They did not assemble them on an occasion like that to repeat praises unde- served ; it was really a tribute of true feeling,and appre- ciation of his worth. (Hear, hear.) , Alderman Surrost said he had known Lord Winmar- 'eigh all his life, and always looked upon him as one of the finest specimens of an English gentleman and as true a, nobleman as any there was in the country. (Hear, sleet.) 'Councillor H. ROBERTS, as one of the younger members t,:f.the Council, and a native of Warrington, wished to J°ln in the expression of regret which had been given Utterance to by theVayor in words which, bethought, extremely well chosen, and also to join with the other rneuabers of the Council. Lord Winmarieieh was a man of whore Warrington had every occasion to be proud. nature had been singularly kind to him, even in his very Presence, but on all occasions, whether in public or in Private, he, if possible, excelled nature's gifts in manner, caurtesy,and grace to all. (Hear, hear.) There was one inr.; that came to him as a young man, and that Was he singular devotion of Lord Winmarleigh to what he considered to be the pnblic service. Orealt occasions, 110 matter what the subject was, whether it was the eause of education, art, 01 something even greater and more responsible than that, Lord Winmarleigh was al.srays to the fore. div.head: COUNCILLOD DIXON ASKS
div.p: COUNCILLOD DIXON ASKS

Councillor DIXON asked the Chairman of the Street Improvement Committee "if any error has been made in allowing the property to be erected by Mr. William Jeffrey, in Padgate-lane, and if one has been made, will he give me the full particulars, and, who is responsible for it 2" Alderman PLATT said his answer to that was that no error had been made, and consequently they could not hold anybody responsible for what had not occurred. Since ' Mr. Jeffrey took a lease of the land le- ferred to it had been added to the borough, and the conditions of building had been somewhat altered from what they were under the Rural Sanitary Authority. Further than that, since the lease was obtained there had been a most important decision of the High Court of Appeal with regard to what they knew as ancient highways. In Warrington for a great many years I they had thought and acted upon the supposition that I they could not interfere with the buffeting line in an ancient highway without purchasing the property, and I that it was not in their power to insist .upon its being made into a 401 t. street, and that they had no power to ask the frontager to pave the street: ' All that, however, had been reversed at a very recent date, and it appeared that they had just as much power over an ancient high- way as over any other street in the borough. They could compel the frontagers to make the street 40ft. wide, just the same as any ordinary street which was laid out ; and further than that, they could compel the owners to pave it. That might be regarded as a hardship by Mr. Jeffrey, but it was a state of things for which no one could be 'held to blame ; and, indeed, it was a very much im- proved state of things. NEW BUILDINGS.—STREET IMPROVEMENTS. '- • •

The minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee contained the following :—That the plans of the following buildings. &c., be approved :—Five houses in Thyrine-street for Mr. John Longshavf; hayloft, &a., near Sankey-street, for Mr. Shawcross ; twelve houses in Marsh-street, off Manchester-road, for Mr. Joseph Matthews; ten houses in Marshhouse-lane for Mr. Stephen Dale.; Awe houses in Padgate-lane for Mr. J. T. Farring- ton ; alterations to shop in Buttermarket-street for Mr. Baines. Also, that an agreement be entered into with Mr. Murray Douglas for the purchase of a strip of land containing about 550 square yards in Liverpool-road and Factory-lane at 12.5. ed. per yard. The Corporation to erect a new wall and to make good any buildings inter- fered with lay the alteration. Mr. Douglas to take down any buildings on any part of the laud not immediately required when requested iso to do by the Corporation ; and that the Finance Committee be requested to apply to the Local Government Board for permission to borrow the money required for the above purchase. Alderman Purr moved the adoption of,the minutes. He said that provision had been made to widen Factory, lane—a most important improvement, as the road led 'down to the riverside. ~Already the road conveyed a considerable amount of traffic; such a quantity of traffic had it to accommodate that it was high time that steps were taken to widen it. A strip or land belonging to Mr. Murray Douglas, extending down Factory-laae and Liverpool-road, was proposed to be purchased in order to make a proper approach. The Corparation would have to take down a wall and make other alterations. It was estimated that the alterations would absorb a sum of between £BOO and £7OO. In answer to a question, ne added that there were certainly a few tumble-down sheds, &c., on the land, and they were included in the purchase, tha amount for the whole' being as already stated. There was one part of the land occupied, namely, at the western end, by a comparatively new building, but it was not anticipated that it would be necessary to deal with that at the present. Mr. Douglas had given an undertaking, however, to pull down all Maid- lags when called upon. Continuing, Alderman Platt said the Committee felt that the sum of MO or £7OO was rather too much to take out of the ordinary revenue at one time, and it was therefore, proposed to have the Finance Committee instructed to apply to the Local Government Board for permis'elon to borrow the money required to accomplish the purposes referred to. There were one or two other small pur- chases to be made by the Street Improvement Com- mittee, and it was proposed when the time came, to take powers to borrow the whole amount required, and have the repayments spread over as many years as it was possible to procure. Alderman &Mama took it that the amount of money immediately required was only part of a scheme, and as the Council only recently objected to the Gas Com- mittee taking powers to borrow money which they did not immediately require, he felt compelled to ask the chairman of the Streets Improvement Committee to lay down what he proposed to do in the future. What might becontained in the other part of the scheme might be more than the Council calculated for. Further, he said that £5OO or £OOO was not such a very large sum to take out of general revenue. The Council surely was not so hard up as that. If it was necessary, he would squeeze the amount out of the Longford works. (Laughter.) Councillor MONKS gave it as his impression that in view of the probable completion of the Ship Canal at an early date this road leading to the river side would be- come an important one. From an inspection of plans, however, it appeared to him that the road was not to be widened throughout. As he understood, only three- quarters of the street was to be widened ; leaving cer- tain cottage property to be dealt with at some distant date, and then, when it was found necessary to finish the work, it would, no doubt, be found that the value of the property had been considerably enhanced. Alderman ?La= said, in reply, that Councillor Monks had, in his opinion, rather overstated the case. It was propesed to deal with the whole of the street except one house. The Council must certainly understand that everything could not be done at once. The present negotiations were the first steps towards the completion of the work. It was not intended to stop short, but the committee had fully determined to acquire the house, and Mr. Douglas had agreed to sell it. In reply to other questions he said that it must be within the recol- lection of the Council that no steps had been taken in regard to obtaining the money for property purchased at Market-gate, and at Bridge Foot. It was proposed by the Street Improvements Committee to go to the Finance Committee and add the small purchases, to which he had referred in his opening remarks, to these, and take powers to liquidate the whole amount in yearly instal- ments. (Heartixiar.) ' The minutes were then adopted. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—TfiIE BOILER QUESTION.

Russell; that the tender of The Castle Rubber Company, Limited, to supply 4 cart sheets at £1 4s. each be accepted. Alderman BURGESS moved the adoption of the minutes. Referring to the recommendation as to the boiler, he said that though he was absent from the committee meeting he thought the committee, in making the re- commendations had taken the best aourse they could have adopted in the matter after the vote of the Council at their last meeting. It had come to him with refe- rence to this within the last six or seven days, since the committee pasied their resolutions, that at the last meeting of the committee the Town Clerk produced an agreement which had been come to by the Corporation with Messrs. Manlove, Alliot, and Company, some ten years ago, he believed, and which had escaped the memory of the Council, and the Town Clerk, and him- self, and other members of the Sanitary Committee at that time. That agreement bound the Corporation, for reasons that were set forth, he believed. (Councillor Flood: That is expired.) That agreement would be found to be in force if they attempted to go elsewhere for material that might be required for. the plant at Longford—for this reason that the firm had now and al- ways had a patent right, and never charged royalty, that being the reason they had entered into the agree- ment with the Corporation. There was a firm putting in three or four new ones, and did the Cor- poration think for a moment, they would go to an in- surance society fora specification 0 boilers which they wanted ? (Interruption). He was quite sure there were persons within the borough who could give speci- fications for any steam boiler. He thought, as Council- lor Roberts said, that everything for the borough should be got within the borough if possible, provided they had practical men, as Mr. Bolton said, to toll them what they wanted: In all his many years' experience there had not been a more disgraceful thine than writing to an insur- surance society for a specification for a steam boiler for Longford. This Committee presented the following return for the year ended June 30th :—Books issued in the reading room, 10,479, previous year, 17,798; books issued in the lendinr, department, 52,003, previous year, 28,845 ; number of borrowers, June, 1892, 2,435, previous year, 1,137. The Committee mentioned the appointment by the County Council 9f Mr. Charles Lister to represent it upon the technical instruction committee af that Coun- cil. Committee recommended :—That the Literary and Philosophical Society have the use of the Lecture Room on the same terms as before, provided the meet- ings are held on Mondays. That the Committee do con- vey to the teachers of the Institute its satisfaction with the manner in which the classes have been conducted during the past session. The other minutes of the Committee were published last week. Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the adoption of the minutes. He referred to the return as to the result of the past year's operations after the freeing of the library. The Council and the public would be very much grati- fied to see the figures produced. Councillor SHAW GREEN; Just double. Alderman HOLMES : You never can get a book out of the library when you want it. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he was very glad to say he could get his books out of the library quite easily. Councillor BOLTON: You are a privileged individual. Councillor H. ROBERTS said the committee would be able shortly through the increased rate they had in operation to add very considerably to the number of books. They hoped to spend pretty nearly £lOO in that department, which would provide a very large addition to the lending books. Their difficulty was this—one that only money and time would overcome— that certain new novels and so forth were much more in _ _ . _
demand than others, and unfortunately they had only

Alderman BUNIONS said Councillor Bolton's remarks, Indorsed by Alderman Platt,were the most cogent of any that had been made on the subject. The Alderman in- , formed the Council that specifications and drawings from the Steam Users' Association were now in the hands of the borough surveyor. They had been asking for this new destructor for some time for a specific reason and that was that the manager at Longford advised this Cor- poration that they were in a condition of very censider- able danger' and that he would not be responsible for anything that might occur through his not having the necessary plant. Councillor FLOOD : That is not the opinion of the Com- mittee.. Alderman BURGESS : I am speaking now, air, of what the manager at Longford advises. I know nothing whatever about the opinion of the committee. There are one or two very singular members on the Commit- tee, and I cannot be held responsible for their opinions. (Laughter.) The minutes were adopted as they stood With the dissent of Councillor Dixon. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended :—That the tender of Mr. J. Fairclough to repair flush cart at £lO be accepted; that Percival's Fold be paved with setts; that in order to ensure greater stability in the repair of paved streets interfered with hy the Gas and Water Committees, this Committee will in future undertake the filling in of the burrstone and the relaying of the aetts ; that the Coun- cil be recommended to adopt "The Private Street Works Act, 1892." The Borough Surveyor submitted plan, estimate, and Specification for the forming and paving of Bramhall-st, The Committee recommended that the Town Clerk serve the necessary notices and take all pro- ceedings for the recovery of the expenses in the event of the owners being in default. Councillor HEAXON moved the adoption of the minutes. The committee, he observed, it would, be seen,were pay- ing some little attention to the paving of the back yards and folds in Warrington. The committee had had a lot of complaints about the Gas and Water Committees tak- ing up the streets and neglecting them, and had decided that they wculd superintend the work, and hoped in future to have no further complaints. Councillor SHAW GREEN asked Councillor Heaton to explain as to the adoption of the private street Works Act. Councillor HEATON said it was not exactly before 'I them that night in proper form, and it was hardly neccessary to explain it till it was. Councillor Snew GREEN: YOU, are asking us to I adopt it. Councillor HEATON t Not to-night. Alderman SUTTON: No, it is coming on again. Councillor HUTCHINSON seconded the motion for adoption. Councillor Bnowim objected to Percival's Fold being passed seeing that there were more important streets in the town in a worse condition; (Where would you begin?) lie would begin with Bank Street. Councillor. HUTCHINSON said the area was much

But it was the intention of the Committee to have several copies of each of these, sti as to meet, as far as possible, the tastes of men like Alder. man Holmes,who liked a little light reading occasionally. (Laughter.) Then they came to the question of the ar- rangements for teaching new subjects next session, which he was bound to say would depend very consider- ably for being carried out upon the terms they received from the County Council. Up to now they had not been satisfied with the treatment they had dealt out to them, but if Warrington had been a county borough they would, of course have received pretty nearly £l,OOO more than they had received at the hands of the County Council. Why they were treating them in this niggardly fashion they could not understand, and it would be a matter for that Corporation to consider very seriously, whether the time had not come for them to have a report which they had been promised for sometirne,as to whether it would not be better to become a county borough. (Hear, hear.) As a Committee of technical instruction they could not afford to lose hundreds of pounds a year owing to the position in which thev stood with regard to the County Council. 04 of the £4:0,900 appropriated by the County Council for purposes of technical instruction the Committee ought to have received in proportion to other boroughs on the basis of population and rate- ability £BBB. They got £6lO grant for one year, and £lOO for the second, and they had earned by scholar. ships about £6O, so that on the two years they had only I received £7lO, instead of £1,710. Contrasted with the treatment they had received from the Lancashire County Council ,the Cheshire County Council had dealt with them I most fairly, and shown a more active interest in thei r pro- ceedings. Councillor Roberts expressed his satisfaction at the appointment of Mr. Lister la testifying the interest of the Cheshire County Council in the scholars who came under the Committee's care from Cheshire. If the Lan- cashire County Council would only do the like, and I appoint some gentleman to represent them on the Com- , mittee, they would he was quite certain have better Itreatment. He moved the adoption of the minutes. , Councillor MONKS seconded the motion. He emphasized the difference in the treatment received from the Cheshire County Council and that from the Lancashire County Council. As a matter of fact, they had no claim whatever on the Cheshire County Council, and what had been done had been done at their (the committee's) suggestion by sending their students to Warrington,and paying the fees. On the other hand,the Lancashire County Council had sent students out of Warrington to Liverpool and Manchester. The War- rington Committee had all along been crippled, owing to I the want of information, which the County Council refused to give. They had not, even up to the last meeting of the committee, any definite idea as to the amount of money they could rely upon, and their classes had been crippled In consequence. Alderman PLATT asked why the representatives of the borough on the Lancashire County Council did not at- tend better to its interests. Councillor BOLTON: Some of them don't attend at all.
