div.p: Councillor SHAW GREEN said the Lancashire County Council were very curious, and treated the Committee setoorreak. trelliel 4 boy, as if they did not know eii-dfityf (Laughtet.) Fle had said more than once ;Theil it was difficult to move the Connty-Council, and he 'thought the time had come wnen the Corporation ought to act independently of them, and apply for a grant in their own favour. _ _ . .

_ Councillor BitowNE congratulated the Committee on the appointment of Mr. Lister, of whom he spoke with high eulogium. Councillor Browne complained that when a member of the library applied for a book which happened to be out, he had to pay a halfpenny and to put his name dowh so that he could have the book in turn. That, to his mind, Was not consistent with the character of a Free Library. He mentioned a case where a well- known book was lying all the week in the library eight persons having paid a halfpenny each for it. Alderman HOLMES said he had long since given on sending to the library for books, there being such diffi- culty in obtaining them, but he dared say this would be overcome. _

Alderman Surrox said that in every Council there were stupid people, as in the Warrington Council. (Laughter.) It was no doubt a difficult matter to induce the members of the County Council to think as they did in Warrington. He had no doubt the represen- tatives of Warrington on the County Council did their duty to the best of their ability. Alderman CHANDLEY suggested that a deputation should be sent to the County Council asking for infor- mation on the subject. They could not wait until the borough be made a county borough. Councillor Itosza•rs said a deputation from the Committee waited upon the Technical Instruction Committee of the County Council a considerable time ago, with the result that they got a little more money than was originally intended but not what they expected, and were put off with a sort of half promise that the difference between what they expected and what they got would be given to them afterwards as subsidiary grant. This had not been done. The Committee had just taken over the care of the School of Art, and with this increased responsibility ought to have an increased grant. The imposition of the halfpenny complained of by Councillor Browne seemed to be rather a pettifogging kind of thing, but it was a relic of the old management, as was also the penny fine, which was found a valuable thing as a source of revenue and as a means of getting back books in rea- sonable time. The halfpenny was charged for intimat- ing by post that the book reserved for a reader was ready for that person. Defending the representatives of Warrington in the Lancashire County Council, Coun- cillor Browne said that authority had a large amount of work to do, and the representatives had done what they could. The interests of Warrington had not been over- looked, and these gentlemen perhaps had not been able to impress them with the idea many people seemed to have that Warrington was the whole of the universe, but they were educating them into that idea—(laugh- ter)—and no doubt in due time Warrington would get , its deserts. (Clear, hear.) The minutes were adopted.

div.head: CEMET-KRY COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE CEMET-KRY COMMITTEE.

The Cemetery Committee reported that the interments for the past four weeks were—adults, 26 ; minors, 35; stillborn and premature, 12. Corresponding per-hod last year—adults, 4!; minors 42; stillborn and premature, 10. The receipts for the past four weeks were £54 Es. Bd.; corresponding period last year, £7O 193. Alderman HARRISON moved, and Councillor Ashtsn seconded, the adoption of the minutes. Councillor Buowss complained of the number of cases that had recently occurred at the Cemetery in which funerals had been delayed by graves being too short for the coffins. Alderman HARRISON said he should obtain information on the subject at the next meeting of the Committee. The minutes were then confirmed. THIs BATHS &C.

The Town Hall, &c., Committee reported that the in- come from the baths for the foar weeks waa £2l 9 s.,and for the corresponding period last year £44 15s. The Committee recommended that the asphalted space around the band'stand be enlarged and finished off with a small stone curb also that the tender of Mr. Stephen MOSS to provide and fix heating apparatus in the new plant house for the sum of £4l 10s. be accepted.
On the motion of Alderman CHANDLEY seconded by Councillor BOLTON, the minutes were confirmed.
THE MARKETS.

The Markets Committee reported that the income of the markets for the put four weeks was £393 ; cor- responding lsst year £379 6s. 103. The minutes were confirmed on the motion of the MAYOR, seconded by Councillor BLACHHORST.
THE GAS COMMITTEE.-QUESTION OF ADVERTISING.

The Gas Committee reported that the average illu- minating Dower of the gas for the past four weeks was equal td 19 80 candles at both works. It also recom- mended the acceptance of several tenders for coal.

Alderman Founts moved, and Councillor R. T. FAIR• cr.kooa seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor PLIMPTON asked if the advertisements in- viting tenders for coal were inserted in the local papers, and, if not, why not? Alderman HoLmss said that was a question he had not expected to be asked, and he did not see the object of it. They had received 30 or 40 tenders as the result of their advertising. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he should like to press the question. He did not see why the tenders shonld not be advertised for in Warrington, as there were other people besides colliery proprietors who might like to tender.

. - Alderman Ilotums said he did not know whether they were advertised in the local papers or not. Councillor H. ROBERTS: They are not; simply in the trade journals. In answer to Councillor Monks, Alderman HOLMES said that there had been a reduction of from 3d. to 81 a ton in the price of the coal tendered for. The m mutes were then confirmed.

div.head: WATER COMMITTEE.-THE WATER MAINS.
div.p: WATER COMMITTEE.-THE WATER MAINS.

At a meeting of the Water Committee, held on the 25th July, at the request of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, it was agreed to hand over to that commit- tee the re-forming of all streets interfered with in the laying of water mains. Alderman FRANCOMB proposed, and Councillor HEE- HERD seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman BURGESS desired to be informed if the com- mittee had arrived at a decisioa to supply the Sanitary Committee with Appleton water for the Longford depot. Alderman FRANCOMB replied that that matter was re- ceiving careful attention. It was believed that the com- mittee wculd consume very nearly the whole of the sur- plus water at Appleton, but he believed that it was possible that the Winwick water would be offered the Sanitary Committee in preference to Appleton water. Councillor FLOOD asked what was the quantity of water allowed to run to waste from Appleton at that moment.

Alderman FRANCOMB adinitted that there was a lot of water allowed to run away, but they could not take up a new concern like that and make the best of of it in h few months. They were anxious to use the water for the purposes_of variou4 manufacturers.
The minutes were Confirrned, and the Council soon afterwards concluded its,sittiag.

div.head: CHOICE CHINA TEAS
div.p: CHOICE CHINA TEAS
THE MODEL LODGING HOUSE
VISITED ON FRIAR'S GREEN.
WHAT THE PEOPLE ARE LIKE WHO LIVE

Almost in the centre of the old historic neigh- hood of Prier's Green, stands Brouchernite's Model Lodging House. There is nothing particularly ex- traordinary in the fact of Warringtompossessing a model lodging house ; but this establishment In itself is one possessing many points of interest. It is not a very extraordinary brick and mortar building to look at. The men whom you see enter- ing and leaving it don't strike you as being either important or interesting personages. Some of them don't strike you as being particularly respectable either. Most of them cultivate quite a Bohemian free- dom of toilet, their well-ventilated and greasy pants; brimless and unconventional-shaped hats, which are the last remains of a defunct fashion, and their fondness for wearing on one foot an elastic-Aded boot, and on the other a blucher, speak eloquently to you of that awful bogie man,the perennial tramp. He, indeed, is the chief character whom you will find in Brouchemite's Lodging House. " Poor, use- less, forlorn, lost mendicant ! ' you say. Well, he just likes that, and, so to speak, chuckles immode- rately up his cleeve, whilst you innocently con- tinue to pay the piper.
TEE -UMBRELLA MAN.

1. Only a few days ago the writer visited the " model "on Friar's Green. To the left at the end of the entrance passage was a long room with forms and tables running along each side and a large stone in the centre. About twenty men were engaged in different matters about the room. Some were sitting at the tables, silently but earnestly plunging into the enjoyments of pickled herring, fried bacon, hot-pot, &c. At the stove stood a man stirring up something which appeared to be amass of boiling rags in a pan. He was not an ordinary- looking roadster. He wore a silk list; judging from its ancient appearance, it was a family heirloom and a little too large for the present possessor, for once or twice when it slipped over his e 3 es he pulled it off his head, and impatiently rammeu pieces of paper into the linings. The frock coat he wore was of a greenish hue, and the sleeves were rolled up so as not to conceal his hands. " That man," said Mr. Brouchemite," is resuscitat- ing old umbrellas. When he came in this after- noon he brought with him a number of old umbrel- las. He would beg them, or give a few coppers for the lot. Those are the covers that he is boiling in a dye. Just now he will take them. out an't dry them. Then he will collect the lost sticks and 'wires together, and by to-morrow at noon he will have fixed covers on them and made them passable second-hand umbrellas. If he hss average luck he will get through all the lot at about 2s. each during the afternoon."

THE TICKET WRITER. ..4.c a table not far away was another man. His head was bent close to the surface of the table ; his somewhat besotted visage bore a look ot earnest concentration. He constantly dipped a small camel hair brush into a saucer containing a mixture of ordinary laundry blue and water; and then he pro- ceeded to fill in the outlines of a black lead sketch of 9s. 6d. which had been drawn upon an oblong piece of cardboard. There were a number of other completed prices lying about the table. This man was what is called a ticket writer. They are a class of men often met in such places. They generally beg small cardboard boxes from benevolent drapers, cut them into squares or oblongs, paint a variety of prices in blue, and then sell them to pawnbrokers or clothiers at about threepence per dozen.

"THE DOCTOR?' I "Do you see that man there? COM 9 and see if yin can tell what he is doing," said the proprietor, and he led the way to a man in his shirt sleeves, whom he saluted thus: "flow do Doctor? How do you 11 find things ?" "Oh, jest slick, gov'nor—fair. hut I business aint overwhelmingly, darn, great shunks. tell yer. See !" The " doctor " continued to pound away at some compound which he was mixing in a wooden vessel. After a while he ceased his opera- tions, and going to his locker, or small cupboard, he came back with a number of small ointment boxes. Without taking much heed of the two on- lookers he perched himself upon the table, charged lan old clay pipe, applied a match to it, and as he smoked on in a meditative manner, he com- menced to scratch off the labels of the boxes. This done he took from his pocket a number of new labels and attached them to the lids of the boxes, and then he commenced to care- fully fill each box with the light-coloured compound. The writer glanced at one of the labels which read " Ointment. I is a speciality ; and non" should be without it. It is acknowledged by medi- cal men to be the best and quickest healer of cuts, bruises, or wounds of any character." It turned out, that the "doctor was one of those travelling healers of the ills that man is heir to, and he often stops in the market on a Saturday night, and philanthropically cures for one penny what physi- cians can't do for pounds. Anyhow, he says, he can when you purchase of him; and when you charge him with fraud the next time you meet him he discoverc that you misrepresented your ailment on the previous occasion. THE DOG-COLLAR MAN.

"You look surprised," said Mr. Brouchemite, light- ing a cigarette, and smiling. "The fact is, my friend, it is in one of these places that you can fully realise the truth of the saying that one haif the world doesn'd know how the other half lives." There was a representative of another profession in this afternoon. I should like to have shown him to you. He is a gentleman who travels from town to town inscribing names on dog's collars. The thing is 'one this way: A specific quantity of muriatic acid and nitric acid is mixed, and formed into a soft wax. The brass part of the collar is first heated, the wax lightly spread over it, and then written through with a broad pen. The wax is then cleaned off, and if the thing has been done properly, the name will be quite legibly inscribed. I remember setting a poor fellow on his feet with that some time ago. It was in winter. I came into the kitchen here, and saw a poor, half- starved-looking fellow sitting on a bench, crying like a child. 'Now, then, what's up ?' I said, 'l'm hard up,' was the reply, and then, between his sobs, he told me that he was a pantomime artiste. Three months before he was playing Pungo the monkey, in 'Sinbad the Sailor,' in one of the Liverpool theatres. His failing, like that of most people who come here, was drink. Owing to his inebriated. condition he made more of an ass of Pungo than a monkey, and he got discharged without salary for negligence. Ile sold his professional skins, and drank the money, and for six weeks before he arrived here he had been on tramp. ' Now, my lad,' said I, 'crying isn't of more account than baby squalling. I'll set you right on fourpence,' and I did. I put a bit myself to his fourpence, bought the acids, made the wax, gave him an hour or two's practice, and sent him out at noon. He came back at night. Ile had 10s. in his pocket, and be was drunk ;so he hadn't done so bad. He left town on the same job two days afterwards."

THE CORNERMAN, ke. These kind of tramps are always the quietest men in the house; but they merely form a section of the class who ate,emble there. You will find there the cornerman and scamp; some born so, and others made 80 by circqmstances. They are the most troublesome men. They depend upon getting their food by either pilfering, bullying, or begging. They suit the method to the individual, i and generally adopt begging when the other man 114 the biggest. When the house was first opened twelve months ago they were ite greatest Pest. They came together in dozens, really to fight either the proprietor and his assistant, or any of the lodgers. But the proprietor who is a man possessing much physical courage and strength, proved to be to the rioters what the laudanum was to the boy—too much. Besides lavishly thrashing them himself, he got for, at least a dozen of them, long terms of imprisonment. Those who got the latter reward appear to hare quite forgotten Mr. Bronchemite, for they never, never, come t* see him now. THE evvr. The most respectable class of lodgers arei the navvies. Except occasionally, when under th be- nign influence of the barm stick on a Saturday night, they never indulge a propensity for rowdy- ism. They turn in for , tea af)out se' en at nignt, play cards and smoke until about half-past gine, turn into bed, and are off to work at four or five o'clock in the morning. Some of them, more modernized than others,don't play cards and smoke. . .

- -- IThey put on their coloured silk kerchiefs,and heavy silver tings, and serge suits, and take systematic courting exercise with 'Arriet or Alice. Of course, there are black sheep in every flock, and those in ..thenavvy flick.chlefly characterize them- selves by the number of pints of beer they drink,' and the extremely scientificznanner in which they Use their rigs. I However, in Brouchemite's Lodging House eine and all are treated fairly and well. There are 76 beclq in the establishment-38 on the second floor, and 38 on the third. Each bed or bunk is in a small, compartment, with all necessary conveniences. The compartments run along each side of the corridor, and are each numbered. Upon payment of 41. the lodgers are given a check number of their bun* and having first removed their boots—when thdy possess them—are each shown their beds. Thire is a warm bath, too, kept near the pay box, and itis open to the free use of all lodgers.

div.head: PROPRIETOR.
div.p: THE PROPRIETOR.

Mr. Alfred Brouchemite, the proprietor, is himself an unusual kind of lodging-house keeper. Hels a Frenchman, and came to Itngland 20 years ago with a carpet bag and a tote- ignorance- of the .English language. Somehow, but without the aid of a tutor, he has now become a proficient English scholar, well versed in British history, ancient, modern, political, and otherwise. Amongst democ- ratic circles in Wigan and Widnes and other Lan- cashire towns where he rune" models,' he is a well- known orator. During the election campaign, he .itn a w halfpenny paper under the head of 'ThetLaoncpaag Lancashire Telephone, edited by A. Brouche- mite." He is what is called a labour man in politics. that is of a socialistic turn, and it requires but a few moments talk on the question with him to show how earnest and well versed he is on the subject. He gives sensible men hard advice- at the "Model," as well as giving notorious characters hard blows. Last year he was an unsuccessful candidate for a seat on the Widnes Local Board.

div.head: WARRINGTON FooTBILL CLUB
div.p: WARRINGTON FooTBILL CLUB
ATHLETIC SPORTS.

The annual athletic sports in connection with the Warrington Football Club, were held in the ground of the club, Wilderspool-road. on Monday after- noon. The weather proved propitious, for, though I there was a slight 8/tower of rain of short duration during the afsernoon, and for -the most part of it the atinsphere was not throughout as bright as could have been de,irel, still with the exception mentioned there was a summery fineness which made tne occasion very enjoyable. It is estimated that the 'spectators numberel nearly 6,000, 'and the number of entries was larger, while they were of a batter character than in any previous year, so that the festival proved a every respect a complete success. Prizes to the amount ot .£lOO were given, and consisted of a large number of beautiful and costly articles, which were arrayed on a table in front of the grand-stand for presentation at the conclusion of the sports. The Warrington United Prize Brass Band was presents and played the following selections of music in ex- cellent style :—Vart 1 : March, " Bostonian ;" over- ture, "The broken chain ;" waltz," Summer Roses ;" I fantasia, "The harvest feast ;" quadrille, " Medusa ;" polka, " Cavendish." Part 11 :—Overture, " Dom ' Pedro ;" waltz, " Fallen leaves ;" fantasia, "The wolf ;" duet, "The village festival ;" quadrille, I Pandora ;" and "God .tive the Queen." The following were the offLnals :—Clerk of the Course Mr. T. Pemberton ; Sutter, Mr. E. Kane; Judges Messrs. Percy Davies. W. Pierpoint, J. Evans, and H Ashton; Committee, Messrs. W. Hewitt, J. W. Evans W. Speakman, T. Bowers, W. Antrobus, F. Barnes, jun. Geo. Smith, John Holmes, T. DAvies, John Boyle, J. T Bate, H. Howe W. Povey, E. Gil iert, and J. Jolley Handicappers, T. it Sutton and J. H. Hardwick: Hon. Treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton; Hon. Secretary, Mr. ,J. E. Warren; referee, Mr. T. R. Sutton. Tne sports commenced at two o'clock, and finished about seven ;o'clock.

The events were as follows :- 100 Yards Local Elandicap.—Twelve heats and a final: confined to persons who have resided over six mouths , within a radius of six miles from Warrington. First prize, clock; second prize, cheese, butter, and biscuit jar; third prize, biscuit box (Doulton's ware). 1, A. J. Mottram, Warrington, St yards ; 2, T. Sudlow, scratch; 3, H. Webster, scratch. rune 10 3-5 seconds. 100 YARDS HANDICAP.—FifLeED heats and a final : First prize, tea and coffee set and tray ; second psize, six-cup egg frame; third prize, two fruit spoons and case. 1. E. H. Williams. Crewe, Alexander, A.C., 8 yards ; 2, T. R. Allen, Warrington. 9 yards; 3, T. Sod- low, Wigan F.C., 7 yards. Time 10 seconds. ONE MILE BICYCLE HANDICAP. —Four heats and a final: First prize, gold cuain ; second prize, case of fish car- vers and crumb scoop; third prize, claret jug. 1, H. Brown, Leyland, 155 yards; 2. G. Blakey, Southport, 150 yards ;-3, J. Buxton, Warrington, 155 yards. Length; length and a half. Time 2 mm. 46 sec. This was a most exciting race and was remarkable for one incident, E. Broadhead of Manchester giving in during the 4th lap of theist heat. 220 YARDS MAIDEN HANDICAP.—Five heats and a dual: First prize, lamp and stitde ; second prize, ink- stand ;third prize, tankard. 1, R. liiratwood, Man- chester Press A.C., 27 yards; 2, James Houghton. Latchford, 20 yards : 3, J. T. Westall, Warrington, 17 yards. Won by a yard and the same between second and third. In the first heat of this race J. J. Deakin, of Widnes, a mere boy, whose pluck in competing with so many older runners was mucii admired, took part, and a feeling of regret was felt that his spirited pitting of himself against them did not meet with some reward. 220 YARDS Mimosas' Kans.—Three heats and a final: —First prize, tea urn; second prize, salad. bowl; third prize; carvers (three pieces) ; fourth prize, fish carvers: 1, J. T. Westall, n yards; 2, E. Osborne, Warrington, 2 yards; 3,5. Holmes, 8 yards; 4,J. Thornton, 11 yards, won by a yard. ONE MILK HANDICAP.—First prize, tea and coffee set; second prize, fruit and flower stand; third prize, hot water jug: 1, A. J. McKee, Belfast, 105 yards; 2, J. ,H. Fair, Warrington, 102 yards; 3, Joseph Marney, Sale Harriers, 125 yards. Won by a yard and a half. Time, 4min. 25:sec. This race was signaliwd by the competition in it of W. U. Morton, of the Salford Harriers, the 20 mites champion of the world, who was allowed 45 yards less start than the competitor in front of him. Morton's style was beautiful to look ' at, his fine, swinging, striding pace covering the ground admirably ; and towards the close of the race he, with- 'Out apparent straining, put on an amazing spurt, and seemed likely to win, but the effort proved too much for him, and he fell further behind. 440 Yantis flasmcap.—Two heats and a final: First prize, case of cutlery (53 pieces) ; second prize, ram's horn inkstand ; third prize, sugar basket : 1, D. Barr, Southport, 28 yards ; 2, J. Wightman, Warrington Har- riers, 26 yards • 3, George Ashworth, St. Anne's-on-the- Sea, 35 yards. Won by half a yard. Time, 501 seconds. _ -

IWO MILES BICYCLE HANDICAP.—Four heats and a final. First prize, gold watch; second prize, six-glass cruet ; third prize, cruet frame: 1, W. H. Snaps, Skel- mersdale, 270 yards; 2, E. Blakey,Southport,2Bo ycli.; 3, J.Buxton,Warrington,29o yds. Won by half a yard. Time. . smin. 28secs. In the first heat of this race, which was a very exciting one, W. J. Bellian, of Warrington, was leading, when he had a fall, and two other competitors fell on him. This, giving the others an advantage, As Whitehead, of Bolton, managed to come in winner, but by such an extraordinary distance, that it seemed that even had the accident not occurred, lie might have ac- complished the feat. In the final of the race, Hollins Allen,of Warrington,had a slip when he had only covered one lap. 380 Yenos HaNiarcae.—First prize: Two cake dishes and covers ; second prize, biscuit box • third prize, Tankard. J. Clark, v. Widnes St. Mary's F.. 0 50 • 1 yards. 2, F. Smith, Sale, 48 yards 3, H. Gretna% wigan, 48 yards. Won by two yards. Time 1 min. 581.5 sec. At the close of the sports, the Mayoress, with whom the Mayor (Alderman (Ireenall) was present, presented the prizes to the successful competitors. On the con- clusion of this ceremony, Mr. P. Davies, president of the club, said he had very great pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks tothe Mayoress for the graceful manner in , which she had presented ths prizes. He was sure they would fed with him that that duty could not have been fulfilled better, than she had done it, and he, as presi- dent of the football club,felt very proud to see her there, and hoped to have the pleasure of seeing her there again. He was sure they could not wish to see a handsomer lady than the Mayoress to take ttuipart she had done. and they would all agree wi:h him that she deserved a very hearty vote of thanks. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Morris seconded the proposition. Be remarked that the Mayoress had performed , her part so gracefully that he felt that he should like to be a recipient of a prize from her himself, and he hoped she would come many times, and can inue to come so long as she lived in Warrington. (Appause.) The proposition was carried with hearty acclamation. The Mayor, who was mcuh aopiauded. on commixing to speak, said he thanked them for he kind way in which they had received Mrs. E. Gr. mall, the Ma 3 oress of Warrington, and he was sure it I,ad given her the greatest pleasure to be amongst th na that day. He thought it wa. not necessary for h.m to ,x lain how much interest she took in local mt. ers. Aat lultVt she was president of the ladies' committee in con: action with a bazaar which was to came on ii aid of tit.. viral- nasium. He thanked them all for so kin ly re (riving him He was always ready to do the bat he cold for the town and t perform his duty with the greatest efficiency that he could. (applause.) After three. hearty cheers for the Mayes the crowd dispersed.

A Bishop THE Bishop of Chester has views on of his own on the drink question. Licensing. Some time ago he intimated that he should like to have a hand in the management of a well conducted public-house. He spoke as if such a thing was a rarity; but we frankly admit, while recognising that there are far too many licensed houses, that some of them are carried on man unexceptionable manner. Bishop JAvNE,in a letter to the " Times," has now propounded a notable scheme for dealing with licensing as a whole. His scheme is a sweeping one; but there is no likelihood of its being accepted in its present form. It involves, to quote his own words, "a complete reconstruction of our public-house sys- tem." He says :

Licensed victualling must change hands. Experience has abundantly shown that private enterprise cannot bear the weight of this vast national responsibility. The State, through its local authorities and instrumentalities, must with a firm and liberal hand undertake the provision of houses of refreshment for the people, in which alcoholic beverages, though frankly recognised, will be deposed from their aggressive supremacy and supplied under less seductive conditions. These conditions would, for example, be comfortable, spacious, well-ventilated accommodation; temper- ance drinks of every kind brought well to the front, invested with prestige, and supplied in the most convenient, attractive, and inexpensive way ; the pecuniary interest of the managers (e.g., in the form of bonus) made to depend entirely on the sale of eatables and non-alcoholic beverages; alcoholic liquors secured against adulteration ; newspapers, indoor games, and, where practicable, outdoor games and music provided ; while the mere drink shop, the gin palace, and " the bar "—that pernic- ious incentive to drinking for drinking's sake— would be utterly abolished.

The scheme is a very pretty one on paper ; but there are some difficulties in the way, and some things to be explained,before it can be regarded as within the region of things practical. It is easy to say that "licensed victualling must change hands"; but the old question crops up—What about compensation for loss of license ? If the Bishop, knowing the law admits of no vested in- terest in a license, is opposed to compensation, he should say so ; and he will then ascertain who are with him and who are against him, at the very threshold. If, on the other hand, he proposes that the State,through its local authorities,should, as a preliminary step,. buy up every existing license, he will find that neither State nor Munici- pality would look at a plan which would be costly to the verge of ruin.

Further, it may be asked, why should the pecu- niary interest of the manager be made to" depend entirely upon the sale of eatables and non-alcoho- lic beverages r' The bishop's answer would, we assume, be that, if the manager had no interest in "pushing" the sale of drink, there would be less drunkenness; and the conclusion, is a sound one. But it would be scarcely fair to the business as a whole to make an invidious distinction ; and it would certainly lead to non-alcoholic drinks be- ing sneered at and jeered at by those who like some- thing more stimulating. There is,. besides, another factor which the bishop would have to reckon with at the outset; and that is aversion—the strong iiversionon the part of a large section of the public to have any part or lot in the traffic in drink. It is this feeling, which prevents the Gothen berg system receiving due consideration in this coun- try—a system far less objectionable than that pro- posed by the Bishop of CH EST.3II. Under the Gothenberg plan,.the ratepayers would control the traffic without being traders in alcoholic liquor. They would determine on the number of licenses 'in a particular town or district ; and leave it to a I Limited Company to conduct the licensed houses under the regulations to be laid down. This Company would.receive 5 per cent, and no more, after all expenses had been paid; and would there- fore have no interest in encouraging drinking with a view to increased gains. Yet, as experience shows, the gains would be great, and they would go to the improvement of the-town, the mainten- ance of Parks, Libraries, Art Galleries, &,c. All the ends which, the bishop aims at could be accom- plished without seriously offending the suscepti- bilities of those who would regard it as an outrage if the State, or the Municipality owned and con- ducted public-houses on behalf of the ratepayers. Having gone so far, the bishop should certainly go a step further, and support the Gotbenberg plan out and; oat. Mr. C DIA,MBERJAIN was amongst the first to advocate the system in this country ; and MI. HOUSTON mads- a most favourable impres- sion when he detailed as advantages to the mem- bers of the Warrington Liberal Council. Its fair- ness i&so obvious, andas merits are so great, that it is a matter of surprise to us that it has not been niece generally advocated by politicians and public' speakers, irrespective of party. Perhaps it needs to be countenanced by a dignitary of the Church ; and we trust that Bishop JAYNE having gone two, : thirds of the way will go the whole way, and be- come an earnest apostle of the new gospot of temperance.

THE first Monday in August is be- Bank Holiday. coming a formidable rival of Whit Monday as a general holiday. It seemed a small matter at first to make provision for banks being closed on that day ; but the closing movement has "caught on "—to use a current phrase—so that August Bank Holiday laas become the second great holiday of the year. It is a matter of course that the great rush for a change should be to the sea-side ; for love of the sea is in an English- man's blood. He lives on a small island, and when he wants what he would call a complete change he believes he can best secure it by going for a short time on a smaller island—to be hugged,so to speak, by the sea. Hence the hunger and thirst, when

August arrives, for a visit to the Isle of Man. Unfortunately for those who make their stay at Douglas, it is, to a certain extent, simply an exchange from the bustle of one town to the bustle of another, For Douglas has become a, large and busy centre of activity, in " the season/ and it is not the place f6r those who requiro rest as well as change of scene and air. Another thing which should be borne in mind is that a sudden influx of visitors to a health resort is not in itself healthy. Sanitary arrangements which aro good for 20,000 persons are the reverse of good when they are called upon to do duty for .10,00 ;CUd it therefore sometimes happens that the last state of. the visitor is worse than the first. Certain evils and discomforts have, it is true, a tendency to right themselves. For instance, after a great influltr special provision is usually made for next year, : when there is, most likely, a falling off in the number of visitors, with the result that there le inure elbow room and better accommodqtiou

Monday last was not perhaps an ideal day for Bank Holiday, but the weather was on the wil°le good, and that means that some hundreds of thousands of people had an opportunity OP thoroughly enjoying themselves. And what facilities for travel are afforded by the Ball" way Companies! They have at any rate risen' to the occasion, with the result that choice' is practically unlimited. And what if trains are late ? The danger of accident is now. reduced to a minimum, and, besides, there is so much more for the money. There is one drawbacli abot this journeying to and fro, and that is people. are becoming less and less inclined to use their limbs. Indeed walking from place to place is nes/ out of the question if there is a train, or a trap; or a waggonette to be had. And yet walking charms which nothing else can give; not walking on the dusty highway merely to cover so DOI miles; but walking in bowery lanes, throng meadows and woods, and along tho banks of th.o beautiful rivers for which our beloved land famous. Use the railway by all means to get W.Ol away from the madding crowd; and then stri.ke. out into a choice bit of country, with a few choice friends ; and if you have a soul open to the he3.ll_ ties of nature and that free converse which In eludes— Mirth which wrinkled care derides And laughter holding both her ides— .11 you have the conditions of a holiday which secure happiness at the time, and boa WO memory hereafter. Thera are people, to be sure; who say they cannot walk ; but if they are n% diseased or lame,that simply means that theYdeter_ ar lazy. And as to the laziness let them be mined and work it off; and they will be aa sn.r: prised as they are pleased with the result, It I no doubt, rather hard, after a bath of fresh air a° f feasting one's eyes on the unsullied lovelineaa na nature, to come back to the whiff of the slums r the ugliness of town life. But what then ?. a glimpse ot paradise than never a thought of 10; and it is only when when we fully realise that °to slums degrade us that we shall set earneseY work to get rid of them. vet

The crop of election petitions is now pretty Plentiful ; but that which ranks first in interest is the one presented against the return of the Right lion. A. J. Balfour for the East Division of Man- °heater. It alleges bribery,treating, intimidation, and general corruption, before, during, and after the election. It will find the Tory leader some- thing to think about until the verdict is given.

It is very difficult to prove treating, 86c., by !gents even when, ordinarily speaking, there can ?6 no doubt about it. Whenever proof can be furnished, it is the duty of party managers to take :proceedings ; for if the Corrupt ,Practices Act is allowed. to become a dead letter honest 'Politicians will hesitate to enter iota ft` 'contest for Parliamentary "honours.' He is a ; and believes' things would soon right "enaselves if bimetallism were adopted.

The cry of " bad trade "on the part of cotton I.lesoufacturers is as old as the trade itself. Thera 1,2 a good story told• of a Blackburn builder who a witness in an important arbitration case. uross-examined es to the cotton trade being bad ite said :—" Well, it's so bad that if it ,gets much worse we shall all be run over." The children attending the Sunday school in connec- tion with the Runcorn Seamens Institute had their annual treat on Monday when about 400 were conveyed in boats along the Bridgewater Canal to London Bridge, Grappenhall and Lymm. A most enjoyable .day was spent. Mr. W. Shaw the missionary carried out the arrangements. JOSEPH PRITCHARD has the best stook :of ladles' silver and gold watches in the town.—Advt. POLICE ti. TRADESMEN AT WIDNES. This annual cricket match took place on Widnes crickee ground on Thursday, but failed to attract that patronage of former years. The police went first to the wickets and ended by Yates of Lancashire County, who made 19, compiled a score of 48. The Tradesmen won very easily their total score reading 101. " Jack " Briggs was on the ground and came in for hearty con- gratulations for his brilliant performance against York- shire at the beginning of the week. Joe yen PRITCHARD keeps spectacles to sill all sights from a shilling a air.—Advt. BANK HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN AND WIDNF.S. Bank Holiday was observed as a general holiday in Runcorn and Widnes, and advantage was taken of the railway facilities afforded to visit the various pleasure resorts in the district. A very large number were booked to Liverpool, where the Lancashire Agricultural Show was the chief attraction. The only amusement provided at home was the annual gala in connection with St, Mary's Roman Catholic Young Men's Society, and it was fairly well patronised. The amnsements consisted of three-legged races, sack races, obstacle races, tug of war, climbing the greasy poll, izc. The weather,though dull, was fine.
If you wantyour watch repaired by skilful workmen, take it to PRITCHARO.—Advt.

DEATH OF MRS. LEICESTER AT RUNURN. Mrs. Leicester, of Leicester Gardens, Runcorn, died on Thursday morning at the advanced age of 92 years. The deceased lady belonged to the old Runcorn family of Rigby, and her recollections of the town went back to the time when the place was much resorted to by those in search of health from its invigorating breezes, and the capital bathing afforded by the Mersey. She had seen the green fields and smiling orchards disappear before the advance of civilization, until Runcorn became the home of soap and chemicals. Mr. John Rigby, M.P., is nephew of the deceased lady, who leaves two sons one of whom is Mr. John Leicester draper, of High-st.

The half-yearly-n;Wiin—g—oFTl7e—P;Oprietors of this Company was held at the Gas Office on Thursday. Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., chairman of directors presided and there were present Messrs. James Handley, J.P., (vice-chair- man), James Pritchard, Thomas Handley, W. Whittaker, J. M. Frith and J. R. Frith (secretary and manager). In their report the directors state that the business of the Company continued to be satisf mtory and they recom- mended the payment of the usual dividend at the rate of 10 per cent, per annurn.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and said the new gasholders was completed and at work, and satisfactory pro- gress was being made with the pew works.—The Vice-Chairman seccnded the motion which was carried On the motion of the Vice-chairman seconded by Mr. Pritchard, the retiring directors—Messrs. Rigby and ' Thomas Handley—were re-elected. The retiring auditor Mr. W. Handley, was re-appoiuted on the motion of the Chairman seconded by Mr. W. Whittaker. A cordial vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and also to the secretary and manaaer. The gas holder mentioned by the Chairman has been erected by Messrs. R. and J. Dempster, of Manchester, and has been a most expedi- tious piece of work. The contract for its construction was not made until April Bth, and as the chairman remarked it was now at work.

Go to PRITCHARD'S for the best five guinea watch a work- ingman can have.—Advt. FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORIES. About half-past nine on Monday morning the " resin shed" of Messrs. Hutchinson's Chemical works of the United Alkali Co., Widnes, was discovered to be on fire. The flames spread with great rapidity and soon a. num- I ber of barrels of resin which were stored in the shed added to the conflagration. The works fire brigade under the command of Mr. A. G. Kyle, were at w )rk a few minutes after the outbreak was discovered, and an immense quantity of water from the adjoining canal was poured over the burning pile. Several police con- staples in charge of Inspector Pattison and Sergeant Strickland also lent valuable aid. Near the scene of the fire were several oil condensers and about 1,200 barrels of resin, but the prompt and welt directed efforts of the firemen saved them from becoming ignited. By eleven o'clock the shed and its contents had become completely demolished and the damage is very heavy. The Widnes Fire Brigade were sent for but they arrived too late to be of any service. Although there were several men engaged in the shed, the origin of the fire is a mystery, but it is stated as probably caused by the overheating of some pipes. Fires have originated in this department on several previous occasions, but they have started so suddenly that no clue as to their cause has been gained. The firemen deserve every credit for their labour as the continual falling of debris and the suffocating fumes of smoke from the burning 1 resin made their work highly unpleasant and dangerous.

That the festival of Saint Lubbock, ü Hank Holi- day is frequently termed,is becoming more and more a general holiday in this district, and on Monday there were far more players thanworkers in the in- dustrial hives of launcorn and Widnes.
That the weather turned out much better than the weatherwise expected, and those who toox advan- tage of the excursions provided, spent an enjoyable day.

That a considerable number of tradesmen cora= plain that the closing of the Runcorn Docks has most injuriously affected their business, and it is a certain fact that, notwithstanding the facilitie. afforded by the Ship Canal Co. for communication between Weston Point and Weston, there are very few of the seafaring community to be seen in the town.

That only one thing remains to be done,and that is to make the best of a bad job, and to hope that the engineers will hurry on the river works, and let the trade of the port return to its usual course quickly.
That an optimistic view of the situation is that the Runcorn Docks will not be re-opened for twelve months! What would a pessimist say?
That the Runcorn Commissioneri, on Thursday, took a step towards having a number of streets made. And not before it was needed say I acd many others.

That the golden pill awarded at Liverpool Assizes will do much to drive out the dirty water, Dr. O'Keeffe, Mr. Wright, and Mr. Neil swallowed when. thrown into the Sankey Canal several , nths ago. What was Mr. Neil doing to receive Tnn than his brother divers?

That perhaps Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. Wright will do the " Continong " togettier now instead of being " baked "on the MediterPaisean coast ; or will they take Mr. Bighain's advice and go to B,)utliport Sands?
That as the School Board and Municipal dections are coining on, perhaps they had better not travel far away, as they may be needed.
THE SECOND CHESHIRE RIFLE VOLUNTEERS IN CAMP. (Continued from Page 6)

, ,The reveille sounded at five o'clock on Monday morning, and the week's training at Douglei, Isle of Man, commenced in earnest. , The efforts of the buglers, at six in the morning, were supplemented by the services of the drum and lite baud, which paraded the camp playing a lively air. At half- past ten the men were marshalled, under the Colonel commanding, and then were put through battalion drill on the beautifully situated drill ground at Port-e-Chee. The march to and from the drill ground was not relished by many of the men, in consequence of the excessive heat, and the consequent dusty state of the road. The three o'clock drill amounted to a march out to the parade ground and back; and the men, ex- cepting theee who were allotted special duty in connec- tion with the guard and picket, were at liberty for the rest of the evening. This freedom was, of course, taken advantage of to the full, and the different places of amusement in Douglas had a good sprinkling of red coats among their audiences. The other days during the week were spent in much similar fashion. On Tuesday. at the second parade, however, the attack formation was gone through, under Majors Hazlehurst and .lolliffe, 'and Captain White, the Colonel having left camp upon having received a tele- gram that his wife whom he left at home in a delicate state of health, had been taken most seriously ill. lie left by the nine o'clockboat for Liverpool, but a gloom was cast over the camp at two o'clock by a message which was received announcing Mrs. Ashton's death. • The attack formation, and especially the volley firing, was remarkably well performed, particularly considering the fact that the battalion had not had a previous op- portunity of concerted practice. The company drill on Tuesday had to be abandoned on account of a-downfall of rain, which did not affect the town of Douglas. ' On Wednesday there was no afterno.in parade, and the men had a balf-holiday. This was because there had been an exceedingly heavy drill at the half-past ten parade. On Wednesday additional officers arrived in the per- sons of Surgeon King and Lieutenant Clough. The inspection took place at Port-e-CheC. on Friday, before Colonel Brownlow, commanding the 22ad Regi- mental District, Chester.

The Medical Officer (Dr. M.;Dou-galit reported that during July there were 37 deaths, of wilkh two were inquest cases ; of the remaining 35 deaths s were due to mesenteric disease, 6 to diarrhce I, 2 to convulsi ms, 2 to cancer, 2 to bronchitis, 2 to jaundice, 2 to inflam- motion of the lungs, 2 to ianatntuation of the bowels, 2 to inflammation of the lining rnembrance of the brain, and one each to natural dccay, incinha- nous, croup, typhoid, inherited disease, heart disease, blood disease, debility, and two diseases of uncertain origin, The 37 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 222, and exclusive of the inquest cases of 21 per 1,000 of the estimated population. lIIGIIWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE. This Committee recommended that the footway of the west side of Regent-st., be flagged and that S. Snow. ball's price for flagging, is. 6d. per sup. yard be accepted ; that the tender of Messrs. H. Heys and Co. for 3in. best barn flags at 53. per sup. yard, less 24 per cent, discount, be accepted ; that the Board advertise for an assistant Surveyor for one year at a salary at the rate of £l5O per annum, to devote his time more par- ticularly to the preparation of plans, specifications, and quantities in respect of the private streets requiring to be made ; that the plan of Mr. Robert Ingham for the erection of four cottages in Dale-st., be approved :1 that the plan of Mr. George Marshall for the conversion ,of Beaconsfield House into two houses be approved. Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minu:es, and, referring to the proposed appointment of an assistant surveyor, said there were about 30 new streets required to be made and they all knew that it was utterly impos- sible for Mr. Barker to do the work within a reasonable time, so the Committee had concluded that they had better get someone for twelve months.—Mr. Grice ' seconded the motion and said the assistant surveyor's salary would really cost the ratepayers nothing. There was a margin of 11 per cent, between the rate of inter- est paid by the Commissioners and the rate they charged, and the advantage derived from this arrangement would be a very great one to the ratepayers. Anyone could see that during the past few years some of the streets had been in a terribly bad condition—many required to be made—and ho thought the public would appreciate the movement of the Committee in this business.—The minutes were approved. -- On the recommendation Ji the Duke of Rutland, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, her 'Majesty !vas appointed Mr. William Wilbraham Blethyn Hutton, IP., D.L., of Hutton Park, near Bolton; to the historic and ancient office of Constable of Lan- caster Castle, rendered vacant by the death of Lord Winmarleigh. div.head: SALVATTON ARMY DICILONSTRATION.
div.p: SALVATTON ARMY DICILONSTRATION.

About 2,000 members, principally from Liver- pool, with contingents from Warrington. Earles- town, Widnes, St. Helens, Present, Runcorn, and Matto Heath, arrived at.Huyton Railway Station and marched to a large Held on Grasmere Park, ac- companied by seven brass bands, where, American camp meetings and various religious exercises were gone through, interspersed with outdoor games. The proceedings were conducted by Colonel Boon, chief secretary for the Liverpool radius of the Army. Major Holden, provincial secretary, and Mrs. Major Miles. Several thousands of visitors wended their way and took part in the demonstration dur- ing the afternoon. GALLANT RRsCUR FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN

A gallant rescue from drowning took place at the Ship Canal Works at the Sprinch on Wednesday. Screams were heard proceeding from the direction of Victoria Bridge. and Thomas Burrows, a ship- wright, ran to the spot, and seeing a child floating under the structure he dived into the water with- out divesting himself of any clothing, seized the drowning child, and swam to the side, where he handed it to some of the men who had witnessed his brave act. Life was nearly extinct, but the usual means for restoration of respiration were used successfully, and the youngster, who, it transpired, was John Brock, aged 3 years, son of a shipwright living in Surrey-st , was taken home. Mr. Burrows was highly praised for his manly deed. ATTACKED BY A DOG AT DARESBURY. _ _

Mr. Richard Abel, of Tower House, Runcorn, met with a serious accident on Saturday last. In com- pany with Mr. John Dykes, Mr. Abel paid a visit to his friend Mr. C. Phillips of the Ring o' Daresbury, and together the three gentleman paid a visit to the garden. On returning Mr. Abel was taking a "short cut " across the coal heap when the coal gave way beneath him and he slipped down to the dog kennel. The dog,a large black retriever, at once set npon him, and before Mr. Phillips who was in advance could come to his rescue the animal had inflicted several wounds upon his face, which bled most profusely. Mr. Abel at once drove to Runcorn, and placed himself under the care of Robinson, and he is satisfactorily recovering from the serious injury he received.

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB FOR NEWTON.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB FOR NEWTON.

The proposal to start a Liberal club in Newton has now become an accomplished fact, and ere many, weeks have passed, we hope to see the effort fully patronised. Several meetings in turtherance of the object have been held, resulting in the selec- tion of the good working committee, with Mr. G. Bowyer as secretary. Suitable premises have been , secured opposite the Town Hall, and a good list of names of intending members has been obtained. It Is intended to open the club, simply as a political meeting place, but in addition to newspapers,games will be provided for those who care to indulge in the pastime. Mr. Luffman is the principal spirit in the movement, and it is expected he will be appointed as president. The subscription for hon- orary members has been fixed at the low rate of 2s. per annum,and far members who desire to make use of the club at 4s. per annum. THE ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN BARMAN: EXEMPLARY SENTENCE.

At the Liverpool Summer Assizes, in the Crown Court, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Denman, John Ward and Bernard McGee were indicted for having assaulted W illian3 Henry Smith, and robbed him of .£.s.—The prosecutor, who resides in Run- corn, was returning from Liverpool Races on the 21st July, and when between Aintree and Sandhills the prisoners, it was alleged, set upon him in the railway carriage. Waite they were assaulting him £5 was taken out of his pocket.—The jury found the prisoners guilty.—llis lordship said he found as regarded McGee that he was a tremendously accomplished gaol bird, and he must go to penal servitude for rive years. Ward was a younger man, but a very dangerous character. Ile must go to penal servitude for three years. Lawn Mowers. —GARLAND, hortieuural ironmonger, War. rington•

A ST. HELENS BANKRUPT RELEASED FR03.1 PRISON. On Friday, at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, Mr. Thomas Roberts, builder and contractor, of North-road, St. Helens, applied to his Honour Judge Collier, through Mr. Septiton, to be released from Walton Gool. The bankrupt was in attendance in charge of a warder. The motion was opposed by Mr. Malkin, on behalf the trustee (Mr. Marsh). The bankrupt had been a builder and contractor at Sr. Helens, and was committed to gaol for contempt of court in not complying with an order to supply the trustee with certain information. He had been in Real for three weeks, and Mr. Sephton, on his be- half, now urged that he was unable to give the trustee any more information that he had supplied, and made an appeal to the court, one of his points being that the bankrupt had an invalid wife, who had to be kept in ignorance of his imprisonment for fear of the consequences to her. His Honour said the commital of anyone to gaol was kale of the most disagreeable of his duties, and one he was reluctant to exercise. Ile would release the bankrupt now, but warned him that if he did not supply the ipfor- mation to the trustee, that gentleman could apply again for his committal. His Honour concurred with the trustee in thinking the bankrupt was keeping something back.• EXTRAORDINARY STORY BY A RUNCORN NEws.

_ BOY. • Wm. Ilerringshaw, a boy in the employ of Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son at the railway station book- stall, was sent on his usual 'round to Weston end Weston Point, on Saturday morning, but loe failed to return either to ", he station or to his home at 5 Chaucer-st. Inquiries were set on:foot but nothing could be ascertained as to his whereabouts. About half-past ten, on Sunday morning, a navvy named Wm. Brown found the canvas bag containing news- papers, books, &c., which had been in possession of the missing boy, and P.C. Hammersley dragged the canal in that place until evening, but without re- sult. The speculations as to his death by drown- ing or otherwise were set at rest at 10 p.m., on Sunday, when he returned to his home and made a statement that he had been stopped on the cane' bank by a navvy who robbed him of 10s. (11 he had collected for his employers, and afterwards threwhim into the water, from which he was res- cued by a boatman, and taken to a house at Weston Point, where he had stopped until that time. On Monday morning when questioned by the police, he retrae ed this statement, and admitted that he had been to Liverpool where he bad spent 35.6 d. He handed over the rem tining 7s. It is improbable that the foolish boy will be prosecuted, but he has lost hie eituation.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
LIVERPOOL PILOTS ON THE CANAL.

Cn Saturday a deputation of pilots consisting of a representative from each cf the pilot boats in the Liver- pool piloting service visited the Ship Canal works. The , primary object of the deputation was to confer with the manager (Mr. Marshall Stevens) with the object of ascertaining whether the Ship Canal Company would , arrange forthe employment of the services of the Liver- pool 'pilots for piloting vessels over the Ship Canal in continuance of their voyage from the sea. The party left the Liverpool Lauding-stage at 9A5 a.m. in the steam tender Fanny, and passed over the entrance channel of,the Ship Canal at dead low water. This is the first occasion on which a vessel has been able tn obtain access to the canal at low water, the dredging of the channel to the 501 t lock having been completed the previous tide. The vessel was raised in the lock 191 t. 6in: to the level of the canal in seven minutes,,and pro- ceeded to the point Which has recently been cluistGeed Saltport. From thence the party went over the works to Manchester. They were, we are informed, fully satisfied in regard to the easinessof the navigation of the canal for vessels of large tonnage.

div.head: NAVVIES UNION.
div.p: THE NAVVIES UNION.

In connection with the Lancashire and Midland Conn- tits district, of the Navvies, Bricklayers, Labourers and General Labourers Union meetings were held at the Big Field, Norton, on Sunday Morning, and in Devonshire Square, Runcorn. in the afternoon. A number of the .members walked in procession through the town headed by the Patricroft Public Band. Mr. A. Blacklock Hayes presided and addresses were delivered by Mr. John Ward, of London, president of the Union, and Mr. E. Cheadle, district secretary. The ad vantages of combina- tion Were pointed out, and examples of the benefits con- ferred by the Navvies Unima were described. About a hundred new members were enrolled.

THE VIEWS OF TFIE "TIMES." Referring to Sir John Harwood's report the "Times " Says :—" The difficulty,- no doubt, will be confronted iLrid overcome, for it may be assumed that the undertak- ing has gone too far to be abandoned whatever burdens in may entail, but the prospects of the original share- holders are dark enough, and the interference of the Corporation will in all probability involve a heavy tax upon the ratepayers of Manchester for many years to come. Lancashire will have its Ship Canal, -Manzhester will boast of being a sea part, and when the lately pro- jected schema for a railway across England between the cotton capital and Lincolnshire) coast has been carried out, as it undoubtedly will be, a great development of the facilities for internal trade will be effected. But a high price must be paid for these luxuries of modern civilisation.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO. SIR JOHN HARWOOD.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO. SIR JOHN HARWOOD.

, At a meeting af the Manchester City Council held on Wednesday, on the minutes of the special committee re Manchester Ship Canal being considered, Councillor i Gutman said he supposed that, n the ordinary course, the report of the committee regarding the canal would mime before the next Meeting of the Council. He wanted to suggest that instead a /medal meeting of the Council should be called to discuss such an important subject. The Mayor (Alderman Boedin T. Leech) said he had no doubt that the matter would be borne in mind, and it was understood that a special meeting will be held.— The ordinary report of the committee, which referred to details of finance, was passed without comment. At a , subsequent period of the meeting a communication was received from the Mayor (Alderman Bosdin T. Leech?, intimating his acceptance of a directorship of the Ship Canal. When the business of the meeting had concluded,' the members adjourned to the banqueting hall, where lunthean having been served, an interesting ceremony took place. ,It consisted of the presentation by the Mayor, as rejaresenting the corporation, of a full-length portrait of Sir John Harwood, the cost of which has been defrayed by subscription. The presentation was made in recognition of the public services of Sir John, who is now directing his high abilities to the task of pilot- ing the canal undertaking through the troublous time it is experiencing.—The Mayor formally made the pre- sentation, and an appreciative address to Sir John was read by Alderman Ileywood.—Alderman Sir John Har- wood replied at length to the eulogistic remarks that had been offered:

div.head: FRODSIIAM,
div.p: FRODSIIAM,

THE UNION CHURCH.—In connectioniwith the above,the annual services on behalf of the Sunday school were held on Smithy, when the Rev. John Yonge, of IVarrington, preached afternoon and evening to very good congrega- tions. The collections realized £l5 4s. 61.

Havrop Nausea Cnuaca.—On Sunday special services were held at this church, when sermons were preached by the Bev. 8. Wilkinson, vicar of Timperley. In the morning the collection was on behalf of the Chester Infirmary, and in the evening it was for the Church Building Society. In the afternoon there was a flower service, when an offertory was taken for the University Mission, Central Africa. ALLEGED THEFT FECAL A LODGING-HOLTSE.—At Frocl- sham Police Court, on Thursday morning, before Mr. A. Tlic.mas, Mary Ellen Taylor was charged with stealing a gnantity of clothing, value 10s.' the property of Moses- OntinskY, hawker, between 7 o'clock on Wednesday night and 8.30 that morning, from a lodging-house, in Frodsham. Sufficient evidence having been given to justify a remsnd, the case was adjourned until Tuesday DaAnr. or Mos, A enToN.—We regret to leave the sad duty of recording the death of 'Mts. Mice AShtne, wile of Colonel Ashton solicil or and magistrates' clerk as .ftuncorn and Froclsfiam. For sonic months Mrs. Ashton had been in delicate health, but nothing serious was apprehended until midnight on Monday, when she was suddenly taken very ill, and Dr. Robinson was celled in. Despite the efforts of that gentleman, she rapidly sank, and diertabout two er'clock. Colopel Islaton aied his son, Mr. Cieorge Ashton, were aw.;y with the Volunteers in camp at Douglas, and they were summoned home by telegram. Mrs. Ashton, who had taken a prominent part in Church matters, and had until recently been secretary of the Frodsham Primrose League, in connec- tion with which she achieved much success. The greatest sympathy is expressed for Colonel Ashton and his family in their bereavement. Tne deceased lady was 40 years of age. div.head: PENKET.H.
div.p: PENKET.H.

CHILDREN'S TAR AT. Yesterday week the scholars of the infant school held their annual tea party. The children, under the superintendence of Miss Burns. the schoolmis- tress, and Miss blarion Foster, the pupil teacher, were marched down to Miss Tinsley's garden, where they went through exercises and drill for the bene- fit of the ladies assembled. The children had tea on the lawn, and dispersed in good time, having en- joyed themselves very much,

div.head: SIICCEBBFUL LOCAL_ ATHLETN.
div.p: A SIICCEBBFUL LOCAL_ ATHLETN.

On Monday, at Huyton annual sports, Mr.W.Jack- son, of Penketh, distinguished himself by carrying off the first prize in the, 2-mile bicycle handicap. The prize is a beautifully-chased metal tea-pot. As this is the first time he beisracecl,the ,4uccess is more appreciated. He rode a "Raglan" pneumatic, lent to him by Mr. T. Earns. Mr. H. Stanley, also of Penketh, ran very well, winning his heat in the quarter-mile Hat race in fine style, but was unfor- tunate in the final.

in the final. EXCURSION TO DELA MERE FOREST. On Monday a party left Penketh to spend the holiday at Delamere Forest. Though rain fell rather heavily shortly after leaving home, the shower soon passed over. Mr. Joseph Pownall, of Brookside Farm, organised the trip, and about thirty persons accompanied him to the favourite Cheshire resort. On their arrival, about 11.30 a.m. the party went direct to the Abbey Arms, and indulged in dancing until dinner, which was a most substantial one, provided by the proprietor, Mr. Wilson.• In the afternoon the lake, forest, and the militia camp came in for a large share of attention, and with keen appetites the party once more requisitioned the services of Mr. Wilson, and severely tested the capacity of his larder. Tea over, they turned their faces towards home, returning by way of Frod- sham, the journey occupying nearly four and a half hours. All were delighted with the out.

PARKS BANKINU COMPANY AND THE ALLIANCE BANK, LIMITED.

Ar. ettraor.linary general meeting of these amal- gamated banks was held at the Old Bank, Warring- ton, yesterday, at noon. Mr. A. Turner (the chair- man) presided, and amongst those present were Colonel Gamble, C. 8., Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. C. F. Parr, Mr. P. Stubs, Colonel McCorquodale, Mr. John Dun, N. Farrington &kersley, Sir T. G. Frost. Mr. Henry Warren-Meade Bing, (directors), Captain Withing- ton ; Mr. H. Davies,Mr. John White,Mr. W. Gamble, Mr. D. Garnett, Mr. H. Milling, and others.

div.head: CHAIRMAN'S REMARKS.
div.p: THE CHAIRMAN'S REMARKS.

In moving the adoption of the directors' report (which was printed in the " Examiner" two ..or three weeks ago), and the balance sheet, the Chairman said that l'when they last met in that room to sanction the amal- gamation of Parr's Banking Company and the Alliance tank. They had now before them the balance sheet showing what the directors considered to be a very satisfactory result of the six months' union. They had not hitherto issued half-yearly reports but they proposed to follow in that respect the example of the leading London and provincial banks. Having quoted from the bklance sheet, he said it was really a gratifying state- ment, more especially, as some of them were painfully aware, as the time ,had not been a favourable one for either merchants, manufacturers, agriculturists, or tradesmen. Referring to the removal of the head office to London, he assured them that that would not I lessen their care and devotion to their northern business. : Mr. Murray would remain at Warrington—(applause) —and Mr. Dun would not always be at call should he be required, but he proposed spending one week in every month at his old quarters. (Hear, hear.) Indeed their directors thought that Warrington, looking to its position on the Manchester Ship Canal and its becom- ing the future western terminus of the great railway now be;ng constructed from east to west, had a bright pro- spect before it—(hear, hear)—and they trusted that the bank would continue to share in its prosperity and would merit a continuance of the confidence of its people. They would observe that in future their meetings would be held alternately in Warrington and in London. Numerically the shareholders of the Alliance Bank were twice as many as those of Parr's Banking Cempany, but as regarded value the figures were more than reversed. At present there were no signs of improvement in trade, but they must hope that fine weather and a good harvest- ' ing of the crops would at least help their home trade, and it was to that trade they chiefly looked for their profits. (Applause.)—Mr. C. Parr seconded the adop- tion of the report, and this was agreed to.

div.head: DIVIDEND.
div.p: THE DIVIDEND.

On the motion of Col. McCorquodato, seconded by Captain Withlngton, it was resolved to adopt the recom- mendation of the directors that an interim dividend of 19 per cent. per annum, free of income tax, be declared for the half-year ending June 30th, payable on aad after August 9th. '

div.head: REMUNERATION OF DIRECTORS.
div.p: REMUNERATION OF DIRECTORS.

On the motion of Mr. R. Davies, seconded by Mr. John White, the directors of the banks were accorded a I vote of thanks and the remuneration of the directors I was fixed at dB,OOO per annum. Mr. Davies mentioned I that the remuneration of the directors of Parr's Bank had previously been £B.OOO and that of the directors of the Alliance Bank £4,000. APPOINTMENT OF AUDITORS, &C. On the proposal of Mr. W. GAMBLE, seconded by Mr. H. MILLING, the remuneration of the two firms of audi- tors, one in Liverpool and the other in London, was fixed at £350 per annum.—Colonel GAMBLE proposed a vote of thanks to the general manager, secretary, and other officers of both banks for their services during the past year. This was agreed to and Mr. DUN responded.—A vote of thanks to the Chaii man,moved by Mr. MORTIMER, and seconded by Dr. BEAMAN, was also passed, and the meeting then terminated.

div.head: BRUTAL ASSAULTS ON FEMALES.
div.p: BRUTAL ASSAULTS ON FEMALES.
MORE WOMEN'S POLITICAL DISSENSION 3.

At the Warrington Magistrates' Court, yester- pay, Wm. McCue, bricksetter, 46, John-st., was charged with assaulting on the 31st ult., Emma. Tomlinson and Emma, her daughter, 48, John-ste and Mary Ellen Whittle, her sister, Wellington-st., and Peter Tomlinson, ironworker husband of Einma,was charged with assaulting Mary Elizabeth McCue, wife of Wm. Mr. P. Davies appeared tor the complainants and Mr. A. Browne for Wm. McCue.—Mr. Davies said the provocation for the assault on Mrs. Tomlinson was a very silly one, i matter of political feeling.: He was informed by his clients that John-street was a hotbed of Liberalism, and they said they believed they were the only Conservatives in the street. There were a number of Irish people of whom Mr. McCue was one, in the neighbourhood. On Sunday night, about a quarter past 10, Mrs. Tomlinson was in her house with her daughter and Mrs. Whittle, Peter Whittle (hex husband) and a man named Alfred Barnshaw, who was courting her daughter. William McCue came drunk, and burst the door open, rushed in, got hold of her by the wrists, pulled her out, and hit her a terrific blew on the temple. She thought he had an instrument in his hand for he cut her head so severely that she fell,covered with blood. Wer husband was terribly afraid of McCue and dare not interfere but Mrs. Whittle did, and McCue. knocked her senseless. Miss Tomlinson 1,1:;.!•.!1y, get into the house, and he got hold of her and /-iulltd I-13e about, stll:'n Din! SO thst she I fainted several times. Then 13arhshaW !lt•-l' Sweetheart Interfered and was violently struck, and knocked in the gutter. Mr, Tomlinson's life wag almost futolerable lh the street ;he hardly dare go to his work, or, indeed come to court. Mrs. McCue on Sunday night cattle to his window and threatened to kill him, and the same night he was brutally a:Vat:fled by men.—Mrs. Tomlin- son gave evidence corroboratitig Misstatement, so far as the assaults were concerned—Cross-examined bv Mr. Browne, she said she was the only Cotiservative in the row of houses she lived in. McCue waft not the only Liberal. The cause of all the row was not that Mr. Browne engaged McCue's house as a committee room. They did not call him an Irishman or a Home linter. with oaths and say they would have no Home Rule committee room there. Dr. and Mrs. Houston's name were not mentioned. It was not true that at every municipal election there was a disturbance there. She denied that Mrs. Tomlinson seized McCue's girl by the ' hair. Dr. Cannell,Mary Ellen Whiteley,and Ellen Tom- linson gave evidence and deposed to assaults upon them- selves by McCue.—ln the course of Mr. Browne's cross- examination of Tomlinson, as to the door being burst open, Alderman Harrison exclaimed "Nonsense." Mr. Browne said he had overheard the remark.—Alderman Harrison : I repeat it emphatically.—Mr. Browne said the breaking in of the door was part of the case of assault. Mr. Browne added he was going to shorten the case, but now he would not.—Mr. Davies objected to this remark, and being detained there unnecessarily. He never heard such cheek in his life.—Mr. Browne : I never said such a thing. I said I was going to make it shorter. —Mr. Davies: And now you won't. What do you mean ?—Mr, Browne : I mean what I say.—Alderman Chandlev said Mr. Browne was elaborating the same points over and over again .—Alfred Barnshaw deposed to the assault upon himself.—Sarah Ellen Hartley, Annie Empson. Peter Whittle, and Peter Tomlinson, also gave evidence in support of the charges against Wm. McCue.—Mr. Browne called George Stoekton. fie said Mrs. Thmlinson seized one of Mrs. McCiie's danghters by the hair, and witness separated theneat Mr. McCue's request. He did not smash open the door. Mr. Tom- linson hit McCue's other daughter. The girls sent for r Mr. McCue. Witness at first said McCue was an entire stranger to him, but afterwards that he had known him two months and drunk with and visited him.—Mary Elizabeth McCue, one of NVilliam's daughters, said Mrs. Tomlinson used horrible language to her, and she sent for her father and when Peter Tomlinson saw him coming he struck witness. Her father WAS sober, and did .not assault Mrs. Tomlinson.—Margaret McCue said that Mrs.Tomlinson pulled her to the "floor." She struck Mrs. Tomlinson in self defence. She cited abominable language on the part of Mrs. Tomlinson...— Annie Bailey, Mary Ellen Oates, and Wm. McCue, gave evidence.—McCue was convicted on the three charges • against him, and fined 403. and costs for the assault on Emma Tomlinson, Dr. Carmen's medical fee, RI Is. being , allowed against the defendant ; and he was fined 10s. land costs in the other cases. The case against Peter Tomlinson was dismis.sed.—The hearing of the cases, though they were all taken together, lasted three hours and twenty, minutes.

div.head: --4.--- THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.
div.p: --4.--- THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

This week the British Association for the advancement of science is for the third time holding its annual meet- ing in Edinburgh. At the first general meeting on Wednesday evening, Dr. Huggins resigned, the chair, which was then assumed by Sir Archibald who, to a large assemblage of British And foreign scientists and others, delivered a presidenital address, which was mainly devoted to a survey of the progress of geological science and inquiry. On Thursday Sir Charles Fremantle delivered his ad- ,' dress as president of the Economic Science and Statistics Section. Mr. C. W. Smiley, who is investigating, the , slum problem for the United States Government and is i making a tour n England with that object, read a paper 'on "The Slums of Manchester." He praised the Jersey- st. dwellings system, saying it was a business scheme which would accomplish more than all the benefit societies put together, and he should recommend its adoption in America as one of the methods of redeeming their slums.
