div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WARRINGTON.

Councilllor Robert Heaton is hardly a success when he has, temporarily, to take the place of the chairman of a Committee. At the Town Council meeting. on Tuesday, in the absence of the &air- man of the Paving and Sewerage Committe, it fell to his lot to answer questions that might be asked in reference to the minutes of the Commit- tee, and Councillor Plumpton having asked why there was so long a delay, notwithstanding pre- vious promises to push on with the work, in com- pleting the paving of streets in Whitecross Ward, Mr. Heaton had the atrocious bad taste to insinuate that Councillor Plumpton was animated by personal motives, inasmuch as he had been called upon to pay for a certain amount of paving that had been done. This was not only bad taste but it was an absurdity as far as Coancillor Plumpton is con- cerned. Before that gentleman was ever elected to the Council he laid particular stress upon the scan- dalous condition in which some of the streets of Whitecross Ward bed been left for a long time by the Corporation. and he pledged himself to raise the subject if he were returned to the Council. ,S;nce his return he has agitated the question on several occasions. The unjustness of his insinua- tion, must be apparent i nt even to Mr. Heaton, unless, indeed, he thinks it s impossible for a mai to raise a public question without having a personal motive for doing so.

But there is another side of the subject which strikes me as being worth a little attention. It seems from what Councillor Heaton says that bay- ing to pay for the making of streets and passages is regarded as a bit ot a hardship by proper.y owners. On the or her hand, of course, it will be considered a favoer when these payments are delayed as long as possible. This being so, it would be interesting to know who they are that own the property where the streets and back passages have been left unpaved for an unusually long time. I have heard it said that, while some comparatively new streets have been made and paved in the most approved man- mer, there are others that have been lett for years .upon years in a muddy and disreputable condition. If this be so, what is the reason of it? Nit to save the pockets of the property owners, or are there , 'yule unusual impediments in the way of carrying out the work ?

Last week there was published with the "Daily Graphic" a supplement containing the portraits of all or nearly all the candidates returned in the recent election. I say nearly all because that of Mr. Robert Pierpoint, the member for Warrington was omitted. I presume that the artist must have had an interview with or sight of each member thus portrayed to sketch him or has obtained his photograph. Possibly Mr. Pierpoint had none to provide him with except the celebrated one repre- senting him as a volunteer. It i 3 hard to conceive that a place so important as Warrington which figures so conspicuously before the world in con- nection with the Ship Canal, and has been brought specially to the notice of the country by local cumstances of late, has been omitted solely through oversight from consideration in the publication of the portraits. I should like, supposing this has not been the case, to know how the matter really stands. Liberal though I am, Mr. Pierpoint is member for Warrington, and I am sorry to see the slight put upon the place and the man by their non-inclusion.

On Mr. J. Crosfield taking his seat on Wednesday as chairman on the county bencli at the Warrington Police Court he was, after a prefatory explanation, presented by the magistrates' clerk with i pair of white kid gloves in commemoration of the fact that there were no cases to be heard that morning. Of course it is difficult to understand the connec- tion between a pair of white kid gloves and the absence ef business at a police court, but the cus- tom of the presentation is an old one, though I fancy that in Warrington it has been more honoured in the breach than the observance. There is often enough no business at the borough police court. but instead of magistrates appearing on the bench to receive a pair of white gloves, the doors of the court hay,: remained closed and the reporters been informed on reaching the building that Oere was no business.

About this custom of presenting white gloves there is one thing that strikes me. I presume the gloves must be of the size of the hand of the mag- istrates to whom they are presented, and that being the case its measurement must be obtained before- hand. If so, the presentation is probably no sur- prise to him when it takes place; and it would be rather awkward if another magistrate than the one they fitted were to present himself. This is a nice point to raise, but I suppose the authorities con- cerned have their own way of managing these , , matters,

The almual display of athleticism Made tinder the auspices of the Warrington Football Club shows no signs of declining popularityludging from the vast assemblage there was to witness it on Bafk holiday. As the committee, too, learn from in- creasing experience their management of the affair improves. They and the secretary and indeed all officially concerned deserve the highest credit for the perfect manner in which they carried it out on Monday, and it says much fGr the abQorbing inter- est of such sports when between 5,000 and 6,000 people can meet to witness them without one single instance of disorder or confusion occurring to mar the harmony of the scene. This is the more remarkable, in the case of a football club festival, considering that the game has in other parts of the country than Warrington'got itself into some die- repute in consequence ofbeing accompanied with scenes of lawlessness.

lam not surprised at Alderman Holmes's com- plaints in the Town Council of difficulty in obtain- ing the books he wants from the Free Library, as this experience is not confined to himself, and I am much pleased to learn that the Committee having the charge of it propose to have more than one copy of many of the most circulated books. It seems, however, from what Councillor H. Roberts says, that it was principally because of the supply of certain novels not being equal to the demand, that this step has been decided upon. But I hope it will be considered whether it may not be neces- sary to multiply copies not only of novels, but of at least some of the sounder hooks. The higher cul- ture of the few is, after all, of as much importance nay, of more to the community, than the amuse- ment, or, at most, lower culture of the many who read mainly for the former and in the process man- age to get a modicum of the latter.

There are some of the best known and most in- stractive of the continental authors whose works are not to be obtained in the library, except in the tongues in which they were written. English edi- tions of these ought to be placed there, for every en- couragement ought to be given to the udent and the higher class reader to cultivate his mind,as welt as to those who make fiction their stock mental food.
MERLIN.
Z THE WESL LAN CONFERENCE.

At the sitting of the Wesleyan Conference at Bradford on Tuesday further appointments to stations were read. Dr. Moulton submitted the proposals for the examina- ti.m of ministers on trial. Appropriate reference was made to the life and work of the ministers who had died during the year. A conversation followed on the need of more vig,oreus religious work, and later the Confer- ence dealt with the Luton baptism case. On Wednesday there was a large attendance, antici- pating the confirmation of stations. It was decided n Tuesday night that at the next conference, to be held in Cardiff, there be two ordination services, one to be eltulucted in the Welsh language. ,The election:of chair- men of districts was next proceaded with. At the afternoon session, the conference proceeded to the consideration of the third reading and confirmation of stations. The Wesleyan Conference, which has been sitting since July 4th, was brought to a close on Thursday morning, The Conference Record was read, and several of the Bradford Methodists came to witness the signinc of the journal and to receive the votes of thanks which were passed to the friends of Halifax and Bradford district for their hospitality.
The eruption of Mount Etna, which had almost sub- sided on Monday, showed signs of renewed activity on Tuesday, and the lava streams commence to flow afresh.

A St. Petersburg telegram reports that cholera has made further advance towards the centre of Russia, cases having occurreo at a town in the province of Orel. The occurrence of some cases is again reported from Moscow. Reports have been received from Simla to the effect that three detachments of Russian troops have occupied the Pamirs right up to the Flindoo Koobh, the dividing line between Afghan Turkestan and Afghanistan.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A MILITARY ROWI!Y.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day, Richard Taylor, a soldier who had joined the 3rd battali m of the South Lancashire Regiment about ten days before, was charged with being drunk and refusing to quit the Rodney inn, Winwick-street the previous night, also with wilfully damaging to the =stint of £5, the windows of the premises, on the same occasion.—?dr. Marsh,the landlord, said the prisoner came into his house drunk, with two others, on Tuesday night about half- past ten, and he told him to go out. He began " squan- dering "his money about the counter, and witness told him to pick it up and clear away. He refused to go and witness ejected him. He then took off his belt and stroshed six squares of plate glass in the windows with it.— A Sergeant from Orford Birracks said the character given to the prisoner was indifferent.—He was sent to jail for two months with hard labour.

div.head: CIIELIMS CASB.
div.p: A CIIELIMS CASB.

At Warrington::Borough Police Court on Tuesday, a woman named Hamlett applied ba the Bench for advice with regard to the custody of a child. From what was stated by the Chief Constable it appeared that the appli- cant and her husband, who had no children of their own, adopted the child of a woman who had since got married. The latter, with her husband, now wanted to claim the child, which was four years of age ; but they had no settled abodeof their own, it being stated by the applicant that they were" here to-day and gone to- morrow." The child was now well cared for and well clothed, and Mrs. Hamlett wished to keep it.—The Chief Constable was instructed to make inquiries into the case and report to the Bench.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDa2.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), and Messrs. Glarnett and Voisey. THE ALLEGED THEFT OF RlNGS.—William Rody, is. bourer, from Chester, was again brought up charged on this occasion, with stealing from a railway van, whilst in transit on the London and North-Western Railway from Wigan to Birmingliam,a box containing gold studs, rings, &c., valued in all at £5O. The prisoner was seve- ral times brought up on the charge of being in possession of two rings, supposed to have been stolen, but as no owner could he found for them he was bound over to appear whenever he might be called upon to do so and discharged. Later on the Chief Constable received a communication from the London and North-Western Railway Company to the effect that a' box which had been sent by rail from Wigan by a jeweller,was missing. The box, it was proved, had got as far as Newton. An assistant to the Wigan jeweller was called, and he iden- tified two of the rings produced as those which had been placed in the box. 'The case was remanded until Satur- day next,to enlble the polies to complete their inquiries. The following is a description of goods stolen from New- ton Station : "Three sets of heavy 18 carat gold studs and links and one pair of links,plain dull gold, a solitaire gold strict and the bottom of a solitaire, one wedding ring, standard size M or N, two ladies' garnet rings, one large and one small ring, one carbuncle ring, very large stone and appears to have been set in solid gold slightly chased on shoulders, one ladies' garnet and p.srl dress ring, two pearls missing, a piece of frosted and figured glass in brass (a heirloom) about the size of a spectacle glass." THEFT OF /Tex.—James Cummings (58), a navvy em- ployed on the Slip Canal at" Big Field„' was charged with stealing a boiled ham and a towel, the pro- perty of William Johnson, from the British Workman Cocoa Rooms, Bridge-st., on Tuesday last. It appeared that Johnson, who is the manager of the rooms, placed a recently boiled ham in the back yard to enable it to cool quickly. Later on a customer called and asked for some ham, but when the manager went into the back yard he found that the ham which had been placed there a short time previously was missing. Information of the rubbery was given to the police, resulting m an appre- hension of tho prisoner. The Bench considered the case proved, and committed the prisoner to gaol for two months with hard labour. A WAHNINO.—Arthur Longshaw, described as a la- bourer, was charged with running away from the borough, on the 23rd July, leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the funds of the Warrington Union. —Mr. T. J. Garnett prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and stated that the defendant and his wife and children had been several times in the workhouse, and the cost of their maintenance to the Union was over £lB.—The magistrates decided to send the prisoner to gaol for two mouths with hard labour. A SWEEP FlNED.—William Delooze, a sweep, was fined in the cests, 2a. 61., for depositing a quantity of soot in Milner-st., contrary to the by-laws. It WAS stated that defendant shook some bags in the street, to the annoy- ance of passengers, several of whom had to leave the footpath. MISCELLANEOUS.—Mary Jane Earl, Blackhurst-st., was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—Peter Sutton,fried fish stealer, and Daniel Dutton, pork butcher, were fined a shilling each for allowing their chimney to

be on fire. GAMES OF CHANCE.—Patrick Farrington (16), Thomas Farrington (19), James Kirkham (17), James Leonard (17), Thomas Flynn (22), Henry Hughes (16,) John Bennett (22), Charles Bennett (17). Benjamin Bennett US), William Narroway (19). Moses Narroway (17), John Varley (13), and Michael Mulligan (17), were charged • wit", playing at a game ef chance with cards in Pier- • point-street for money. The prisoners admitted the •offence.—Varley was fined 2s. 6d., and all the rest ss. each. WIFE DESEAyioN.—John Plunkett, described by the •Chief Constable as a" lob," was charged with deserting his wife, Charlotte.—The prisoner did not appear, but the Bench made an order 'against him to pay 10s. a week towards his maintenance. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) in the chair, and Aldermen Francomb, Holmes, and Harrison. DEVINE AND DISORDERLY.—CIara Beaumont, in Bridge- .st., Agnes Constantine in Winwick-st., John McLauch- lan, in Scotland-road, and Peter Clough in Academy-st., ' all on Saturday night, and Henry Beach in Bridge-st., 'llfr and John Woods in Win wick-road, both on Sunday . morning, were all fined ss. and costs; in default seven days' imprisonment. UNSEEMLY WOMEN.—Margaret McLauchlan and Jessie Sefton were charged with unseemly b<haviour, the former on Saturday night at Bridge Foot, and the latter .on Sunday morning, in Springfield-st. McLauchlan was sent to prison for two months' hard labour, and Sefton was discharged on promising to leave the town. CUAROE OE BEGGING.— Patrick Lennardy, aged ten, and Benjamin Jaundrell, aged nine, were harged with being found begging, in Wilson Patten Street, early on Sunday morning.—lnspsctor Cphall agent for the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. said Leonard was in the street with a basketin his hand containing bread, and in company Arith Jaundrell. He had found them begging frfguently, and had warned their parents.—The Chief-constable said Lennardy was a pest, and was very abusive to women. Even the Town Clerk had been pestered by him—The Mayor said he himself had been bothered by Lennardy although he knew what he was and that he was on the Bench.—The magistrates considered that the charge was net proved, the lada not having been caught
in the act of begging and 110 money having been found on thCm ;lificrUiey diainiSS-elrfhWrage leaving-Inspector Uphill to.take what steps. he chose. _ _ _

• - A SATV7RDAY NIGIFT Row.—VIGLENT ASSAVLT WIT'S A Jun .—Martin • Hart; •a, corner-man, was clatrged with being drunls and disorderly in ,Friars' Green on Saturo day night, • also with assau.ting F.C.'s Turner and Forster and a man named John Crow. P.C. Turner said Hart's mother came aud complained to him that her son had struck Crow at her house with a quart jug. He went to the house, and found Crow with a deep cut under his eye, which he was informed had been caused by the jug. The house was flowing with blood as if it were a slaughter-house. He, with the assistance of Forster, took Crow to the Police Station, and all the way he was kicking and striking them. Crow had been in the Infirmary, but was able to appear in court, but he said he did not remember anything about the matter or how the cut was produced. The defendant's mother was called, and said the prisoner and his sister had a quarrel, and she was going to strike him with a jug,but struck Crow instead.—The magistrates refused to be- lieve her tale, and sent Hart to jail for three months' hard labour. DESERTING HIS CUILDREN.—John Painter was charged by Mr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guar- dians, with leaving his two children chargeable' to the Union.—The case was adjourned a month. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. E. J. Guest (chairman), and Mr. W. Owen. _ _ - -

THEFT OF A DRESS—Annie Ryan was charged with ' stealing, on Tuesday afternoon, from 3 Navior-st., a print dress, value 25. 6d., the property of Edith Annie Turner, a fellow lodger of hers at that address.—She pleaded not guilty, and said they had been drinking all day together, which the complainant admitted, and borrowed the skirt, which was denied.—D.S. Monaghan , deposed to the complainant reporting the theft and his finding that the prisoner had sold the dress at Catherine Gibbons's second-hand shop in Mersey-st., for 15. Corroborative evidence was given by the complainant and Gibbons.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner was an associate of Bodelia linockton and a worse char- acter in the street than Bodelia.—lnspector Bowen said the prisoner was a pest to: Bridge-st. She went about half drunk, and watched the policemen clear out of the way, and if another girl of her own character was pass- ing thought nothing of striking her.—The prisoner was sent to jail for two months with hard labour.

THUMB ay.—Before Alderman Chandley. (chairman), Councillor Jas. Fairclough. and Captain Ridgway. DRUNK AND DISOBDEBLY.—EIizabeth Ellen Fleming, in Lime-st., the previous night. A cemstable deposed to seeing her kicking at the door of Walker's Vaults. She would have broken the window but for him.—Mr. G. Riley, School Board officer, who was present at the soli- citors table, volunteered a statement that he saw the woman on Wednesday night cursing and swearing and using shameful language. She was fined ss. and costs. EDUCATION CASM.—Win. Ratcliffe, 27, Tilley-at., was charged by Mr. Geo. Riley, with not sending his child I regularly to school. Mr. A. Browne defended, and con- tended that the lad had been properly educated, having passed the 4th standard, and only failed in the fifth , last year, in one subject, composition, and the master of Heath Side School which be attended raised him to thelsixth standard, and gave him books that he would undertake the School Attendance Committee did not know.—The Chairman said Mr. Browne had no right to I reflect upon the School Attendance Committee, because he had no opportunity of judging of their qualifications. Mr. Browne said the lad had passed the 4th standard, hence was entitled to be a half timer.—Mr. Riley, Contended that he was not, having pet passed theZandard. He was consequently under his supervision till he was 14, he being now 12. Ernest Ratcliffe, the boy, said he hail passed the 4th i.standard, and Mr. Finney, the maiteeof the school had I told him so.—The defendant, who is a time-keeper at Longford wire works corroborated,, and said Mr. Riley had suggested that the lad should be a half-timer. as he was at present. He was employed helm 7 a.m. till 12.30 p.m. daily by Smith and Son, news agent.—The Chair- man adjourned the case for production of a certificate of passingAhe 4th standard, from the master.—The follow- ing cases were also disposed of at the instance of Mr. Riley.—William Cartwright, 29, Tilley-street, case adjourned.—John Barnett, moulder, Daley's lodging- house ; Thomas Brown, labourer at Lewis's coal yard ; William Burton, 5, Edward-street, Frederick Cooper, 53, Forshaw-street ; William Pollard, labourer, 5, Birchen- street ; John Crimes labourer, Glass House Row, and , Matthew Smider, labourer, 20, Silver-street, and Joseph Kinsey, railway man. FIIIDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison (in the chair), Chandley and Platt. DAMAdE BY Boys.—Patrick Lennardy, a boy, was charged by Mr. Thompson, farmer, with damag- ing, between the 22nd and 25th ult.' certain growing oats, the property of Colonel J. S. Black- bume. Mr. Thompson said he had suffered damage to the amount .of £6 or £7 already through boys.— Patrick and Peter Lennardy and John McCormick, and Wm. Morland, all lads, were charged with doing dam- age to a fence on the same spot on the 30th of July. The Lennardy's were tined ss. each and ordered to be locked up till to-day (Saturday), sad the others were ordered to be detained the same time and to pay 2.8. 6.1. each. NEurxer OF FAMlLY.—Edward Norman, outdoor railway porter, was charged by Mr. Basil Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with leaving his wile and child chargable to the Union. A inonth's hard labour.—The Prisoner: Can't you give me 20 2—The Chairman : I would if I could, but unfortunately .I cannot..

CRUELTY To Hoaszs.—James 'Mercer and Thomas Grundy were c!Aarged,the former with travelling a horse while in an unfit state and the latter with causing the offence on the evening of the horse fair. D.S. Monaghan and Inapt. Dowty proved the cases. Grundy was fined 15s. and costs 63. and Mercer dismissed—J. Middlehurst of St. Helens, was charged with unmercifully flogging his horse on Warrington fair day.—lnspectors Wilson and Dowty proved ;the cases. It appeared that the horse was covered with weals and bleeding, and the whip used had gutta percha at the end of it, which Mr. Dowty said would out like wire.—The defendant's father said the weals were caused by others, as was the common prac- tice at fairs, lashing a horse when they saw a lad on its back.—The defendant was fined 104. and costs, 225. in all.—John Rimmer, sen., Cadishead Moss, for causing a horse to be travelled while hi an unfit state, on War- rington fair day, was fined 203. and costs, LI. us, in

She was remanded until Monday and admitted to bail. A NAVVIF.S NIGFIT ADVIZIPTIMIL—Reuben James was charged with frequenting the enclosed premises of Samuel Becket Chadwick with ictent to commit a felony on the Ist inat.—P.C. Gregory deposed to seeing the prisoner climb the garden wall, and go into a shed.—The prisoner said he only went into the shed to shelter from the rain and to have a rest. He had come to see a friend and lost his way en returning. Superintendent Ather- ton said the man was a navvy and lived at a hut on Frodsham Marsh. He did not think the man had any felonious intent inasmuch as he had a silver watch and a sovereign in his pocket.—The prisoner was discharged with a ,caution.

div.head: PETITION AGAINST MR. BALFOUR
div.p: PETITION AGAINST MR. BALFOUR

A petition has been lodged against the return of Mr. A. J. Balfour as member for East Manchester, the allegations including bribery, illegal hiring of vehicles, and treating. The " Star " says :—" From all quarters evidence continues to accumulate in support of our proposition that the Tories had, during the recent elections, recourse to the most shameless forms of corrupt practice. Cor- respondents innumerable are making the gravest and most circumstantial complaints, and actually in not fewer than seven constituencies petitions have, on grounds of bribery, treating, or other corrupt practices, already been lodged against the return of Tory candi- dates. These petitions are directed against : Mr. A. J. Baifour,in East Manchester : Hon. G. H. Allsopp,in Wor- cester ; Alderman Davies, in Rochester ; Mr. Vv. Isaac- son, in Stepney; Mr. F. James, in Walsall ; Sir Prvce Jones, in Montgomery ; Mr. Smith Wright, in S. Not- tingham.f.' It is stated that tfie petitions against the election of Mr. Arnold Morley for East Nottingham and Mr. S. Wright. for South Nottingham have been abandoned.

WARRINGTON v. BOLTON,—This return' match was played at Bolton on Saturday, and the Boltonians re- peated their performance at the first encounter' by a rather eady defeat of the visitors. S. M. and J. J. Crosfield opened the account for Warrington' and made a fairly good start, though the captain went after con- tributing 14, being caught off Ellis. J. J. batted in good form, and F. Williamson made a valuable stand, whilst Voisey hit up 13. The rest could do little with the deliveries of the Bolton trundlers, and the innings closed for 98, the pro, Smith, being absent on the Warrington aide. On Bolton taking up the batting, Walker was early caught and bowled by S. M. Crosfield, but Ellis was in good form, and after a little help from Mallett, Stanley joined the pro, and the fielders had a high eld time of it, the newcomer batting with the utmost free- dom and in fine form. BOLTON P. WARRINGTON (2fin Etaveiss.)—The return match between the above clubs was played at Warring- ton on the Arpley ground on Saturday last. Bolton winning the toss were first represented by Messrs. Stan- ley and W. Smith, the bowlers being Messrs. J. Bibby and C. Unsworth. Stanley, however, was soon disposed of by Bibby in his second over. Crowther came to the assistance of Smith. and the telegraph board had not beeo altered when Bibby took Crowther's wicket. Ten runs were on the beard, and Bashall helped Smith to put seven more on, when the latter had to retire, another good delivery from Bibby taking hismiddle stump. Carson was the only one out of the remainder to reach double figures, their innings closing for 50, owing to the splendid bowling of Bibby and Crompton who took 6 wickets for 17 runs, and 2 for none respec- tively, the latter only bowling three overs. Messrs. C. Russell and R. Frown started for the home team, but their stay was only a short one, Russell being caught and bowled by Shepherd and Brown bowled by the same man. Unsworth had to go back after contributing one. • Disaster luckily stopped here. Bibby and Crompton now got together and made a good stand, 'runs coming freely from both, and 40 were sent up in quick time. At 41 a separation was effected, Bibby being bowled by Bashall. Parry came next and made two good hits when he was lbw, having to retire for 7. Crompton was now joined by Evans, who scored very quickly, knocking 4 boundary hits, when the former's wicket was taken by Bashall. Evans kept on batting well, and helped the score up to 93, at which total the 9th wicket fell, and the innings was closed, the match ending in a win for the home team. Score

div.head: BOWLS.
div.p: BOWLS.

A bowling match waa ployed ots the ground of the Warrington Liberal Club on Saturday afternoon between the members d the club and a team from Winnington, with the result that the latter were defeated by exactly 100. The weather was fine, and the ground in excellent condition, and there were about 60 spectators. ' Subse- quently the players partook of tea in the Committee room, Mr. J. Albioson'presiding. A vote of thinks was passed on the motion of the secretary of the Winnington club, to the Committee, and the steward, for their arrangements.—Mr. Albinson responded to the vote,and, referring to the fact that most or all of the Winnington players were in the employ of Mr. Brunner, M.P., said he was more pleased at the return of that gentleman than at the victory that afternoon.—A vote of thanks was given to the visitors on the proposition of Mr. Thos. Critchley, seconded by Mr. S. Dunbobbin ; and this hav- ing been responded to, the company dispersed.

• A match was played at Bank Quay bowing green, Warrington, on Bank Holiday afternoon, between Henry Fogg aud V,iltiam Dutton, both of Warrington, for £lO a side, in the presence of about 300 spectators. Fogg won easily.

UNsUCCESSFUL PROTEST AGAINST WARRINGTON.—The question " What constitutes a professional "has fumed the subject of inquiry at a special meeting of the Execus • tive of the Counts, Bowling Association, arising out of a protest made by Newton-le-Willows against Warrington, the two teams who met in the semi-final in the Associa- tion division at Didsbury on the 21st of July. Newton complained that T. Critchley, a member of the War- rington team, had been engaged ins match on a public bowling green, for the sum of £lO with W. button, also of Warrington, on the 12th of that month, and should , be regarded as a professional ; and that according to the special rule" any club allowing such a member to play must be disqualified. Evidence in support of the pro- test was given by members of the Newton club, one of whom was present at the match. Several members of the Warrington club were heard in reply, the substance of their evidence being that the match was not played for money but for a suit of clothes, that the green was not open to the public on the day in question, and that both the parties engaged were members of the green. After a .lengthy discussion the committee decided the charge had not been proved. The spe.ial rule referred t 3 recites that" any member of a club who plays in a public competion for money is ineligible to play in a county competition." The decision placed Warrington in receipt of a valuable county prize. BOWLINGJJAIN AT PADGATE. Last Saturday the employes 9f Messrs. J. Crosfield, and Sons, repaired to the bowling green adjoining the " King and Queen " Inn, for the purpose of deciding then' annual main of bowls. The turf—always good— was on this occasion in the pink of condition and ex- tremely inviting, and the weather (except a couple of easy showers), was all that could be desired, all impor- tant elements conducive to a scientific exposition and pleasureable game. The list of prizes consisted of an assortment of varied and valuable articles with a for- midable complement of cash generously contributed by the following ladies and gentlemen of the town :—Mrs. Hatton, Mrs. Hartshorne, and Mrs. Brundrett, Messrs. J. Crosfield, J.P., J. J. Crosfield, A. H. Crosfield, R. Pierpoint, M.P., Drs. Gornall and Markel, J. Fleming,A. Browne, John Walker, W. P. Skelton, R. Roberts and Son, W. Welsby, J. Urmson, R. Proud, H. Clayton, H. N. Plotiglitan, Piokinere, Welding, J. Fiulingson, S. Clare, W. H. Robinson, P. Cordwell, T. Parkinson, R. Martin, G. Hemerson, W. Forshaw, C. Chorley, C. T. Huffman, J Hedgccck, W. Chester, W. Beswick, T. Peek. "a Friend," and the Warrington Slate Co. The following were the successful competitors and recipients of prizes In order of merit :-Ist, J. Wilcock, copper kettle and 7s. ed. ; 2nd, J. Woods, copper kettle and 7s. 6d. ; 3rd, L. Dobson, time piece and ss. ; 4th, J. Barton, case silver spoons and 55.; sth, P. Weave, spirits and 3s. 6d.; 6th, J. Jackson, brass stool and 3s. 6d. ; 7th, to 12th, J. Rougbley, W. Handles, T. , Lowe, W. Longinore, E. Handles, and S. Jones, ss. each ; 13th to 22nd, A. Tilling, 8. Millfngton, C. Harrison, W. Woods, A. Chalmers, J. Jackson, fi. Dagnall, P. Hill, H.WilliaMson, jun., and J. Lawton, 3s each. In a subsequent "consolation" game prizes were secured as upder.:-Ist, J. Willett, spirits and 3s. ; 2nd. J. Smith, kettle and 2s; 3rd, T. Handles, ornaments and is. 6d;; 4th, W. Norman, 2s. 6d. ; sth and 6th, P. John- son and P. Whittle, 2.3. each. The event itself was per- haps one of tho most successful ever conducted on this green; the players and their friends maintained the utmost good-humour throughout. Immediately antr the main the numerous contestants retired to the hotel, where theg partook quantum stellicit of a substantial repast provided by the proprietor. As a mark of esteem and admiration Messrs. P. Hill and W. Williamson, the oldest servants of Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons present, were respectively elected chairman and deputy chair- man. After the president (in the unavoidable absence of Mr. A. H. Crosfield) had suitably awarded the prizes, and offered a few appropriate remarks. he read a letter from the latter gentleman expressing regret at his non- attendance but suggesting that the contest might be repeated a reasonable time hence, offering a handsome donation, and a promise to make a special effort to be amongst them, an announcement which was received with applause. In the course of a report read by the Secretary, Mr. J. Willett, he remarked that it afforded him the greatest pleasure after another year's labour, in joining his co-workers in an afternoon's pastime of that natnre, and assured those present his only object in working up these events was for the welfare and the interest he took in his brother toilers. Songs were afterwards rendered by Messrs. J: Wilcock, J. Willett, 'l'. ftandles', S. Millington, P. Johnson, J. Eden, and J. Jackson, which contributed largely to the evening's conviviality, Mr. A. Long ably presiding at the piano. The gathering terminated with various toasts• —" Success to the firm of J. Crosfield and Son" which was responded to with musical honours, "the prize donors "and the " Host and hostess," Mr. Clare in his acknowledgment naively remarking that it was a source of pleasure to the "King and Queen " to be honoured by so distinguished an assemply within the precinct& ot their " Royal Courts".

At South Shields, on Monday, Catherine Stewart, a widow, of Sunderland, was committed for trial chargeo with attempting to kill her child and commit suicide by wilfully going in front of an approaching train.

On Saturday, a most inteiiitingt fiktdre in con- nection with the above club was carried out. It consisted of an inter-Club run with the niembers of the sale Cycling Club: Starting about 30 p.m'. from headquarters abont a score of the Warrin,tlton Cycl- ing Club ran to Mere, near Hoo green, where they met a party of About 18 of the Sale Cycling Club. The .combined clubs then ran together via Knutsford and Chelford to the Sale Cycling Club farm Which is beauti- fully situated on the banks of Hodes Mere at SiddingtOn. After a substantial repast to. which ample justice was done, a stroll was made down to the Mere where several members refreshed :themselves with a dip. 'A cricket match was the next feature and this created a good deal 'of interest on both sides. The Warringtonians went in Ito bat first, and, thanks to Podmore who made 34 wit out, the total was taken to 58. On the Saleites going in they managed to make 26 for six wickets, the game thus ending in a draw. Shortly afterwards the members returned hone, the Sale Cycling Club going by way. Alderley Edge and.Cheadle. and the Warrington Cycling Club by way. Monks Heath and Knutsford. The afternoon was voted by everyone present to have been most enjoyikble and succesSful, and thanks are due to the hon. secretary (Mr. E. Pickavance; jun.) for the admirable way in which he carried out the arrange- ments'. It may be mentioned that he is at present arranging for a greater series of runs of the above des- cription to take place during the next season. „

div.head: NOTES ON: GAMES AND ATHLETICS. .
div.p: NOTES ON: GAMES AND ATHLETICS. .
CRICKET.

The Lancashire victory over Gloucestershire, says the "Athletic News," was very badly wanted by the County Palatine. The feature of the two days' cricket was the admirable innings of A. C. MacLaren, who was batting three hours and a half for 135—his largest contribution in a county match. The old Harrow captain has pre- viously topped the century, scoring 108 against Sussex a couple of seasons ago, when he was but 18 years of age. His return to form must be very gratifying to his father, the respected treasurer of the County Club, who was out at Aigburth on tr.th days, and who,! am pleased to say, is looking very much better.

S. M. Crosfield makes a capital captain, and although I would not like to say he equils A. N. Hornby, it is pretty certain that not a better choice would have been made than the one which gave the Warrington amateur charge of the team in Ur. Hornby's absence. He is always on the alert to take advantage of a batsman's peculiarities, and does not object to moving his field about, while, although, as he told me some time ago he has a personal abhorrence to fielding -in the slips; he occasionally goes there when an extra hanci is necessary. "

• Bolton set their return with Warrington apart,for the benefit of their two professors " Jerry "Ellis and Halley, and a rare good benefit they had, too. The spectators numbered something like 2,000, which in that part of the country is a pretty large muster for a club cricket match. Bolton wog comfortably, beating the " wire- pullerS " for the second time thia year. They have an uncommonly good record for the season, their colours having been lowered by Manchester and Leyland only, and in the case of the latter the indignity has been avenged.

Notts and Surrey entered the arena on Monday with an equal number of points--seven—to their credit, and with the knowledge that 01'e-result of the match would almost certainly settle the county championship. The genie was worthy of the occasion, but the grand quali- ties of the Notts team again polled them through;as they won with four wickets to spare. The match which took place at the Oval is a record one with regard to the attendance of spectators. On Monday 30,780 people people paid for admission, on Tuesday 29,370, and on Wednesday morning 3,633; or a grand total of 63,763, which is a record at a match in this country. Up to Wednesday Notts had not beaten Surrey atthe Oval since 1886. for their splendid and thoroughly well-earned victory they have particularly to thank the batting of Gunn, Barnes, and Daft ; and the bowling of Shacklock, but the fine fielding of the whole team on Tuesday after- noon had also something to do with the result.

Runs were'about as plentiful blackberries in the match between Durham and Yorkshire. The north countrymen may be said to have done unlommonly well In making 352,0 ff the cream of the Yorkshire bowling,. Indeed, no fewer than 945 runs were totalled in for three com- plete innings. Three batsmen were credited with a century each, both Wardall and Wainwright hitting very finely on Saturday. •

The positions which Yorkshire and Lancashire till will not cause a tremendous amount of delight to thrill the bosoms of theadmirers of those counties. Both contin- gents seem to la.? blessed or otherwise with the hardest of luck, in their championship games, and then develop an extraordinary ability to score in a match of no im- portance to the statistical gentleman' but which may perhaps be quite as strongly contested as some of their encounters in the select company of first-class counties. The Yorkshire Football Committee have so far climbed down from their almighty attitude towards the Alliance ten as to profess the most friendly feelings for them, and to solicit the favour. .of an interview with them with tho view, of arriving at an amicable settle- ment. How such settlement is to bfi obtained over the heads of the English Union it is difficult to see, unless the Yor {shire Union were to take up the cause of the Alliance and themselves beleaguer the parent body. In View of recent „events, that would be an interesting situation. •

The subscriptions to the Yorkshire Union are due this week. If not paid the clubs cease to be members, and will not be found in the Cup tie draw to take place a tortnight hence. It would be interesting to know if any of the clubs in .the Alliance have forwarded their subscriptions. If they have not they cense to. be mem• hers of the Yorkshire Union,who therefore cease to have authority over them, though they would still retain membership of the English Union. The possibility of this turn of affairs—perhaps we might almost say the probability of it—appears to have roused the Yorkshire autocrats to their senses.

The idea of providing a separate dressing-room for the .referee has its advantages; for it is not 'pleasant to hear certain remarks from the players when you are divest- ing yourself of your official attire, and donning the everyday garb of civil life. With nothing on but your shirt, for instance, you feel a loss of dignity which pre- vents you arguing knotty points in a manner which becomes a Saturday afternoon gmperor, and on ,various grounds the idea of reserving private apartments, for a referee is to be commended, and might he followed by , other clubs. TIIE ROYAL SHOW AT LIVERPOOL.

The Royal Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society's Show was brought to a close on Monday at Newsham Park, Liverpool. The total receipts for the four days have been over £4,000, which is double the amount realised at last year's show. The fifty- guinea championship cup for leaping was won by William Dodsworth, of Nottingham. No fewer than 32,000 persons visited the show on Monday.

THE ACCIDENT TO WIDNES GENTLE-
mgN AT SANKEY BRIDGES.
CLAIM FOR DAMAGES.

At ,t+jcs,LipOol Asaizes, on ,Thesday, before Mr. Justlie Williams and a special jury, the base of Wright v. London and North-Western Rail way Company was hefted . •This Was. an aEtion by ilavid . , , Wright, grocer and pr °vision dtale. dt Widitcs, to recover damages for personal injuries sustained through the negligence, ai alleged, of the defendant company's serOanta. Negligence was denied, and con- tributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff alleged. Mr. M'Call, Q.C., and Mr.' 'Pickfurd appeared for the plaintiff ; and Mr.. Bigham, ,Q.C., and Mr. C. A. Russell for the company.—Mr. M'Call said he thought the issue would really be one of damages: The plaintiff was chairman of the health committee of the Widnes Local Board, and In the course of his public duties he went on January 26th to inspect one of the infirmaries at War- rington. He was accompanied by Dr. O'Keefe (medical officer at Widnes), Mr. G. J. Neil (a member of the board), and Mr. Sinclair (surveyor of the board). They sat in a trap back to back, the horse being driven by Mr. Neil. After inspecting the Infirmary, they proceeded to return about half-past five 'o'clock in tae evening. About a mile and a quarter frorn Warrington, on the road leading to Widnes, there fs a bridge !crossing the. canal belonging to the defendant' company. It is is bridge that cast be opened and shut, and there were bars to place across and prevent anyone passing wheU the bridge was open. The - trap was driven at a' moderate pace, and as there was no warning that the bridge was open it went all) ng and tumbled into the canal. One hundred yards from the bridge the 'trap had slowed down in order to let another vehicle pass. All the occupants were thrown into the cold water and injured. The plaintiff was most severely injured as a portion of the trap struck him in the back. There were bars which could he laid acrass the roadway to pre- vent anyone crossing when the bridge was open,but they were not up on the present occasion.—The plaintiff stated that if he had not grasped the trap he would have been drowned. They were got out and taken to an hotel. Nobody connected with the company came to look after them except a porter who asked for their names and ad- dresses, as he said the company were going to charge them for getting the horse and trap out of, the canal. (Laughter.) He (plaintiff) was not yet better, and his doctor had advised him to take a two months' trip,which would cost £loo,as he Would have to take someone with him. His grocery business brought in 10. a week less than before the accident, and he had incurred great ex- penses, including £4O for doctors and nurses. He could not do the baking, and reckoned his loss £2 108. per week. Cross-examined: He would like to take a trip to the Mediterranean—say to Constantinople. „,(Laugh- ter.) His shop was rated at £l9 a year.-7-Mr. Neil, Mr'. Sinclair, and Dr. O'Keefe described the accident.—Dr. M'Lellan said it would be three to six months before the plaintiff would be able to do his work as well as betore, including the lifting of weights. Cross-examined : The witness said he had charged the plaintiff a guinea a visit, Plaintiff was still a little nervous.—This closed the case for the plaintiff.—On behalf of the defendants, Francis, the bridge man, raid that before the accident he lighted the lamps at the bridge. There was nothing to prevent any one at a distance 9f 200 yards seeing the bridge was open. While• in the cabin he heard a cry of" Heigh-up !' and on going out saw strap come along at a rapid pace—about 14 miles ian hour—and tumble n the canal. The bars were not usually put up.—Cross-examined : Since the accident he had received instructions to regularly put up the bars.—Re-examined : He reported to the company that the men in the trap were driving at a furious rate.— John Hough, jun., said the lamps at the bridsm were lighted.—John Rose, a boatman, said that when the trap was 20 yards off he called out that the bridge was open. Itwas a Wet and misty night.—Tho case had not concluded when the court rose. • ,

The case was resumed on Wednesday, when Mr..Birr- ham, in bumming up the defendant's case, arguedthat the pony was driven at a "apid pace when it. tumbled into the canal. It was ridiculous to say that the puny was going at a walking pace--like a horse going into the sea with A bathing machine. (Laughter.) It had been endeavoured to make a point of the lac: that the protec- ing bars were not across the roadway, but he would re- mind the jury that if they bad, the occupants of the trap would have met with more serious injuries. It was a case in which there had been contributery negligence. Then as to the damages demanded, he eontended that they were extravagant. It was curious that the three plaintiffs:who had brought scions, each wanted £l2O to take a two months' trip to the Mediterranean.—His Lordship said that Mr. M‘Call did not seriously suggest that.-41r. Bigham : The plaintiff did.—His Lordship: I should have thought that for a man suffering from nervous disposition to go and bake himself in the Medi- terranean for three months is idle and childish, and no sane man would think of doing anything of the sort. (Laughter.)—Mr. Bigham : I sheald have thought a fortnight at Southport would have been better.—Mr. Weal( argued that the company was liable in not tak- ing better precautions against accidents.—The jury found that the accident was caused by the negli- gence of the company, and that Neil, who drove , the trap, could not have avoided the accident by ' the exercise of reasonable skill and care. They awarded the plaintiff £275 damages.—The parties could not at I first agree to a settlement in the action brought by Dr. John M. O'Keefe, medical officer of health for Widnes, 1 who was also injured.—Mr. Weal( opened the case and said that the plaintiff wail 53 years of •age, and had a considerable practice. He still suffered from the effects of the accident, and had to give up his night calla. His expenses and loss of practice amounted to £2OO,—Dr. O'Keefe was then called, and while, under examination the counsel came to terms. It was agreed that the plain if should receive £275,—A third action was heard in which George J. Neil, pawnbroker, of Widnes, sought to recover damages for personal injuries, injury to his trap, and the price of the pony, which was drowned. The plaintiff was cross-examined as to his sale-book, which Mr. Bleb= suggested had been written up at one time. This the plaintiff denied, but he admitted that he could not 'find his sale-books prior to 1891. He had set down £2O for extra assistance. While he was away two extra Assistants had been employed each Satur day, one receiving 51. add the other 2s. Bd.—Mr.Big.ham: Then will you tell me how you make up the £2O ? Plaintiff: I could not bring it to anything like that. (Laughter.)—ln further examination he said the horse was worth at least £5O His saddler told him that the harness was damaged to the extent of £4 10s. He took a trip to the Mediterranean with his wife ; it was ordered by his doctor, lasted two months,and cost £lOO. He was charging £l5 for the keep of his children while he was away and the house shut up.—Mr. Bighain : Is it your view that when you fall into a canal, and a railway corn pany is held liable, they are to support your family from that , time forward,, (Laughter,)—Plaintiff : They wonld have been kept cheaper at bome..—Dr. O'Neil, of Widnes, and Dr. Whitford, of Liverpool, gave evidence that they considered the plaintiff was suffering from an incipient form of epilepsy, due to the accident,—ln summing up to the jury, Mr. M'Call said ,he did not object to the defendants criticising the plaintiff's claim, but he did complain that they slivuld make charges of fraud in connection with the book without producing the slightest tittle of evidence.—The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff for £250.

div.head: GREAT BRITAIN AND MOROCCO.
div.p: GREAT BRITAIN AND MOROCCO.

--- Since the rupture at Fez between the Sultan and Sir Charles Roan Smith there has been no renewal of nego- tiations. It is truo that the Moorish Minister for Foreign Affairs called on the British Minister on the latters return to Tangier, but no mention wis made of a resumption of negotiations, n)r have any envoys yet arrived at Tangier from the Sultan with that object. The report published by some London newspapers titat negotiations had actually been rGsum-d is therefore unfounded.

div.head: BISHOP OF LINCOLN CASE.
div.p: THE BISHOP OF LINCOLN CASE.

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council on Tues- day gave judgment in the case of the Bishop of Lincoln, who was charged with certain alleged illegal ritualistic practices. The charges came originally before the Arch- bishop of Canterbury mid other Church dignitaries, and that court found that some of the alieg,ed acts were not proved, and that others complained of were not illegal under given circumstances. Against this judgment com- plainants now appealed, but their lordships dismissed the appeal with costs.
MINERS' CONFERENCE AT BIR- MINGHAM.

The Miners' Coliference opened in Dirtninglitn on Tuesday, and there were delegates present from *early all the chief coal-getting districts of the country. The 1 proceedings were private. On Wednesday, when the proceedings were public, thanks were voted to the miners of Nottingham for their action during the late general election in opposiio,_ ' Broadhurst, who was a declared opponent of the rEight Hours Bill. A resoluticn was passed uraing upon Par- liament the importance of appointing a Labour Minister, and it was determined to use every effort to carry an Eight Hours Bill next session, the sugg ion of local option in the matter being repudiated. On Thursday the Coal Mines Regul, lun Act was dis- cussed. Durham having decided 1,. juin the Federation! the secretary was instructed to I ward the . necessary information. The sliding scale (-..tficulty in South Wales was under consideration, and it was resolved to send a Federation deputation to the men. Mrs, Fraser, wife of the bank clerk who, at Pol amt, Stirlingshire, on the night of Tuesday las!, Ifillt.d two neighbours and Seriously wounded a third, has suffered so much from the shock that it has been found necessary to remove her to the Asylum for the Insane at Larbert. . , • .„.

THE SECOND CHESHIRE RIFLE VOLUNTEERS IN CA.M.P!

The anfittal,week'e. training of. the _lnd Battaliol Cheshire Regiment teok place this week at the Isle of Man. The battalion coasist sof men fruit' Chester (five companieS); North evich, Ruticorn. end Frodee ham, and they travelled by train to Lime-.t., Liver- • pool; on 'Saturday last, Flare the three bands of the corps—Chester,Frodeham, and Runcorn—were inassed• and; under Bandmaster Carr, preceded the inee to HA Landing-stage playing the most lively airs es route. , . The origin of bookkeeping, like that of most other useful arts, is involved in great obscurity. Systematic, bookkeeping is generally admitted ,to have been,first practised at Venice, in thetifteenth, century. Lucas de Borgio published a regular treatise on the subject, in the Italian language, in 1496. Beekman, in his "History of Inventions," says that the Banians of India have bee from time immemorial in possession-of the method of bookkeeping by double entry;.apd tbat.iVeniee was the imporium of Indian commerce at. th 6 time Friar Lucas's tres!A appeared. Other authors think that doubleAtry was kilown to the ancients, and revived only' in •ItuV with the revival of com- merce; and certain gabtations are' "adduced in support of this opinion, which.. show -that -.the ancients entered the receipts! and, payments -of,, money on opposite pages in the way of nebtor and ' creditor; but nothing beyond single-entry can be Inferred from this practice. The first treatise on boekkeeping in the' triglish language, ''ot"vihich there is any aCeount;' Was' published in the year 160, by Hugh Oldcastle,d schoolmaster. . •

IT was said of Hannah More that when she, was told a tale against another in her village, her reply usually was," Come, we will go and ask if that be true." The effect was something wonderful. The tale-bearer, taken aback would begin to say, "Well, perhaps, there might have been a mistake," and to beg that no notice might be taken of the matter. But no; the good lady would go there and then, taking the scandal-monger with her, to make inquiry and compare accounts. If all tale-bearers could be treated in this way how few tales would be told!

THE poet Cowper says that "domestic happiness is the only bliss that has survived the Fall." The great Martin Luther said, speaking of marriage— " The utmost blessing that God can confer on a man Is the possession of a good and pious wife ; " and again he said, "To rise betimes and to marry young are what no man ever repents of doing." One old English poet pronounced a true marriage " a pattern of celestial peace," and another called it 'heaven on earth"—
IT is 'indolence that exhausts, not action, in which there is life, health, and pleasure. The spirita may be exhausted and wearied by em- ployment, but they are utterly wasted by idleness.

div.p: tetter to the attar.
THE NEW PARLIAMENT AND THE DIRECT
VETO.

Sir,—lt may interest many of your readers to know that 297 members of the new Parliament have promised to support a measure giving to the people, in their res- pective localities, a direct veto power over the issue and renewal of licenses for the common sale of intoxicating liquors, viz. :—Gladstonians : England, 193 ; Wales, 27 ; Scotland, 49 ; 269. Liberal Unionists: England, 8; Scot- land, 7 ; Ireland, 2 ; 15. Conservatives: England, 2 ; Scotland, 2; Ireland, 9 ; 13. There are only 6 Glad- stonian Liberals unpledged in support of this question.— Yours truly, J. H. 8, Esplanade, Waterloo, August 4th, 1892.

div.head: BISHOP JAYNE.
div.p: BISHOP JAYNE.

Sir,—lt appears from the Press that his lordship has written to the London School Board complaining that the girls at the Industrial Schools at Stockport and Sale are not allowed to be prepared for confirmation. Before doing so, he ought to prove the rite to be Sriptural,and so act up to Article Six. Possibly the authorities con- nected with these schools have been searching for them- selves on this matter, and have concluded that it is not Scriptural. Article Twanty-tive classes it as a false sacrament. Archbishop Cranmer said it was never in- stituted by Christ ; his chaplain, T. Becon, wrote it was brought into the church by man. Bishop rtyle in his second charge, October, 1884, says :—" Confirmation is not a sacrament ordained by Christ Himself, and gene- rally necessary to salvation; it is one of the most impor- tant ordinances which the Church of England has pro- vided for its members." Archdeacon Taylor, of Liver- pool, in his catechism on confirmation says :—"lt was not enjoined by Christ or the Apostles; it rests upon the authority of the Church." It is one of the chief pieces of work the bishop has to do for his £3,500 a year. J K. Blunt, in his Bible Dictionary, p. 143, says :—" There is no verbal institution of this rite by our Lord," and in his key to the Book of Common Prayer, p. 88, says := " None shall be admitted to the Sacrament of the Body and Blcod of Christ (except at the point of death) unless he has been confirmed, or has been reasonably hindered from receiving confirmation." There is not a shadow of Scripture to support such teaching. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, August 3rd, 1892.

div.head: LIVESEY.
div.p: LIVESEY.
THE NEW PARLIAMENT.
SCENE AT THE OPENING.

There was the usual rush for seats in the House of Commons this morning, on the part of gentlemen famous for enterprise of this description. Mr. Ernest Spencer, who on the last occasion was just beaten, by Mr. Dixon Hartland, turned the tables on that gentlemah by putting in an appearance before eight o'clock this morning. Mr. Bigwood was the next arrival, followed after a brief interval by Mr. Dixon Hartland, whose consternation was great when he discovered that his was not the first but the third place in the race for seats. A more striking personality was the next corner Sir Charles Dilke, who secured his old place, but at first took up a position on the Conservative side, apparently forgetful that the Government of Lord Salisbury was still in office. This mistake was promptly rectified, and the member for the Forest of Dean retired to the library Mr. Jacks, who was a member of the short Parliament, arrived at the House shortly before ten, and was speedily followed by others. At 11 o'clock there were some 15 members in the House. Mr. Walter M'Laren was the first local member to put in an appearance. As early as eight o'clock there was a considerable display of popular interest outside Palace Yard, little crowds of people collecting at the gates watching for the arrival of members. At ten o'clock the Yeomen of the Guard from the Tower reached the House, and at once began their search for possible gunpowder barrels. Marching to the House of Lords, and each carrying a lantern, they descended by the trap door at the back of the throne to the vaults, where they made the usual formal inspection. The beefeaters then marched to the Commons, filed down the iron staircase by the Speaker's chair, and searched the chambers below. Mr. Miehael Davitt took a seat on the Irish benches, undeterred by certain whisperings that his right to take the oath would be contested. He looked in much im- proved health, and was very warmly received by his colleagues, a large number of whom had assembled in the lobby. Mr. Da.vitt subsequently secured the seat formerly occupied by Mr. Parnell. At a quarter-past one o'clock nearly every seat on the Opposition side of the House was appropriated, but on the Ministerial side of the 11 ,use the benches were only scantily occupied. The first gentleman of first bench rank to arrive was Mr. John Morley. Mr. Balfour was loudly cheered by the crowd on his arrival, but the re- ception of Mr. John Burns was mixed. At a quarter to two o'clock the mace was brought in by a messenger and deposited under the table. The ex- Speaker (Mr. Peel) entered the House at five minutes to two o'clock, and was immediately surrounded by a num- ber of members who warmly shook him by the hand. Afterwards he took the seat at the corner of the third bench on the Ministerial side. Mr. Chamberlain came in a few minutes later, and sat down beside Sir H.James and Mr. Courtney on the front Opposition bench.
88-CEPTION OF MI2. LADSTONE.

Mr. Gladstone left Carlton House-terrace for the House of Commons in a pair horse brougham, accom- panied by Mrs. Gladstone, and met with an enthusias- tic reception from the crowd and also in the House, the Irish members rising in their places and waving their hats and cheering, and the Liberals joining in the latter part of the demonstration.
SUMMONS TO TUN LOOM.
At ten minutes past two the Yeoman Usher of the Block Rod (Colonel Butler) summoned the House of Peers to hear the commission read, and there was an immediate exodus.
ELECTION OF SPEAKER.

When the House re-assembled the Clerk standing up, pointed to Sir Matthew White Ridley, who moved that Mr. Peel be re-elected Speaker of the House. Ma. GLADSTONAS, who was again loudly cheered, seconded the motion. He said he joined in the hope that there would be no discordant note in the proceed- ceedings or in the discussion. The position of the Speaker was one of great influence and power, and it was desirable that any gentleman called to that office should possess the unquestioned confidence of the House. In recent years, certainly since the time of the Speaker- ship of Mr. Manners Sutton, afterwards Lord Canter- bury, there had been a great change in the duties of the office, which at that time was comparatively small. They are now voluminous and onerous. They did not expect that the Speaker would be infallible, but they looked to him to possess wide knowledge,great patience, and a thormigh mastery of procedure, whilst to his per- sonal honour not a breath of suspicion must attach. All these demands were satisfied in the case of Mr. Peel, and therefore lie had the greatest Pleasure in seconding the motion. The motion was carried unanimously, and Mr. Past returned thanks for the honour conferred upon him. This was the fourth occasion on which he had been elected Speaker, and if he filled the chair again he would feel under a lengthened chain of obligation to , the Rouse, to which at large he would lookfor support in his efforts to uphold the traditions which for centuries had gathered round the chair of the House. Mr. •Gladstone and Sir Matthew White Ridley then con- ducted Mr. Peel to the chair, the members rising in their places as the right hon. gentleman took his seat. On the motion f Mr. A. J. BALFOUR the House adjourned till twelve o'clock next day..

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.

--- The House of Lords met at two o'clock, when Parlia- ment was formally opened by Royal Cominissiam The Royal Commissioners were the Lord Chancellor, the Duke of Rutland, the Earl of Lathom, Viscount Cross, and Lord linutaford,

In accordance with precedent, and in obedience to a summons from the Black Rod, there was a large attend- ance from the Commons to hear the Royal Commission read. The Commission was read, and the Commons having retired the Bishop of Ripon read prayers, after which the peers present were sworn in and subscribed to the roll of Parliament. Their Lordahipg adjourned at twenty minutes past two during pleasure.

Nowt ridiculous in id? Henry th' Eighth dud id? Just sooa, boil, he hed a differ- ent wife every time, whereas this mon keeps geddin wed to th' same wife ; an' his own too !
