Dud yo' ever hear o' sich tumfc 'ery o' yo'r lives ? An' Lh' nineteenth century, too. Aw've bowt Brussels carpets as torned eawt tapes- try, an' aw've bin as puzzled o'er Brussels spreawts as grow i' England, but this Brussels young woman is a corker, an' no mistake ; iv hoo'd ha' shot hereer —an' aw dorn'd think boo wod ha' done—aw sup- pooase her friend wod ha' bin browt up for morther, or manslowter? Aw heyn'd time to argy th' matter pro an' con, but aw'll mek th' subject a present to eawr judges, an' to Mutual Improvement Societies ; no deawt th' Daily News or Tallygrafil hey a corres- pondence sterttd on id. Ov coourse aw blame th' general lection for o' these cases o' temporary insanity—just as aw blame Id for th'G.O.NL's cowd ; an' there's one instance aw heyn'd mentioned, but aw will. Yo' see it's this way. Jeffrey Fairhurst were comin' eawt o'th' Huntsman's Arms, at Haydock, on th' twenty- seckond °last month, when a collier o'th' name o' Pat Donoghue axt him wor be a Gladstooan mon ? Jeffrey sterted explainin' wod he wor, when Pat grabbed his watch an' off wi' id; " Six months herd" were additidnal time thrown in bi Denman last Monde' at Liverpool. Aw thowt th' Judge wod ha' t'en into consideration th' aggravation Pat hid. Aw've stood listenin' to chaps as tried to explain wod they wor, an' aw know heaw a motes senses leeave him at sicn a time,an' as he's nod ref,p)nsible for his actions. Fancy yo'rsel's hearkenin some- body tell yo' he were a Gladstoonian, but he wor'd i' favour o' Hooam Rule ; yigh, an' doin' his level best to prove id. lirod'nd yo' be justified i' leatherin' him, or steylin' owt he hed—eksept his pollaticks ?

ANI see th' Committee are sparin' no pains to mek thad Dental Exhibition i' Manchester next week a big success. They seldom do spare ony "pains," an' non- committeemen back 'em up weel ; aw know thad fro' experience. They're beawn to hey peppers read on th' subject o' tooth drawin', an' t pepper 'll be illustrated wi' drawin's ; &ma there 'll be some gain, by gum Aw daresay they'll ax some fooak th' audience to step up an' be operated on, an' a tooathri may oblige 'em, but aw wod less aw'd sets top an' bottom. •
Dear o' me! Aw meant to tell yo' abeawt Perlyment meetin' on th' 4th„an' gooan an' cleyn fergetten ! Well, id 'll happen keep till next week.
THE ALLEGED ASSAULT ON A DAUGHTER.

At the Liverpool Assize. on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Denman, John Richard Massey (35), barber, was indicted for having, at Warrington, on the sth June, assaulted his daughter, Edith Massey, a girl twelve years and five months old. Mr. Hope prosecuted, and Mr. Madden defended. Evidence, similar to that previously reported in our columns, was given by six neighbours in snpport of the charge.—Upon the girl being sworn she said that her father did not assault her. The girl wrote down the name of an individual, and his lordship, after looking at it, said he would pass it to counsel. During the further hearing of the case it transpired that the in- dividual the girl referred to was a labourer in Warring- ton, and that he had undergone a term of twenty months' imprisonment for an assault.—On being putinto the box the prisoner denied that that he had ever assaulted his daughter.—The jury, after a short consultation, found the prisoner not guilty, and he was discharged. The hearing of the case lasted for several hours.

div.head: LA.NCASIIIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: LA.NCASIIIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The Lancashire County Council met at Preston on Thursday, under the presidency of the Right Hon. J, T. Ilibbert, M.P. Mr. Guthrie presented the report of the Finance Committee and the budget for the year. Reference was made in the Report to the disallowance by the District Auditor of sums amounting to £114,554 paid out of the Exchequer Contribution Account in aid of the main roads expendi- ture. At the previous meeting of the Council the Dis- trict Auditor was condemned as acting in an absolute and illegal fashion. In the meantime the matter has been before the Court of Queen's Bench, who have decided the points at issue in favour of the County Council. Mr. Guthrie's budget provided for an expendi- ture during the year of £205,447, as against £191,874 in the previous year. Mr. T. Snape, M.P., who submitted the report of the Technical Education Committee, said that the work of the Committee was proceeding excell- ently. A resolution was proposed requiring contractors to sign a declaration that they pay the trade-union rate of wages and observe the hours of labour and conditions recognised by the trade unions. By 53 votes against 9 the resolution was defeated.

div.head: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The Cheshire County Council had under consid- eration on Thursday reports on the subject of asylum accommodation in the county. It appears that if the asylums are to continue to receive patients from the city of Chester they will have to undergo considerable extensions. A committee was appointed to inquire into certain aspects of the qnestion and report. If was reported that the Techni- cal Instruction Committee have under consideration a scheme of technical education which has fur its crown- ing feature the establishment of an agricultural college in the centre of the county. An interesting discussion took place on the administration of the county charities and it is understood that at the next meeting a motion will be submitted asking the Local Government Board to give the Council power to take under its control all the charities in the county that are improperly adminis- tered.

div.head: RUNCORN MATTERS.
div.p: RUNCORN MATTERS.

At the quarterly meeting of Cheshire County Council, on Thursday, there was presented the report, of the committee appointed to take into con- sideration the memorial from the Widnes Local Board and the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners as to the erection of a vehicular bridge across the River Mersey between Runcorn and Wid- nes was received, but it was adjourned sine die in order to enable the local authorities of Runcorn and Widnes to produce further evidence in support of theirmemorial. It was resolved that the further consideration of the memorial be adjourned until after the adjourned meeting of the conference. The Technical Instruction Committee reported that at a meeting held at Crewe, on May 27, it was decided to recommend Runcorn for a grant of £ll4, and Altrincham £4BO.

CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. The anniversary in connection with the Clergy Widows' and Orphans' Fund and the Clergy Dough- ters' School was held at the institution on Thurs- day. The usual business meeting was first held. Mr. George Barbour, of Chester, presided. The Secretary of the Clergy Widows' and Orph ans' Fund (Canon Penrhyn) read the minutes of the previous meeting, which were adopted. The Rev. Canon Pesinnyx, as the honorary secretary to the Clergy Widows' and Orphans' Fund, in his report regretted that the hope the committee expressed in their last report, that their late treasurer (Mr. Ed. Greenall) might be restored to health, had not been rea- lised. He had been called to his rest, and they had also to mourn the removal of a still older and not less warm friend of the institutions in person Lord Winmar- leigh, as well as another more recent member of the committee, Mr. Fletcher Rogers, of Liverpool. Two other members of the committee had also been lost to them. Canon Moberley and the Rev. F. C. French had left the dioceses respectively of Chester and Liverpool. It was recommended that their places should he filled by the Rev. Canon Blackburne and the Rev. W. Willink,that ot Lord Wininarleigh,in the diecese of Manchestor,by M. W. H. Hornby, M.P., and that of Mr. Fletcher Rogers by by Mr.R. A. D's Willis. No other names having been sent in to the secretary the retiring members of the Commit- tee were re-appointed, viz: the Rev. Canons Turner and Blackburn, Lord Egerton of Tatton, and Mr. T. H. Lyon, of Chester; the Right Rev. Bishop Cremer Roberts, Canon Stowell, Mr. J. T. Storming, Mr. W. N. Heald, of Manchester, and the Rev. Canons Livingstone and Diggle, Mr. J. W. Fair, and Mr. R. A. Do Willis, of I Liverpool. Since the last anniversary 4 small special grants had been made amounting to £3l. During the year 4 of the pensioners had died, and two in the diocese of Manchester had withdrawn. They had no fewer than 9 new applications—one widow and one orphan from Manchester. There were now on the list :--Chester, 20 widows, and 9 orphans ; Liverpool, 11 widows and 10 orphans ; Manchester, 29 widows and 17 orphans. Free education in the clergy daughters' school was provided for 6 orphans. The meeting would be asked to sanction pensions, donations, and payments for free scholars, to the amount of £2,070. The amount last year was £2,080. The income of the charity for the year ending December 31st, 1891, was £2,224 183. 9d. made op as follows :—Special donations £ll4 4s. 6d. ; interest on capital, £667 19A. 9d. ; collections, £522 83. 4d. ; sub- scriptions, £774 9s. 9d. Unappropriated fund, Chester and Liverpool £134 ; bank interest, £ll 17s. sd. The report concluded with an appeal for more subicriptions. The RECTOR of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis) honorary secretary of the Clergy daughters' school read his report :—He had much pleasure in speaking very favourably of the school in all respects. During the past half year Bible classes had been held for each of the three divisions once a week, while the school had been in residence. The conduct was all he could wish, the interest evident, the answers intelligent. The Examiner's report was also read, which was of a satisfactory character, and the three reports were adopted. The DEAN of Manchester proposed that the list of , pensions, donations, Sze., be approved, and expressed the wish that the Committee had more money at their disposal. The list was approved. The SECRETARY announced that the preacher this year ould be the Bev. Canon Munro, of Liverpool, and that IMr. Gilmour, of Liverpool, would be invited to be president. Canon Brian' moved that the recommendations of the Corn:nittee in regard to vacancies he approved, and the places of Canon Moberley and the Rev. F. C. Trench I be tilled by Canon Blackburn and the Rev. J. W. I Willinck, and those of the late Lord Wintnarleigh and Mr. Flettther Rogers by Mr. W. H. Hornby, M.P., and Mr. D's Willis. Mr. GRAFTON seconded, and the motion was adopted.

_ On the motion of the Bishop of Chester, seconded by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton' a vote of thanks was ac- corded to the president, for his past services, which he atetnowledged, and the meeting concluded. The Bishop of Chester subsequently preached in the Parish Church from Joshua 23 c. and part of 27 v. He said his hearers would readily understand the applica- tion of his text. The Warrington institutions on behalf of which he was preaching, were a witness, a great con- secrated witness, between those who were still living and labouring in the management of the institutions and those who founded them, a witness again between the representatives of the diocese of Chester and the dioceses of Manchester and Liverpool. The prayers were read by the Rector, and the anthem taken from Proverbs. Doth not wisdom cry ?" A collection was made in aid of the institutions, which realised £37 ss. 2d., £l6 ss. 2d. more than last year. Luncheon was then partaken of, Mr. G. Barbour pre- siding. There were also among those present :—The Bishop of Chester, the Dean of Manchester, the Arch- deacon of Chester, Canons Postance, M. Wood, Penrhyn, Stowell, Birlev, Blundell, and Mason, Mrs. Mason, the Rev. F. W. Willis, Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, theßevs. Hutchings, C.Lowe Wilkinson, Woosnam, G. Booth, and Fitzroy, the Rev. J. and Mrs. Langham the Mayor (Mr. E. cireenall) and the Mayoress, Mr. john White and Mrs. White, Dr. Watkins, Mrs. Lister Kaye, Mrs. Beamont, Captain and Mrs. Withington, Mrs. Buckton, Miss Beal, Mrs. Mark- ham Parr, and Mr. arid Mrs. Edelsten,most of the gentle- men named having been present at the preceding meet- ing. The usual loyal toasts having been drunk, the CHAIR- mem proposed that of the bishop and clergy of the diocese of Chester Manchester, and Liverpool,coupled with the name of the Bishop of Chester. (Applause.) The Bishop of Chester, he said, had set such an example of hard work and energy, and of doing good in the high position in which he was placed, as the clergy and laity alike would do well to try humbly to imitate. He was sure they could see from the Bishop of Chester that the office of bishop was no sinecure. He was determined that at any rate in his diocese the Church should not sleep, that it should not be the Church of one close, but the Church of the people, deeply engraven in their hearts, and cherished in their affections. The BISHOP OF CHESTER, in responding said he had long been supplied with most stimulating examples both amen.' the clergy and the laity. They wanted the world as full as possible of inspiring patterns, and he at least was richly supplied with these. He congratulated the meeting on having the Mayor present—(applause)— and said he could not help rejoicing when he saw him there, that the municipal life of Warrington, and they might be sure the diocese in general, was heartily at one with them. The Dean of MANCHESTER proposed the health of the president, and made an urgent appeal for the increase of support to the institution, and the Chairman responded. Mr. JOHN WHITE proposed the toast of "Success to the Institutions." Be referred regretfully to the deaths ot Mr. John Tinsley, Mr. Edward Greenall. and Lord Win- Winmarleigh, that great nobleman, he said, who was one of the earliest and greatest benefactors of the insti- tutions ; and than whose loss there had never been al greater in this generation to this district. He coupled with the toast the name of Canon Penrhyn, who re- ' sponded. The Archdeacon of CHESTER proposed the toast of "The town and trade of Warrington." The president, he remarked, had said a very heavy burden rested upon his shoulders in proposing the healths of the bishops and clergy of the three dioceses. Then surely it must be a heavy responsibility upon him to propose the present toast. when he was told that there was no trade not re- presented in the town of Warrington. He had every satisfaction in knowing that the toast would be responded to by one who la re the honoured name of Oreeuall, and he hoped they would always have some member of that family to walk in the steps of those who had gone before, and maintain the traditions of that name. The MATOR responded. He said as a Warrington man he was r mud of Warrington as a town, and still more to be its representative on that occasion, knowing that Warrington could claim a north of England reputation for uprightness and sterling common-sense. During the last few years the municipal life of Warrington had greatly improved in many respects, namely in the in- crease of church accommodation, widening of streets, sanitary improvements, the institution of a gymnasium, and the commencment of public baths. The health re- turns of the town compared favourably with those of other towns, and it ranked as one of the best paved towns in the north. Warrington in other respects, was a prosperous town, and, with good management, he had no doubt, would continue to prosper. There was every prospect that the Manchester Ship Canal, and the Lan- cashire, Derbyshire, and East Coast Railway, providing greater and cheaper facilities of transit to the coast and opening up accesss to new districts,would do much to im- prove the trade of the town. He felt sure that Warring- ton owing to the exceptional advantages she possessed, and was likely to obtain, would ere long rank as one of the most important towns of the North of England. (Applause.) The Bishop of Chester proposed a vote of thanks to the Rector ot Warrington, and his lady and gentlemen colleagues for the manner in whtth they had organised the festival, and this toast having been heartily drunk the company dispersed. 4. THE FATAL STRIKE RIOTS IN AMERICA VERDICT OF TEfE JURY. Pirrsnuno, THURSDAY.—The arrest ef two of Messrs. Carnegie and Company's officials at Homestead yester- day, on information laid by Hugh Ross, one of the men accused of murder and riot, was attended by very tur- bulent scenes. The strikers gathered around the con- stables and their prisoners and muttered threats against them. So threatening became their attitude that it was found necessary to call out the militia, who forced the crowd back, and arrested one of the rioters. The coroner's jury who inquired into the killing of seven strikers and three detectives at Homestead have returned their verdict. They declare that the strikers were killed while in unlawful assembly upon Messrs. Carnegie's property to prevent the landing of the Pinkerton guards and as regards the Pinkerton men, they were killed by an unlawful assemblage, and the jury added " we find that the shooting was done by some party or parties un- known with felonious intent.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 6, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 6, 1892.

110.1 N TINIEST TO THE LATE MR. T. JOLLEY. Some time ago a movement was set on foot for the purpose of raising a fund for the erecting of a , memorial to the late Mr. T. Jolley, a young man ' who had attained prominence as a footballer and a cricketer, and whoss death occasioned so much regret throughout the town. The Committee which undertook the raising of the fund was a large one,and its members represented the Football, the Cricket, and the Conservative Clubs of which the deceased was a member, and also the Whiteeross Works at which he was employed. The secretary was Mr. Strettle, and the treasurer Mr. Knowles. A substantial amount was raised by the Committee, and a handsome and imposing monument has now been raised over the grave of Mr. Jolley in the ceme- tery. It takes the form of a Runic Cross composed of the best Bolton-wood: stone, and stands about eight feet high. There is a beautiful carved figure of an angel in front, one hand pointing upwards, and the other holding a laurel wreath. On a scroll are the borough arms, and there are also shown the tools of the deceased's trade, a football, a cricket bat, and other accesories of the games in which he took so much interest. The monument has been the work of Mr. F. A. Essenhigh, of this town, and ,it has been admirably executed. The cost was be- tween £5O and £6O.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this authority was held at the Workhouse, yesterday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present, Messrs. Fairclough, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, A. Jolley, Humphreys, Dignum ; S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), F. Kerfoot (inspector), Dr. Seph- ton (medical officer). THE CEMETERY AT RIXTON.—A CURIOUS DirEicur.Tr. —me CLERK read a letter from the Locat Government Board, with reference to the application for power to borrow £1,700 for the making of a cemetery at Itixton. They pointed out that a cemetery could not be made within 200 yards of a dwelling-house unless with the written consent of the owner or the lessee.—The Clerk explained that in this case there was only the owner of enti small cottage whose consent had not been obtained. He believed it was a Mr. Devonport, of Widnes. Ile had no objectiou to the cemetery but he declined to sign his name to a paper.—Mr. W. Houghton thought they might write to the Local Government Board to explain this circumstance. —The Clerk Clerk said that, in that case they would probably reply that the law was laid down and they could not depart from it. Perhaps if Mr. Devenport would not sign the paper he would let him (the clerk) sign it for him. (Laughter.)—The MEDICAL OFFICER said that the house was nearer the old cemetery than it would be to the new one —On the motion of Mr. W. HOUGHTON it was decided that the Clerk should take what steps he deemed desir- able to get the signature of the property owner referred to. _ .

THE COST OF ISOLATION.—The CLERK said that an ac- count amounting to £37 16s. had been sent by the War- rington Corporation as the cost of isolating in the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital the three persons who were taken from the Authority's district suffering from small-pox.— In answer to a question he said he thought the charges were very reasonable, taking everything into account. He added that he did not think the Authority would be in a position to recover any part of the charges from the relatives of the patients.
LYMM.
EX(XIiSIONISTS AT LYmm.—On Monday there were a large number of visitors in Lymin, many being brought to the village by bfeat along the canal and others by rail.

OUTBREAK OF SHEEP SCAB.—This disease has broken out on the farm of Mr. Jesse Norcott, at Cowley, 13 sheep and lamps being affec'ed. The matter has been reported to the police, and the animals have,been isolated and dressed.

UHL/CENSE]) HAWKER.--At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, before Dr. Brabazon, James Royle, a tramp, was charged with hawking small wares without a license Evidence was given in support of the charge, and pri- soner was committed for seven days imprisonment with hard labour. DEATH OF MRS. WIESTANLEY.—The remains of Mrs. Winstanley, landlady of the Farmers' Arms, Lymm, who died on Thursday, last week, after a short illness, were interred at the Parish Church, Lymm, on Monday, in the presence of a large number of relatives and friends. The deceased lady was one of the oldest inhabitants in Lvmm, and was highly respected by a large circle of Mends.

LY3III FOOTBALL aue.—The annual general meeting of the abovt club was held last evening week. The secretary, in his report, showed that the last season had been a successful one, the club having played 10 matches, of which 6 had been won, 3 lost, and one drawn, and scoring 28 goals, against the 17 of their op- ponents. After some discussion, it was unanimously decided to enter a team for the Cheshire Junior Cup for the coming season. The following officers were elected for the season, 1892-3 :—Captain, Mr. T. H. Peters ; sub-captain, Mr. G. Whelan; treasurer ; Mr. J. Pearson; secretary, Mr. W. Gould ; committee, Messrs. Catneron, Upson, Gleave, ar.d Dodson. .. 1 , 140CA.L BOARD MEETING:—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the clerk's office, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Jas. Gregson (chairman) presiding. There were present—Messrs. H. Harrison, R. Whitelegg, J. Holt, W. 1 Brazendale, J. Perrin, S. Appleton, T. J. Ridgeway (law clerk); W. Mullard (clerk), Jas. Mort (surveyor), and W. Severs (gas manager). The report on the examination in drawing was read, from which it appeared that 12 presented themselves before the examiner, and one passed in the second class. This entitled the Board to the Science and Art Dedartment's grant of 10s., less 144th, and it was resolved to make application for the money.—A letter was read from Mr. It. P. Ward, organ- izing secretary to the technical Instruction Committee of the County Council, asking for particulars as to the expenditure of the grant received inns the County Council, and the sum raised by the Board for the purposes of technical instruction. Mr. Ward also inquired whether the Board had levied the id. rate for technical instruction for the current year.—The Clerk presented a statement which he had prepared, and from this it appeared that the total income was £197 4e. 5d., the chief sources being :—Grant from the Council,l £ll9, the rate or grant from local authority, I £76 ss. 6d. The expenditure included :—Salaries, art £lO. other subjects £53 Bs.; maintenance, £9 135.; apparatus and books, £3 3s. 7d. The balance to 1892-3 was £44 4s. 6d. The number o, students under instruction in the classes during the year ending June 30th, 1892, was—males, 63; females, 105 ; total 168. The subjects taken were—Drawing (free- hand). geametry. shorthand, French, dressmaking (theoretical and practical), and cookery ; 14 were pre- sented for examination in freehand drawing, and three in geometry. There were no examinations in the other subjects. Mr Ridgway informed the Board that the Governors of the Grammer School had given two foundation scholarships—one to the Parochial school and one to the school at Ouglitrington. These would entitle a boy from each school to free education at the Gram- mer school for two or three years. It would, of course, depend on their conduct and behaviour, and whether they made sufficient progress to justify keeping them at the school.

SUCCESSFUL WARRINGTON SWIMMER. ' At the first annual swimming gala, held at the Boundary-road baths, St. Helens, for the benefit of the manager. E. A. Jones, of Warrington, won the let prize in the 100 yards open handicap. Ist heat : J. Preston (6 secs.) ; 2nd heat: D. W. Holland (12 secs.,) 1 ; J. Finegan (Liverpool), (30 secs.) 2 ;3rd heat E. A. Jones, Warrington, (go), 1 ; J. Sherwood (11 secs.), 2. The final was a good race, the result being that Jones, whose first, public appearance this was, carried off the first prize, a regulation clock, Preston taking second place. and Holland being third.

WARRINOTON.
SALE OF WORK AT THE IZECTORY GBOI:NDS.

The sale of work which was opened on Thursday week at the Rectory grounds, in aid of Warrington mission fund and also the Society for the Propaga- tion of the Gospel,was continued on Saturday. The weather was very favourable, and there was a good attendance.

div.head: TouniNG IN THE NETHERLANDS.
div.p: TouniNG IN THE NETHERLANDS.

The party of Warrington gentlemen who left Warrington aboni. a fortnight ago under the care of the Rev. T. M. H. Hughes, curate of St. Paul's Church, for a tour in the Netherlands, returned home on Saturday. The tnurists spent a most en- joyable holiday..

div.head: WEDDING PARTY.
div.p: A WEDDING PARTY.

On Monday afternoon a party, at which there were about 70 guests present, was held in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-st., to celebrate the wedding of Miss Lee, of Friars-green, and Mr. Isaac Hough- ton, of Bewsey-road. The hall was tastefully deco- rated, the whole of the arrangements being under the care of Mr. D. Lowe. During the afternoon the party were photographed. The wedding itself took place at St. Paul's Church, and the presents to the bride were numerous and valuable. The newly- wedded pair went to the Isle of Man to spend their honeymoon. .

div.head: SAD END.
div.p: A SAD END.

The death was recorded by the police of Francis Holmes, a bookbinder, 45 years of age, as having taken place on Sunday. Deceased, it is stated, had for the last twelve months, been of drunken habits, and during the last three months has only worked about a day in the week. On Saturday afternoon he was seen the worse for drink in Bridge-st., and he was, about midnight, found in the closet of a lodging-house. He was considered to be helplessly drunk and was taken into the house, but as he did not awake. he was, about half-past six, sent to the workhouse hospital where he died in the afternoon. FATAL RESULT OF AN ACCIDENT AT SANKEY BRIDGES.

Ann Worrell, aged 56 years. wife of William Worrell, a labourer living in Wright-st., Sankey Bridge.., died at eleven p.m. on Monday, through injuries sustained by falling downstairs the pre- vious night. Deceased was in the house by herself. Her nepnew, Joseph Lingley, lodges with her, but he left home at five o'clock on Sunday night. At that time she was in good health. When lie returned he found her lying at the bottom of the stairs near the back door. She told him she had fallen downstairs, whereupon lie obtained the assis- tance of her daughter-in-law, who put her to bed, and sent for Dr. Braids. ller injuries were about the neck and arms. She died at the time stated above. HOUGHTON HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.

The gardens of the above society's district (which includes the townships of Houghton, Middleton and Arbury, Poulton-with-Fearnhead, Winwick- with-Hulme and Hermitage Green) entered for competition for the prizes offered by the society for She neatest and best cultivated cottage garden were judged on Monday by Messrs. J. Randall and G. Watkins. of Newton, the appointed judges. The number of the gardens entered for competition was 13, and they presented a very satisfactory appear- ance. The judges' decision will not be known until the 2nd of September. the day of the annual show Messrs. W. Sweetlove and T. Smith accompanied the judges to the gardens, but took no part in the judging of them. W ARRINGTON VOLUNTRERS, F COMPANY.

The above company, to the number of 26 men, paraded at one o'clock on Saturday, and proceeded to Widnes, for third class tiring, under the command of Lieut. R. J. (Thorley. Prizes to the amounts of 7s. Oct., 55., 21. 61, and Is. 6d. were offered, providing 20 men attended on the day appointed. Great credit is due to the officers and sergeants for having raised the requisite number of men. The weather was all that could be desired, and resulted in some good scores being made. Results : Lance- Sergeant J. J. Heslreth 69 points, Private G. Uns- worth 69, Private J. J. Mather 67, Private J. Wood 167, Col.-Sergeant J. T. Bennion 65, Corporal W. gabberly 65, Lance-Sergt. F. IChorley 60, liance-Serseant A. Pitt 59, Private J. Scott 59, Private J. T. Kay .58, Private J. C. Tenge 54, Lance-Corporal F. Jones 54, Private J. H. Dobson 51, Private J. Graley 49, Private R. W. Marsh 42, Private A. Craddock 33, Private C. Powell 31. , Recruits : Private T. Massam 65, and Private J. Lloyd 58. WALKING DAY AT STItETTON.

This annual fete took plade at Stretton. yesterday week, the weather being most favourable. The children assembled in the schools at one p.m., and proceeded to church, headed by the Warrington Blue Coat School Band, tke latter playing " Onwata Christian Soldiers," the children carrying banners and flags. A short service was held, and an address given by the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Dodd. After leaving the church, they wended their way to the vicarage grounds, where they were served with buns, &e. They again formed in procession, and marched through the village headed by the band, which played lively airs. Arriving at the schools, the children and friends, nunsbering WO, sat down to a substantial tea, full justice being done to the good things provided. After tea, various games were indulged in, and prizes given for racing. Much amusement was caused by a tug of war be- tween the Blue Coat School and the Stretton choir boys, the latter winning after a severe struggle. The usual ball was held at night, in the schoolroom, over thirty couples taking part in t!,e dancing.

WHITE GLOVES FOR A-C-OUNTY MAGISTRATE. On Wednesday morning when in the usual course the Warrinwon County Sessions would have been held, Mr. E. Greenall, the magistrates' clerk, said he was pleased to inform the Chairman (Mr. John , Crosfield) w ho was accompanied by Mr. J. J. Bleckly, that there were no cases at all for him, and it was his pleasing duty to present him with a pair of white kid gloves.—Mr. Crosfield : I am very much obliged to you, and very pleased to hear that War- rington and the neighbourhood is in such an excel- lent condition. hope there may be no more cases for the next twelve months.—Mr. Blackly : lam very pleased to express the same opinion. I have Ito congratulate Mr. Greenall on the sinecure he occupies to-day. HOUGHTON ODDFELLOWS' ANNIVERSARY. The members of the "Sir Gilbert Greenall "Lodge of the Loyal Order of Oddfellows' Friendly Society held at the Plough Inn, Houghton Green,celebrated their anniversary on Monday afternoon. The members met at the lodge at one o'clock, and at two sat down to a substantial dinner, served by Mr. G. Derbyshire, the host and treasurer, in good style. The number present was 45. Afterwards dancing was enjoyed OM the green and in the large club room, there being a good attendance. Mr. Thompson's quadrille band of Warrington, played lan excellent selection of music far dancing in capital style. From the society's annual report for the year ending 31st of December last, it appears that the society at that date, numbered 142 mem- bers, and the total amount of funds was £690 16s. 81., being a gain for the year of .£22 15s. 80., and the average amount of funds per member, .£4 17s. 30.

- - , PADOATE CHURCH SCHOOL SERMONS. The annual school sermons in connection with the Church Sunday School were preached on Sunday in Patigate Church. In the morning the Vicar (the Rev. .1. J. Langharn) preached to a large congrega- tion, from the words, "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old he will not depart from it," and pointed out that in the day and Sun- day schools the future of a child was laid. He remarked that they were fined in the day schools at Padgate for their poverty. They had to realize a certain proportion of their income. This they bad not done during the past year, and, therefore, they had received less from the (icvernment than they ! had earned. . Under the,circumstances he appealed to the congregation to increase the income, and thus place them in a position to obtain the full grant earned. In the evening the pulpit was occu- pied by the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., rector of War- rington, who based his discourse on the words: "Take this child away, and nurse it for me, mad I will give thee thy wages." In his remarks, the rev, gentleman said that it was the duty of every parent to see that his children were baptised and admitted into Christ's Church, that they attended both Church and Sunday school, that they were taught to pray, and that they were confirmed when they became of the proper age. In the morning an anthem, taken from Psalm ciii., was rendered by the choir, Master T. Beavers singing the solo in a creditable manner. At the evening service the 'anthem was taken from Psalm cxxxiii., the bass solo being admirably rendered by Mr. William Howard, and the duet by Masters T. Beevers and T. Antrobus. Mr. Fornear was at the organ. Offer- tories were taken during the day in aid of the day and Sunday schools, and amounted to ..Cl6 Os. 9d. FEVER EPIDEMIC. The London Hospital fever patients now number 3,244. .
THREE AT A BIRTH.
At Kettering, on Thursday, the wife of a labourer named Holland was safely delivered of triplets. All are doing well. The Queen's bounty has befin applied for.
TWO FISHERMEN DROWNED.

The steamship Hartville, bound for Greece, ran into the fishing smack Telephone, of Ramsgate, off the North Foreland, in the night. Out of the three hands two were drowned. The captain was saved, and brought to Dover yesterday morning.
THE EMPEROR AT COWES.

The special correspondent of the Press Association at Cowes telegraphs that the German Emperor has now expressed his intention of remaining at the Isle of Wight till Sunday morning. His Majesty yeaterday went for a short cruise in the steam lifeboat Duke of Northumber- land, which the Prince of Wales inspected on Thursday. TrIE PETITION AGIINST MR. BALFOUR. 04 From inquiries made yesterday morning,a Manchester correspondent learns that the legal formalities attending the filing of the petition against Mr. Balfour for East Manchester have been practically completed. It is said that the trial cannot take place before November. It will probably be held at the Manchester Assizes.
THE PROPOSED MISSION TO CABUL.

If the Ameer (telegraphs the same correspondent) re- ceives the deputation suggested by the Government, Lord Roberts will he selected to head the mission. The Viceroy's choice will command public confidence both in India and in England.

THE SHOEBURYNESS MEETING. The Artillery Volunteers ot the Ist division left camp yesterday in field artillery. The firing umpires have placed Captain Carr's team, 3rd Kent, first in order of merit in the ranging competition with 16-pounder guns. Captain Bracebridge's team, 3rd Middlesex, are first in order of merit with a total score of 1989. points. The officers, under Major Grey, have had a ranging compe- tition with 16-pounders, and the results were excellent. The weather is fine. THE RUSSIANS ON THE AFGHAN FRONTIER. REPORTED COLLISION.

A "Times "Simla telegram says it is reported that a party of thirty Russians has come into collision with Afghans at Samatash, on Yeshill Lake, in Shignan. The Russians lost five men killed, and had sixteen taken pri- soners. On application for the release of the latter the Afghans refused, stating that in future they would neither give nor take quarter. The story comes in a roundabout way, and is possibly exaggerated. The party probably consisted of Kirghiz, with Russian offi- cers.
SERIOUS COLLIERY ACCIDENT. SIX LIVES LOST.

A Dewsbury correspondent telegraphs that late on Thursday night six miners were drowned at the pit be- longing to Messrs.flaigh, colliery proprietors, Dewsbury, through an inrush of water from some old workings at Ravenswharfe. . . . .

A later telegram says that in consequence of the mine being flooded no bodies have yet been recovered. The following are the names of the men who have lost their lives :—John Swallow, aged twenty, of Heckmondwike ; Joe Beaumont,aged sixteen ; John W.Hirst,aged twenty; Richard Swallow, aged forty-nine ; John Swallow, aged seventeen; and James Swallovv,a,ged twenty-three,father and sons, all of Dewsbury. Out of seven men in the mine only one, named Moor, was saved.

div.head: POLITICAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE POLITICAL CRISIS.
THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

The following members of the Privy Council left Lon- don yesterday morning to attend the Council at Osborne to consider the Queen's Speech :—Lord L'athom, Lord Cranbrook, Lord Cadogan, and Sir Charles Lennox Peel, clerk to the Council. It is stated that the Queen's Speech, to be read on Monday, will be of unusual brevity the major portion of the document being devoted to foreign affairs. It is officially stated that in the House of Lords the Earl of Denbigh will move and the Earl of Powis second the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. It is stated that Mr. Dunbar Plunket Barton, Q.C., one of the Ulster Conservative members, will move the Address in reply to the Queen's Speech in the House of Commons, and it will be seconded by the Hon. W. Ti. Cross, son of Viscount Cross. THE COMING CHANGE OF GOVERNMENT. The division on Mr. Asquith's amendment to the Address in answer to the Queen's speech will be taken on Thursday. It is expected Lord Salisbury will go to Osborne on Friday and Mr. Gladstone be summoned by , the Queen on the following day. The Council for hand- ing over the seals could then take place on Tuesday week, and new writs moved for and the house pro- rogued on the same day. RUMOURED APPOINTMENTS.

There was (says the "Standard ") much speculation in the lobby yesterday afternoon regarding the composition of the new Government. It is understood that Mr. Glad- stone has made a number of provisional arrangements for the constitution of the coming Ministry; but the only appointments that can be regarded as definitely settled are that he himself will be Prime Minister, that the Earl of Rosebery will be Foreign Secretary, that Sir W. Har- court will be Chancellor of the Exchequer and that Mr. John Morley will take the Irish Secretaryship.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS. THE QUEEN AND THE NEW SPEAKER. SWEARING-IN OF MEMBERS.

The House of Lords met at twelve o'clock. After prayers had been read by the Bishop of Ripon, the Lords Commissioners, consisting of the Lord Chancellor, the Duke of Rutland, Lord Cross, Lord Balfour of Burleigh, and Lord Bnutsford, took their seats on the bench in front of the Throne, and the usher of the Black Rod was directed to summons the House of Commons. Shortly afterwards the Speaker-elect, who was attended by the usher, met Black Rod and the Sergeant-at-Arms, and accompanied by a large num her of members of the House of Commons, appeared at the bar. The Speaker- elect then informed the Royal Co mmissioners that, in obedience to her Majesty's command, the House of Com- mons had chosen him as their Speaker, and requested the Royal confirmation of his appointment.

The Lord CHANCELLOR replied that her Majesty was so fully convinced of Mr. Peel's sufficiency to discharge the arduous duties which the House of Commons had selected the Speaker-elect to discharge, that she did most readily confirm his appointment. The Speaker then, in the usual form, submitted him- self with all humility to her Majesty's gracious com- mands, and laid claim to the usual fights and privileges of the House of Commons, including freedom Of speech, access to her Majesty and freedom from arrest. lie also begged that if any error were committed it might be imputed to himself, and not to her Majesty's faithful Commons. The Lord Chancellor then stated that the Royal Com- missioners had it in further comina.nd to ,onfirm all the rights and priveleges ever conferre't upon the Com- mons by herself or by her predeces, s, and assured the 'Speaker that her Majesty would p.,,ce the most favour- able construction on his actions. The Speaker and members of the House of Commons then retired from the bar: The Lord Chancellor shortly afterwards took his seat on the Woolsack, when several peers were sworn. Amongst the Peers sworn in were Earl Spencer, Lord Esher, Lord newton, Lord Brassev, Ear! Carnpei down, Lord Abingar, Lord Raglan, Earl Bradford, ai d Earl GallOWAy. The House adjourned at five minutes past four until eight o'clock on Monday.

The Spe iker pp- ired punctually at noon, without his usual rotas), awl very soon afterwards was summoned by Black Rod to the House of Peers to receive the approbation a tier NI of the choice made by the Commons. 11..turni1g in a few minutes, the Speaker retired for a mowent, and reappeared in his full official costume, when he announ- ced that Her Majesty had through the Commissioners approved of the choice of the Commons, and that he on the part of the house had made claim to all the ancient rights and privileges of the members, which her Majesty abynyC:)hinerislli Royal nal hadprecdoecnteisrsmoresd in as ample a manner as The Speaker then took the oath and signed ths roll, members following in batches of five, Privy Couocillnt6 taking precedence. The members followed in a continuous lino, taking the oath as administered by the clerk at the table, and after_ signing the roll each was formally introduced to tor Speaker by the chief clerk, Mr. Palgrave. Then nasa out, the sworn members left the floor clear for new arrivals. Among the first hundred members sworn 31!. Michael Davitt was included. At one o'clock Balfour and Mr. Goschen took the oath and signed JO' roll. By half-past one the majority of the members bad bee!' sworn, but the crowding about the table was is) flten‘' that the Speaker had again and aasain to call for order- Mr. Naoroji, a native of India, and the member for bury, did did not take the oath but affirmed, as did a retr siderable number of other members. After a short 50: journment, an additional table was brought in, and fro this time the swearing in process proceeded at a faster ratf• By half-past three had been reached, all the available. . members were sworn. In one of the latter baLches Wtaba Mr. Keir Hardie, who made his declaration after Scottish fashion with right hand uplifted. The defendant, who is thirty years old, made the plaintiff's acquaintance in 1886. Be proposed marriage and was accepted, but in 'January iastuddenly broite off the engagement. Mr. rpleridge; for defendant, admitted the promise, and the jury irwarded £5OO damages.
